The article examines how the Western Han dynasty philosopher 严遵 (Yan Zun) interpreted the Daodejing "以老释老" (using Laozi to explain Laozi) in his commentary 《老子指归》 (Laozhi Zhigui).

KEY ARGUMENTS AND STRUCTURE:
The article argues that 《老子指归》 uniquely offers holistic, passage-level interpretations rather than character-by-character annotations (unlike the commentaries of Heshanggong or Wang Bi). Its goal is to grasp the core meaning of the Dao De Jing and use it as a gateway for theoretical explanations of heaven-earth, yin-yang, husband-wife, father-son, ruler-minister, and myriad things. The article analyzes "以老释老" across three dimensions:

1. TEXTUAL LEVEL (文句与修辞): The Zhigui inherits the Laozi's vocabulary—both core concepts (道、德、无、无为、自然、常、虚、静、柔、弱) and low-frequency words (e.g., "市" and "长生久视" used repeatedly). It adopts and innovates Laozi's sentence patterns including "……，是谓……" (defining terms), "……若……" (reformulated as "……而若……" for balance), causal constructions like "……是以…………故……", and rhetorical questions ("夫何故","何以明之"). Both texts employ extensive parallelism and antithesis.

2. THINKING LEVEL (类比与对反): The Zhigui follows Laozi's analogical and oppositional modes of thinking. It reuses key metaphors from the Laozi—Water (水, symbolizing softness overcoming hardness), Infant (婴儿/赤子, representing guileless, non-striving states), Mother (母, as origin), and Bellows (橐龠, symbolizing empty yet inexhaustible). It also inherits the "反者道之动" (reversal is the movement of Dao) thinking, elaborating on how fortune/misfortune, gain/loss, advance/retreat mutually generate one another. Yan Zun analyzes how 祸福 are "同营异域" (same origin, different domains) and how only sages who abandon cleverness and follow 无为 can escape their vicissitudes.

3. MEANING LEVEL (核心概念与思想主旨): The Zhigui constructs a cosmological conceptual system of 道—德—神明—太和, derived from the Laozi's "道生一，一生二，二生三，三生万物" and "天下万物生于有，有生于无". The concepts of 自然 (naturalness) and 无为 (non-action) are treated as core themes: 自然 stands above 道 and 德 in the sequence 自然—道德—神明—（太）和, determining success/failure of heaven, earth, and human affairs, and serving as the sage's governing principle with "自然之验" (verification of naturalness). 无为 is extended from 道 to all levels (道德、神明、太和、万物), expanded from rulers to the common people, seen as the root of good governance (versus 有为 as the source of chaos), and systematically elaborated through 26 paired concepts—13 "生之徒" (虚、无、清、静、微、寡、柔、弱、卑、损、时、和、啬) versus 13 "死之徒" (实、有、浊、扰、显、众、刚、强、高、满、过、泰、费)—most of which trace to the Laozi text.

CONCLUSION: The Zhigui, despite its verbosity, demonstrates a clear "以老释老" tendency. Later scholars praised it—the 《三国志·魏书·方技传》 notes Yan Zun's works served as a standard for measuring philosophical acumen, and 晁说之 regarded the Zhigui as a source for Wang Bi's Laozi Commentary. Through this interpretive style, Yan Zun unified the Laozi text with resources from the Zhouyi and Zhuangzi, and connected heaven-earth, yin-yang, and social hierarchies, realizing "柄自然之归，以统万方之指" (holding to naturalness to unify all approaches).

URL: https://kemingbaike.com/baike/20230889141.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from 可名百科 (Keming Baike), a Chinese encyclopedia platform, presents Chapter 39 of 《老子道德经注》(Annotations on Laozi's Dao De Jing), annotated by Wang Bi (王弼) during the Wei dynasty (魏). The chapter discusses the concept of "obtaining the One" (得一), explaining that Heaven, Earth, spirits, valleys, all things, and feudal lords each obtain the One to achieve clarity, tranquility, spirituality, abundance, life, and righteous governance, respectively. Wang Bi's commentary elaborates that the One is the beginning of numbers and the ultimate of things, and warns that clinging to achievements rather than the source (the One) leads to failure and ruin. Key philosophical points include: one must use the One to achieve clarity rather than use clarity itself; maintaining the One preserves clarity while using it risks fracturing; honor is rooted in humbleness and height in lowness (贵以贱为本，高以下为基); feudal lords calling themselves "orphaned, solitary, and unworthy" exemplifies this principle; and excessive renown results in no renown (致数誉无誉). The commentary notes that jade and stone are not desired because they are entirely confined to their physical forms. The page includes the original text of Chapter 39, compares it with the original Dao De Jing text, and credits Wang Bi as the annotator. It was last updated on 2023-08-14 with 2,107 reads.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
昔之得一者，天得一以清，地得一以宁，神得一以灵，谷得一以盈，万物得一以生，侯王得一以为天下贞。其致之，天无以清将恐裂，地无以宁将恐发，神无以灵将恐歇，谷无以盈将恐竭，万物无以生将恐灭，侯王无以贵高将恐蹙，故贵以贱为本，高以下为基。是以侯王自谓孤寡不谷，此非以贱为本耶，非乎？故致数誉无誉，不欲琭琭如玉，珞珞如石。;用一以致清耳，非用清以清也。守一则清不失，用清则恐裂也。故为功之母，不可舍也。;贵乃以贱为本，高乃以下为基，故致数誉乃无誉也。玉石琭琭珞珞，体尽於形，故不欲也。;一，数之始而物之极也。各是一物之生，所以为主也。物皆各得此一以成，既成而合以居成，居成则失其母。

--- SOURCE 8: 老子河上公章句 - 维基百科，自由的百科全书 ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The page is a Chinese Wikipedia article on 《老子河上公章句》(Laozi Heshang Gong Zhangju), also known as 《老子河上公注》(Heshang Gong's Commentary on the Laozi). It is a commentary on the Dao De Jing attributed to the mythical Warring States-era sage Heshang Zhangren (Heshang Gong), but its actual composition date is disputed among scholars. Theories range from the end of the Western/Eastern Han transition (Wu Xiangwu), the Eastern Han (Chen Jinliang, Wang Ka placing it in the mid-to-late Eastern Han, Wang Ming dating it to the reign of Han Huan/Siling), to the Eastern Jin (Takeuchi and Naitō attributing it to Ge Hong or his clan) and Southern Qi (Shimabukuro Zōnan attributing it to the recluse Chou Yue). Some scholars (Kusuyama Haruki and Kobayashi Masami) propose it was composed in stages, with an original text from the late Eastern Han later supplemented with Daoist longevity doctrines and internal deity concepts, possibly rewritten by Tianshi Dao "Three Caverns" priests or Maoshan sect Daoists.

The commentary interprets the Dao De Jing through the lens of "wuwei governance and quietist health maintenance" (無為治國、清靜養生), holding that the Way of heaven and human affairs are connected, and that governing the state and governing the body are the same. Its health maintenance methods comprise three practices: circulating qi (行氣, preserving "harmonious qi" through gentle breathing), preserving essence (固精, conserving seminal essence and avoiding dissipation), and nurturing spirit (養神, keeping the deities resident in the five viscera tranquil and preventing them from leaving the body).

The work bridges the Han-era Huang-Lao tradition and Wei-Jin proto-Daoism, exerting great influence. Zhang Lu's 老子想爾注 drew upon it, as did the Southern Qi commentator Gu Huan. During the Southern Dynasties, Daoists taught and recited the Dao De Jing, the Heshang Gong Zhangju, and the Xiang'er Commentary in sequence; these three texts became core classics of the Taixuan section of the Daoist Canon. In the early Tang it was used in official schools, until replaced by Emperor Xuanzong's 719 imperial commentary. Thereafter it and Wang Bi's commentary became the two main commentaries on the Dao De Jing. It was criticized as a forgery by scholars such as Liu Zhiji (Tang), Chao Gongwu (Song), and Yao Nai (Qing).

The ancient editions number in the dozens and fall into six categories: Dunhuang manuscript fragments (S477, S4681-P2639, S3926); Japanese old copies and printed editions (e.g., the Keichō-era movable-type edition, which include a preface attributed to Ge Hong); Song woodblock editions (Jian'an Yu-shi and Liu-shi Mashaben); the "Zuantu huzhu" edition; the Zhengtong Daoist Canon edition (closest to Tang copies and of high value); and Ming-Qing editions (e.g., the Ming 中都四子集 and Qing Siku Quanshu editions, of little value).

The chapter text (twenty-two characters in the Jinglong stele version) reads: "谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之門，天地根。綿綿若存，用之不勤。" (The valley spirit does not die; this is called the mysterious female. Key scholarly discussion points:
1. The reading of "谷" (valley) vs. "浴" (bathe) vs. "穀" (grain) — several scholars (Bi Yuan, Yu Yue, Xu Zi, Hong Yixuan) discuss whether the character should be 浴 (as in the Heshang Gong version), 穀, or 谷. Qian Yi (謙之案) concludes "谷神" is correct, citing the Liezi, poems by Yu Jianwu and Yu Xin, and noting that in the Daode Jing itself 穀 and 神 are paired (chapter 39: "神得一以靈，穀得一以盈").

2. Interpretations of "谷神不死": Sima Guang (司馬光) explains "中虛故曰谷，不測故曰神，天地有窮而道無窮，故曰不死" (empty within, hence 'valley'; unfathomable, hence 'spirit'; heaven and earth are finite but the Dao is infinite, hence 'does not die'). Yan Fu (嚴復) similarly says: "以其虛，故曰谷；以其因應無窮，故稱神；以其不屈愈出，故曰不死。三者皆道之德也。"

3. The word "勤" (qin): Hong Yixuan connects it to 廑 (meaning weak/scarce). Yu Xingwu (於省吾) argues it should be read as 覲 (to appear/be seen), citing bronze inscription evidence — "用之不覲" meaning "using it, it is not seen," consistent with the preceding "綿綿若存."

4. The rhyming pattern (音韻): Jiang's (江氏) rhyme analysis places 死/牝 in the Zhi 脂 category, and 門/根/存/勤 in the Wen 文 category. Various scholars (including Gu Yanwu, Jiang Yong, Yan Kejun) analyze the ancient pronunciation of 牝 (bi vs. pin) and 谷. Gu Yanwu notes that 谷 had the "欲" (yu) pronunciation in antiquity, citing examples from the Book of Changes, Book of Documents, Zuozhuan, and Shiji.

5. Textual variants: The stele versions (Jinglong, Suizhou, Dunhuang) have 21-23 characters, while Heshang Gong, Wang Bi, and Fan Yingyuan versions have 24-25, and the Fu Yi version has 26 characters. The Heshang Gong version titles this "Chapter 6 of Chengxiang (成象第六)", Wang Bi titles it "Chapter 6", and Fan Yingyuan titles it "Chapter Six on the Valley Spirit Not Dying (谷神不死章第六)".

**Overview:** The Xiang'er commentary is one of the earliest Taoist commentaries on the Dao De Jing. Its authorship and date are debated among scholars—theories attribute it to Eastern Han Celestial Masters founder Zhang Daoling (張道陵), his grandson Zhang Lu (張魯), or place it in the Six Dynasties or Northern/Southern Dynasties periods. The text deleted filler characters to make 5000 characters (called "五千文"), and its commentary often freely interpreted or even deliberately altered the original text, occasionally in ways that contradict the scriptures' meaning. During Zhang Lu's rule of Hanzhong, the work was used to educate followers and held high status; it was still revered in the Six Dynasties as a classic recited by Celestial Masters priests. It was lost around the end of the Tang dynasty, with only one Northern Dynasties-era fragmentary copy remaining, discovered in the Dunhuang caves.

**Content and Thought:**
- Featured a "神道設教" (teaching through spiritual authority) method, personifying "道" (the Way) into a willful deity speaking in first person ("吾")
- Emphasized following "道誡" (Way precepts, known as the "想爾戒" - Xiang'er precepts) to achieve longevity and blessings
- Promoted longevity practices combining 精 (essence), 氣 (vital energy), and 神 (spirit), rejecting fatalism in favor of achievable immortality through cultivation
- Believed in a celestial bureaucracy (天曹) governing lifespan adjustment and a terrestrial office (地官) governing the dead; virtuous practitioners could attain rebirth after "refining in 太陰" (Great Yin)
- Criticized other Taoist sects, Confucian classics, sacrificial rites, the "守一" (Guarding the One) meditation on inner deities, and sexual practices (房中术) such as "還精補腦" (returning essence to replenish the brain)

**Status and Versions:** Under Zhang Lu's rule it was treated as scripture; in the Northern/Southern Dynasties it was a foundational text for Celestial Masters priests, listed in the Daozang's 太玄 section, with status second only to the Heshang Gong commentary. It declined as the Heshang Gong commentary grew in importance, and was lost in the late Tang chaos; it was not included in the Ming-era Orthodox Daoist Canon. Only one Northern Dynasties handwritten fragment survives, held at the British Museum (catalog number S6825), covering chapters 3 to the end of the Dao Jing section. Jao Tsung-i (饒宗頤) produced an annotated edition (《老子想爾注校證》), and Stephen R. Bokenkamp produced an English translation published by University of California Press in 1997. The text is considered important modern research material for early Taoist history.

This webpage is an academic article by 李芙馥 published on the website of the Institute of Philosophy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (中国社会科学院哲学研究所), dated 2024-06-01, originally appearing in 《中州学刊》2024年第4期. The article examines how the Western Han dynasty philosopher 严遵 (Yan Zun) interpreted the Daodejing "以老释老" (using Laozi to explain Laozi) in his commentary 《老子指归》 (Laozhi Zhigui).

KEY ARGUMENTS AND STRUCTURE:
The article argues that 《老子指归》 uniquely offers holistic, passage-level interpretations rather than character-by-character annotations (unlike the commentaries of Heshanggong or Wang Bi). Its goal is to grasp the core meaning of the Dao De Jing and use it as a gateway for theoretical explanations of heaven-earth, yin-yang, husband-wife, father-son, ruler-minister, and myriad things. The article analyzes "以老释老" across three dimensions:

1. TEXTUAL LEVEL (文句与修辞): The Zhigui inherits the Laozi's vocabulary—both core concepts (道、德、无、无为、自然、常、虚、静、柔、弱) and low-frequency words (e.g., "市" and "长生久视" used repeatedly). It adopts and innovates Laozi's sentence patterns including "……，是谓……" (defining terms), "……若……" (reformulated as "……而若……" for balance), causal constructions like "……是以…………故……", and rhetorical questions ("夫何故","何以明之"). Both texts employ extensive parallelism and antithesis.

2. THINKING LEVEL (类比与对反): The Zhigui follows Laozi's analogical and oppositional modes of thinking. It reuses key metaphors from the Laozi—Water (水, symbolizing softness overcoming hardness), Infant (婴儿/赤子, representing guileless, non-striving states), Mother (母, as origin), and Bellows (橐龠, symbolizing empty yet inexhaustible). It also inherits the "反者道之动" (reversal is the movement of Dao) thinking, elaborating on how fortune/misfortune, gain/loss, advance/retreat mutually generate one another. Yan Zun analyzes how 祸福 are "同营异域" (same origin, different domains) and how only sages who abandon cleverness and follow 无为 can escape their vicissitudes.

3. MEANING LEVEL (核心概念与思想主旨): The Zhigui constructs a cosmological conceptual system of 道—德—神明—太和, derived from the Laozi's "道生一，一生二，二生三，三生万物" and "天下万物生于有，有生于无". The concepts of 自然 (naturalness) and 无为 (non-action) are treated as core themes: 自然 stands above 道 and 德 in the sequence 自然—道德—神明—（太）和, determining success/failure of heaven, earth, and human affairs, and serving as the sage's governing principle with "自然之验" (verification of naturalness). 无为 is extended from 道 to all levels (道德、神明、太和、万物), expanded from rulers to the common people, seen as the root of good governance (versus 有为 as the source of chaos), and systematically elaborated through 26 paired concepts—13 "生之徒" (虚、无、清、静、微、寡、柔、弱、卑、损、时、和、啬) versus 13 "死之徒" (实、有、浊、扰、显、众、刚、强、高、满、过、泰、费)—most of which trace to the Laozi text.

CONCLUSION: The Zhigui, despite its verbosity, demonstrates a clear "以老释老" tendency. Later scholars praised it—the 《三国志·魏书·方技传》 notes Yan Zun's works served as a standard for measuring philosophical acumen, and 晁说之 regarded the Zhigui as a source for Wang Bi's Laozi Commentary. Through this interpretive style, Yan Zun unified the Laozi text with resources from the Zhouyi and Zhuangzi, and connected heaven-earth, yin-yang, and social hierarchies, realizing "柄自然之归，以统万方之指" (holding to naturalness to unify all approaches).

Yan described Dao as beginningless, endless, and self-existent, while De derives from Dao and also possesses infinite power, being formless and imageless unlike the created things which have form. --- SOURCE 1: 苏辙《老子解》全文 ---
URL: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/463976485

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a ZhiHu (知乎) article titled "苏辙《老子解》全文" (The Complete Text of Su Zhe's Commentary on Laozi) published in the column "道德经解释" (Interpretation of the Dao De Jing) by author 大风 (Big Wind). The article presents the complete text of Su Zhe's (苏辙, a Song Dynasty scholar, 1039-1112) commentary/annotations on the Dao De Jing (Tao Te Ching) by Laozi. The article has received 37 approvals ("37 人赞同了该文章").

The article contains Su Zhe's line-by-line annotations of Laozi's classic text, organized by chapter. The content covers chapters 1 through 50 of the Dao De Jing, with each chapter presented with the original Laozi text followed by Su Zhe's commentary (注解). 

Key chapters and themes covered include:
- Chapter 1 (道可道章第一): On the ineffable nature of the Dao; only what cannot be spoken is constant/eternal; the distinction between the named and unnamed
- Chapter 2 (天下皆知章第二): Relativity of beauty and goodness, opposites arising mutually
- Chapter 3 (不尚贤章第三): On not valuing worthies, avoiding contention
- Chapters on water's virtue (上善若水), the usefulness of emptiness (三十辐共一毂/无之以为用), sensory overstimulation (五色章), fame and disgrace (宠辱章)
- Later chapters discuss governing philosophy, returning to simplicity (素朴), the concept of "无为" (wu wei/non-action), and the cultivation of inner nature

The text is divided into volumes ("道德真经注卷之一" and "道德真经注卷之二"), with editorial notes marked (#1, #2, #3) noting textual corrections based on the 宝颜本 (Baoyan edition). Each volume is attributed to "眉山苏辙注" (Commentary by Su Zhe of Meishan).

The commentary frequently references other classical texts including the I Ching (《易》), the Shurangama Sutra (《首楞严》), and Confucian teachings, showing a synthesis of Confucian, Daoist, and Buddhist thought characteristic of Su Zhe's scholarly approach.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"道可道，非常道。莫非道也。而可道者不可常，惟不可道，而后可常耳。今夫仁义礼智，此道之可道者也。然而仁不可以为义，而礼不可以为智，可道之不可常如此。"

--- SOURCE 2: 蘇轍行蹤考 苏辙行踪考 上冊 - DOKUMEN.PUB ---
URL: https://dokumen.pub/8b67f8e7f3e508726a4308c68882c5ba.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from dokumen.pub and presents the full text (preface, table of contents, and opening chapters) of "蘇轍行蹤考" (A Study of Su Zhe's Travels and Whereabouts), Volume 1, by author Li Changsheng (李常生), published in 2020. The book is a 400-page companion volume to the author's earlier "蘇軾行蹤考" (A Study of Su Shi's Travels), both documenting the complete life journeys of the brothers Su Shi (蘇軾) and Su Zhe (蘇轍).

**Prefaces and Context:**
- The author Li Changsheng spent nearly 12 years (from 2008) following Su Shi's footsteps and wrote "蘇軾行蹤考," published August 2019 in Taiwan.
- After completing the study of Su Shi, he continued with "蘇轍行蹤考," and intends to eventually write a combined biography ("蘇軾、蘇轍史傳").
- The author, born 1949 in Changzhou, was originally a real estate developer with a background in architecture; he earned three doctorates (urban planning from Southeast University, history from Nanjing Normal University, and literature from Wuhan University) starting at age 53.
- According to the preface by Professor Wang Zhaopeng (王兆鵬), the book's three incomparable qualities are: (1) the author's spirit/sacrifice (he spent millions of his own money, suffered from severe diabetes, and wrote at the age of 70+ while financially strained), (2) his methodology (integrating "poetry-history mutual verification" 詩史互證, "history-geography mutual verification" 史地互證, and "text-image mutual verification" 文圖互證, including on-site field investigations and hand-drawn maps), and (3) his extensive illustrations (over 700 maps and images comprising about half the book).

**Key Biographical Facts about Su Zhe (蘇轍):**
- Su Zhe (字子由), younger brother of Su Shi, was born on the 22nd day of the 2nd month, 1039 (仁宗寶元二年) in Meishan, Sichuan. His wife was Lady Shi (史氏).
- Both brothers passed the jinshi examination together at age 19 and both passed the special examination (制舉). Emperor Renzong remarked: "朕今日為子孫得兩宰相矣" (Today I have gained two prime ministers for my descendants).
- From the "宋史·蘇轍傳": "轍與兄進退出處，無不相同，患難之中，友愛彌篤，無少怨尤，近古罕見" (In advancement and retreat, appointments and demotions, Zhe was always inseparable from his brother; in times of hardship their fraternal love grew deeper without any complaint—a rarity in modern times).
- Su Zhe died in 政和二年 (1112) at age 74, having retired to Yingchang (潁昌, modern Xuchang) where he farmed for 11 years after returning from exile. His brother Su Shi died at age 66 in Changzhou (常州) after returning from Hainan.
- Su Zhe's career peak was during the Yuanyou era (元祐, 1086-1093): in 1086 he became 右司諫; in 1092 he rose to 太中大夫、守門下侍郎 (Vice Chancellor), reaching the highest point of his power.
- His works include 《欒城集》 (over 2500 pieces), 《詩傳》,《春秋傳》,《古史》,《老子解》,《龍川別志》,《龍川略志》,《論語拾遺》 etc. He was posthumously given the posthumous name 文定 in 1176.
- Su Zhe's travel routes: north to the Liao capital 中京, south to Leizhou Peninsula, and central locations including Daming, Jinan, Xuchang, Ruzhou, Shangqiu, Zhoukou, Gao'an (Jiangxi), and Jixi (Anhui).

**Historical Context and Genealogy:**
- The Su family of Meishan traced their origins to Su Weidao (蘇味道), a Tang dynasty official from Luancheng (欒城), Hebei, who was demoted to Meizhou as governor during Wu Zetian's reign; one of his sons stayed in Meizhou.
- Su Zhe's grandfather Su Xu (蘇序) is when the family began to prosper; Su Xu's son Su Huan (蘇渙) was the first in the family lineage to hold government office.
- Su Xun (蘇洵), father of Su Shi and Su Zhe, began studying at age 27; he and his two sons are all among the "唐宋八大家" (Eight Great Prose Masters of Tang and Song).
- Su Zhe's mother Lady Cheng (程氏) personally taught the two brothers reading; she famously encouraged them to emulate the upright official Fan Pang (范滂).

**Book Structure:**
The book is organized chronologically into 17 chapters covering Su Zhe's life from his childhood in Meishan through his various official posts, exiles, and retirement. The exhaustive table of contents shows the chapters cover: Introduction, Meishan Su Zhe, First trip to the capital and return for mother's funeral, Second departure from Sichuan, Second period in the capital, Posting as official in Daming, Return for father's funeral, Return to the capital after mourning, Chenzhou instructor, Qizhou secretary, Yingtianfu judge, Exile to supervise salt/wine tax in Junzhou, Jixi county magistrate, Capital service and embassy to Liao, First exile to Ruzhou/Yuanzhou/Junzhou, Second exile to Leizhou/Xunzhou/Yuezhou, and Retirement in Yingchang, plus appendix.

**Research Methodology and Sources:**
- The author emphasizes the importance of on-site field investigation (實地考察) combined with historical documents, because previous scholars who wrote chronological biographies (年譜) of the Sus often made errors in travel direction, distance, timing, and geographic ordering since they never physically walked the routes.
- Key reference sources include: various chronological biographies (年譜) by Sun Ruting (宋·孫汝聽), He Lun (宋·何掄), Kong Fanli, Zeng Zaozhuang; geographic works like 《輿地紀勝》,《方輿勝覽》,《太平寰宇記》,《水經注》,《元和郡縣圖志》; historical works like 《宋史》,《續資治通鑒長編》,《東都事略》; and the standard editions 《蘇軾全集校注》 and 《欒城集》.
- The author notes that study of Su Shi far exceeds study of Su Zhe (roughly 10:1 ratio in quantity of research).

**Opening Chapter Content (Second Chapter - "眉山蘇轍"):**
The chapter provides a detailed year-by-year account of Su Zhe's childhood:
- 1039: Born in Meishan (born at 亥時, 9-11pm, on the 22nd day of the 2nd month).
- 1040-1042: Western Xia attacks under Li Yuanhao; Su Shi began studying around age 7-8.
- 1043: Su Shi entered elementary school under Daoist teacher Zhang Yijian (張易簡) at Tianqing Temple (天慶觀), with classmate Chen Taichu.
- 1044: Su Zhe followed his brother to study at Tianqing Temple.
- 1045: Father Su Xun traveled, mother Lady Cheng personally instructed the brothers in reading.
- 1046: Su Zhe wrote his first poem at age 8 ("無人共噄饅頭") in a group poem session.
- 1047: Grandfather Su Xu died at age 75.
- 1048: Father Su Xun, in mourning, stayed home and personally taught the two sons; the brothers also studied under teachers Liu Weizhi and Shi Qingqing in Meishan.
- 1049: Su Xun wrote "名二子說" explaining the names "軾" and "轍" (Su Shi = the ornamental crossbar of a chariot; Su Zhe = the wheel track), prophesying their different personalities.
- 1050: Su Shi's sister Baniang (八娘) married her cousin Cheng Zhicai; she was mistreated and died at age 18 in 1052, causing a 42-year estrangement between the families.
- 1053: Teenage Su Zhe, who suffered from lung illness ("少年常病肺"), wrote "孟子解", "論語略解", and "春秋論", studying with his father and older brother as teachers.
- 1054: Zhang Fangping appointed governor of Sichuan.

The Aixuan School, founded by Lin Guangchao (林光潮), differed from Cheng Yi's tradition by taking a more tolerant attitude toward Buddhism and Daoism, which is clearly reflected in Lin Xiyi's fusion of the Three Teachings (三教). 1. **Harmonizing the Laozi with Neo-Confucianism (理學)**: Early research began with the relationship between the Laozi and Confucianism. Liu Sihe (2013) first noted this, arguing Lin was closer to Zhuangzi and Chan Buddhism than to either Zhu Xi or Lu Jiuyuan. Huang Yun further developed this, analyzing Lin's concept of "無容心" (non-attachment of mind), distinguishing two stages of mind, and linking it to Cheng Hao's views. The article notes there is as yet no dedicated study on Lin's relationship to mind-study, suggesting this as a fruitful research avenue for understanding the continuity of mind-study between Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming.

3. **Using Buddhism to Interpret the Laozi (借佛解老)**: Liu Sihe (2013) argued Lin maintained his Neo-Confucian position, using Chan concepts only as tools (e.g., using "悟"/enlightenment merely as a means to grasp 天理), with Buddhism in a subordinate position. Huang Yun disagreed, arguing Lin engaged in an equal dialogue between Buddhism and Daoism, focusing on experiential understanding (體悟) rather than subordinating one to the other; this blurred distinctions between the two traditions. Several scholars, including Huang Yun and Zheng Tianxi, noted Lin's misreadings of Buddhist concepts but did not determine whether these were intentional or unintentional distortions. Zheng Tianxi also analyzed Lin's views on the "無心" (no-mind) state of those who attain the Dao, influenced by both Mencius's "不動心" and Chan's "無念," and Lin's cultivation practices emphasizing self-realization and the idea that "道體在我" (the Dao substance is within oneself).

4. **Literary/Language Commentary (文章學點評)**: Wang Weiqian's 2012 article first discussed the characteristics of the commentary - Lin used simple, colloquial language (口義 style) with clear explanations, rhetorical devices like metaphor, strong overall coherence, and cross-referential interpretation of chapters. Key arguments and content:
1. **Context and significance**: During the Song-Yuan-Ming period, Neo-Confucians (理學家) increasingly used "reliance on Confucianism to interpret Laozi" (援儒解老) methods. Wu Cheng's work is identified by scholars like Liu Gu-sheng (劉固盛) as best exemplifying how Neo-Confucianism influenced Laozi studies (老學), and is one of only four Laozi commentaries included in the Siku Quanshu for the Song/Yuan/Ming period.

2. **The "Dao equals Li" (道理合一) interpretation**: Wu Cheng equated the Daoist "Dao" (道) with Neo-Confucian "Principle" (理/天理), infusing the Dao with Confucian moral attributes (仁義禮智 - benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom). He used the "Li Yi Fen Shu" (理一分殊, one principle, many manifestations) concept to interpret the Dao-De relationship as "Dao producing myriad virtue" (道一分殊). He viewed "Dao" as metaphysical principle and "De" as its manifestation in all things.

3. **Mind-nature theory (心性論)**: Wu Cheng drew on Lu Xiangshan's (陸九淵) concept that "mind is principle" (心即是理), arguing that all principles of things are inherent in the mind (萬事萬物之理皆備於我). He emphasized "inner contemplation" (內觀) over external seeking, distinguishing "virtue-knowledge" (德性之知) from "hearing-seeing knowledge" (聞見之知). Wu Cheng's philosophy reconciles Zhu Xi and Lu Xiangshan, though leaning toward Lu's "revering virtue" (尊德性).

4. **"Removing external delusions, taking inner truth" (去外妄，取內真)**: Wu Cheng argued that external desires (五色, 五音, 五味, fame and profit) harm life and obscure the pure human nature. He advocated returning to the infant-like (嬰兒/赤子) state of simplicity and true purity (真樸), achieving unity with the Dao.

5. **Cultivation practices (工夫修養)**: Wu Cheng proposed principles for nurturing form, qi, and spirit (形、氣、神). For recluses (出世之人): preserving form, qi, and spirit (存形、存氣、存神); for those in the world (住世之人): nourishing them (養形、養氣、養神). Additional methods include: exhausting one's nature and reaching destiny (盡性達命), overcoming self and being brave in goodness (克己勇善), inner contemplation of the mind (內觀本心), seeing truth and guarding it firmly (見真守固), mind-environment dual forgetting (心境兩忘), using qi to ward off externals (以氣禦外), mind empty without things (心虛無物), and preserving stillness and returning to destiny (守靜復命).

Wu Cheng, a fourth-generation disciple of Zhu Xi who was also influenced by Lu Xiangshan (known for "和會朱陸" or reconciling Zhu and Lu), was a Yuan dynasty Neo-Confucian scholar who commented on the Laozi while at Qingdu Temple in 1307. His commentary is characterized by "以理釋《老》" (interpreting the Laozi through the concept of li/principle).

The paper's central arguments are threefold:
1. **The interpretive foundation**: Wu Cheng understood the Laozi's "道" (Dao) through the Neo-Confucian "縱貫縱講" (vertical/creative) interpretive framework rather than the "縱貫橫講" (horizontal/subjective) framework that Mou Zongsan later applied to Daoism. In Wu's commentary, Dao is not merely a state/boundary (境界形態) but possesses real creative ontological status, generating the universe ("無名者，道也，天地亦由此道而生"). Wu interprets the creation sequence as 道→一(沖虛一氣) →二(陰陽) →三, incorporating "德" (virtue/de) as the "一" into the cosmic generation scheme, thereby bridging the gap that Han dynasty 氣化宇宙論 (qi-based cosmology) had created between Dao and all things.

2. **A critical reassessment**: The paper challenges scholars like Huang Zhao and Liu Yijun who equate Wu's interpretation of the Dao with the Neo-Confucian "天理" (Heavenly Principle). The author argues against this for two reasons:
   - **First**, in Wu's commentary, 無為 (non-action) serves as the ultimate value, while 仁義 (benevolence and righteousness) remain secondary virtues. This places Wu's interpretation firmly within the Daoist system, differentiating it from Neo-Confucian thought where 仁義 constitutes the Heavenly Principle itself. Wu's commentary on chapters 16/18 emphasizes that filial piety and loyalty should be practiced naturally as "常分" (ordinary duty), not through external promotion.
   - **Second**, Wu's purpose in commenting on the Laozi was to distinguish (分判) rather than reconcile Confucianism and Daoism. In the 《吳文正集》, Wu explicitly criticizes the Laoist view of "自無而有" ("有生於無") as implying 理氣二分 (division of li and qi) and 理先氣後 (li prior to qi), which Wu rejects in favor of the Neo-Confucian position that 理氣 are inseparable and without priority. Wu regarded the Laozi's teaching as "異端似是之非" (heterodox doctrine resembling the truth).

**Conclusion**: While Wu's commentary does grant the Dao real creative ontological status similar to the Neo-Confucian 天理 (justifying the "以理釋《老》" characterization), the author argues that Wu maintained a clear distinction between the Daoist interpretation of 道/理 and the Neo-Confucian 理. Wu never equated the Dao of the Laozi with the 天理, as the ultimate values differ (無為 vs. 仁義) and their respective relationships with qi differ fundamentally (理氣二分 vs. 理氣不二). Thus, prior scholars' claims of full identity between Wu's Dao and the Neo-Confucian 理 constitute over-interpretation.

The bibliography is presented twice on the page.

--- SOURCE 1: 苏辙《老子解》全文 ---
URL: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/463976485

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a ZhiHu (知乎) article titled "苏辙《老子解》全文" (The Complete Text of Su Zhe's Commentary on Laozi) published in the column "道德经解释" (Interpretation of the Dao De Jing) by author 大风 (Big Wind). The article presents the complete text of Su Zhe's (苏辙, a Song Dynasty scholar, 1039-1112) commentary/annotations on the Dao De Jing (Tao Te Ching) by Laozi. The article has received 37 approvals ("37 人赞同了该文章").

The article contains Su Zhe's line-by-line annotations of Laozi's classic text, organized by chapter. The content covers chapters 1 through 50 of the Dao De Jing, with each chapter presented with the original Laozi text followed by Su Zhe's commentary (注解). 

Key chapters and themes covered include:
- Chapter 1 (道可道章第一): On the ineffable nature of the Dao; only what cannot be spoken is constant/eternal; the distinction between the named and unnamed
- Chapter 2 (天下皆知章第二): Relativity of beauty and goodness, opposites arising mutually
- Chapter 3 (不尚贤章第三): On not valuing worthies, avoiding contention
- Chapters on water's virtue (上善若水), the usefulness of emptiness (三十辐共一毂/无之以为用), sensory overstimulation (五色章), fame and disgrace (宠辱章)
- Later chapters discuss governing philosophy, returning to simplicity (素朴), the concept of "无为" (wu wei/non-action), and the cultivation of inner nature

The text is divided into volumes ("道德真经注卷之一" and "道德真经注卷之二"), with editorial notes marked (#1, #2, #3) noting textual corrections based on the 宝颜本 (Baoyan edition). Each volume is attributed to "眉山苏辙注" (Commentary by Su Zhe of Meishan).

The commentary frequently references other classical texts including the I Ching (《易》), the Shurangama Sutra (《首楞严》), and Confucian teachings, showing a synthesis of Confucian, Daoist, and Buddhist thought characteristic of Su Zhe's scholarly approach.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"道可道，非常道。莫非道也。而可道者不可常，惟不可道，而后可常耳。今夫仁义礼智，此道之可道者也。然而仁不可以为义，而礼不可以为智，可道之不可常如此。"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: 道德真经注（宋苏辙） ---
URL: https://gushu.net.cn/guji/%E9%81%93%E8%97%8F/%E6%AD%A3%E7%BB%9F%E9%81%93%E8%97%8F%E6%B4%9E%E7%A5%9E%E9%83%A8/%E7%8E%89%E8%AF%80%E7%B1%BB/%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%9C%9F%E7%BB%8F%E6%B3%A8%EF%BC%88%E5%AE%8B%E8%8B%8F%E8%BE%99%EF%BC%89.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the text of "道德真经注" (Commentary on the Daodejing) by Su Zhe (苏辙) of the Song Dynasty, also known as "老子解" (Explanation of Laozi). The text is preserved in the "正统道藏" (Orthodox Daoist Canon) in the "洞神部玉诀类" (Dong Shen section, Yu Jue category), consisting of four volumes (卷). The source text is based on the Orthodox Daoist Canon edition, with a reference edition from the Wuqiu Beizhai (无求备斋) reprint of the Baoyan Tang (宝颜堂) edition.

The content provides Su Zhe's philosophical commentary on the first fourteen chapters (章) of the Daodejing. Key commentaries include:
- Chapter 1 (道可道): Distinguishes between the "道" (Way) that can be spoken and the eternal, unspoken Way. While Confucian virtues (仁仁义礼智 - benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom) are "speakable Ways" and therefore changeable, the true Way is unchanging and undefinable.
- Chapter 2 (天下皆知): Discusses how distinctions like beauty/ugliness, good/evil, being/non-being, and long/short are relative and interdependent; the sage practices non-action (无为) and wordless teaching.
- Chapter 3 (不尚贤): Argues against elevating worthies, valuing rare goods, or displaying desires; the sage governs by emptying the mind, filling the belly, weakening ambition, and strengthening bones.
- Chapter 4 (道冲): The Way is empty yet inexhaustible, the ancestor of all things, preceding even the Emperor (帝).
- Chapter 5 (天地不仁): Heaven and Earth treat all things like straw dogs - without favor or disfavor; the bellows (橐钥) analogy shows how emptiness produces movement.
- Chapter 6 (谷神不死): The valley spirit (谷神) is formless, deathless, and is the "玄牝" (mysterious female), root of Heaven and Earth.
- Chapter 7 (天长地久): Heaven and Earth endure because they do not live for themselves; likewise the sage places himself after others and outside himself.
- Chapter 8 (上善若水): The highest good is like water, which benefits all without contending and dwells where others dislike.
- Chapter 9 (持而盈之): Warns against excess, fullness, and arrogance; advocates retiring after success, following the Way of Heaven.
- Chapter 10 (载营魄): Discusses the soul (魂) and bodily spirit (魄), cultivating unity of spirit and body, and reaching the state of an infant; includes commentary on the "six entrances" (六入) citing the Buddhist Śūraṅgama Sūtra (《首楞严》).
- Chapters 11-14: Cover the utility of emptiness in wheels, vessels, and rooms; the dangers of sensual indulgence (five colors, five sounds, five flavors); understanding favor and disgrace; and the invisible, inaudible, intangible nature of the Way that unifies into the One (性 - nature).

Su Zhe's commentary frequently draws on the Book of Changes (《易》) and engages with the concept of "性" (innate nature) and "神" (spirit), reflecting Song Dynasty Neo-Confucian and Chan Buddhist influences in interpreting the Daodejing.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"莫非道也。而可道者不可常，惟不可道，而后可常耳。今夫仁义礼智，此道之可道者也。然而仁不可以为义，而礼不可以为智，可道之不可常如此。" (Chapter 1 - distinguishing the speakable from the eternal Way)
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E8%80%81%E5%AD%90%E8%A7%A3_(%E5%9B%9B%E5%BA%AB%E5%85%A8%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC)/%E5%85%A8%E8%A6%BD

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikisource (維基文庫) page presenting the complete text of "老子解" (Annotations on the Laozi/Lao-tzu) by Song dynasty scholar 蘇轍 (Su Che/Su Zhe), from the 四庫全書 (Complete Library of the Four Treasuries / Siku Quanshu) edition. The work is a major Daoist commentary on the Tao Te Ching, divided into two volumes (卷上 covering the 道經/Book of the Way, and 卷下 covering 德經/Book of Virtue).

The introductory 提要 (preface) notes the work was edited in October 1775 (乾隆四十年) under imperial auspices by 紀昀, 陸錫熊, 孫士毅 and 陸費墀. The preface discusses Su Che's approach, which advocates that Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism share a common origin (佛老同源), citing 中庸 (Doctrine of the Mean) to connect the teachings. Su Shi (Su Che's brother) praised the work, asserting that had it existed in the early Han dynasty, Confucianism and Daoism would have been unified, and if in the Jin-Song period, Buddhism and Daoism would not have diverged.

The commentary covers all 81 chapters of the Tao Te Ching with detailed annotations. Notable commentaries include: chapter 1 on the Constant Way, chapter 4 on the empty "Chong" Dao, chapter 6 on the Valley Spirit, chapter 10 on the union of soul and spirit, chapter 14 on the undifferentiated unity, chapter 16 on returning to the root, chapter 19 contrasting Confucius and Laozi's approaches, and chapter 29 quoting the Yi Jing (易經).

The end of the work contains two personal postscripts (題老子道德經後) by Su Che. The first, dated 大觀二年 (1108) December, records his exile in 筠州 (Yunzhou) where he conversed with a Buddhist monk named 道全 about the unity of Buddhist and Confucian thought. The second, dated 政和元年 (1111) December, recounts his elder brother Su Shi's appraisal — that the text "使戰國有此書則無商鞅韓非使漢初有此書則孔老為一使晉宋間有此書則佛老不為二" (had this book existed in the Warring States, there would be no Shang Yang or Han Fei; had it existed in early Han, Confucius and Laozi would be one; had it existed in Jin-Song times, Buddhism and Daoism would not be two).

The text is in the public domain (作者逝世已超过100年) and confirmed as PD-old.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"老子解" is a Daoist commentary on the Tao Te Ching by Song dynasty scholar 蘇轍 (Su Che), presented here in the 四庫全書 (Siku Quanshu) edition, divided into volumes on the 道經 and 德經.
</key_excerpts>

<key_excerpts>
摘要: 第一章 道可道（可以语言交流的道）， 非常道（非真正意义上的道）； 名可名（可以明确定义的名）， 非常名（非真正意义上的名）。无名，天地之始（天地在开始时并无名称）， 有名，万物之母（名只是为了万物的归属）。, [延伸阅读1]王弼《道德经注》: 可道之道，可名之名，指事造形，非其常也，故不可道，不可名也。凡有皆始于无，故未形无名之时，则为万物之始。及其有形有名之时，则长之育之，亭之毒之，为其母也。, [延伸阅读2]苏辙《老子解》: 莫非道也。而可道者不可常，惟不可道，而后可常耳。夫今仁义礼智，此道之可道者也。然而仁不可以为义，而礼不可以为智，可道之不可常如此。, 全文【翻译】: 道可以说，但不是通常所说的道。名可以起，但不是通常所起的名。可以说他是无，因为他在天地创始之前; 也可以说他是有，因为他是万物的母亲。, 王弼注: 两者，始与母也。同出者，同出于玄也。异名所施，不可同也，在首则谓之始，在终则谓之母。玄者，冥也，默然无有也。众妙皆从同而出，故曰众妙之门也。

--- SOURCE 6: 历代老子注书评介 ---
URL: http://share1.chaoxing.com/share/mobile/mooc/tocard/81894819?courseId=81892128&name=%E5%8E%86%E4%BB%A3%E8%80%81%E5%AD%90%E6%B3%A8%E4%B9%A6%E8%AF%84%E4%BB%8B&code=null&appId=0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive scholarly review of commentaries and textual editions of the Daoist classic Laozi (道德经/老子), organized chronologically from Han Dynasty to the Ming period. The content is divided into several major sections.

**Part 1 - Han Fei's Commentaries (《解老》and《喻老》):** The text analyzes Han Feizi's explanations of Laozi chapters, noting he emphasized the lower half of the Daodejing (chapters 38+) and focused more on political and life philosophy than metaphysics. Two errors in his 《解老》 are identified: (1) His claim that Laozi advocated "重视变法" (valuing legal reform) is a misinterpretation, and (2) his interpretation of "十有三" (three out of ten) as referring to "four limbs and nine orifices" is incorrect—Wang Bi's reading of "十分有三分" (three tenths) is correct. The 《喻老》 uses historical stories to illustrate Laozi, including interpretations about rulers maintaining power and the use of reward/punishment as state instruments.

**Part 2 - Wang Bi's Commentary (王弼《道德真经注》):** Wang Bi is praised as the greatest contributor to Laozi studies, with his grasp of Laozi's core concepts of "顺自然" (following nature) and "因物之性" (following the nature of things). His commentary on passages like "道法自然" and "国之利器不可示人" clarifies that Laozi opposed harsh punishment and did not advocate political trickery. However, several errors in Wang's commentary are identified, including: misinterpreting "刍狗" as two separate items (grass and dog) rather than a single ritual object made of straw; misreading "其事好还" as "returning to wu-wei" when it means retribution; and misinterpreting "以正治国" and "廉而不刿" (where "廉" means sharp-edged, not "clean/upright"). The text then provides extensive textual corrections to Wang Bi's edition based on the Heshanggong, Fu Yi, and silk manuscript versions—including changing "王亦大" to "人亦大" (chapter 25), "轻重失本" to "轻则失根" (chapter 26), removing spurious text in chapter 28, and many other corrections involving chapters 2, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23, 29, 34, 39, 45, 47, 62, 66, 71, 75, 76, 77, and 80.

**Part 3 - Heshanggong's Commentary (河上公《老子道德经》):** The Heshanggong edition is noted as most widely used among common people. Its strengths include clear, concise annotations (e.g., "道法自然" as "道性自然，无所法也"). However, its errors include misreading "道冲" as "中" (middle) instead of "empty"; misinterpreting "死而不亡者寿" as physical longevity rather than the survival of one's spirit/ideas after death; and its wrong textual reading "致数车无车" for "至誉无誉". The most serious problem is Heshanggong's pervasive Daoist/fangshi (alchemy) lens, interpreting passages through bodily cultivation, qi refinement, and immortality practices—what scholar Wang Li calls "根本错误" (fundamentally erroneous) since Laozi was not about physical longevity. Corrections to the Heshanggong text are also listed.

**Part 4 - Comparative Assessment:** The text concludes: regarding commentary quality, Wang Bi far surpasses Heshanggong; regarding textual accuracy, both have merits and faults, though scholars generally prefer the Wang Bi edition.

**Part 5 - Sui/Tang to Five Dynasties Commentaries:** Includes brief evaluations of: Lu Deming (陆德明《老子音义》, phonetic notes on Wang Bi edition), Wei Zheng (魏征《老子治要》, excerpts from Heshanggong with fangshi content deleted), Fu Yi (傅奕《道德经古本篇》, an important critical edition derived from Wang Bi that corrects various textual errors), Yan Shigu, and Cheng Xuanying (成玄英《道德经开题序诀义疏》)—whose commentary is criticized for mixing in Buddhism, Daoism, and Zhuangzi concepts that distort Laozi's philosophy. Li Rong's commentary has Daoist coloring. Wang Zhen (王真《道德经论兵要义述》)—remarkably an army general who wrote an anti-war treatise to Emperor Xianzong, emphasizing Laozi's "无为" (non-action) and "不争" (non-contention) as the core of his philosophy and urging the cessation of warfare. Lu Xisheng's commentary interprets Laozi through Confucian-Confucian lens. Gu Huan and Qiao Feng also contributed works.

**Part 6 - Song through Yuan Dynasties:** Evaluates commentaries including: Wang Anshi (who first punctuated chapter 1 with "无"/"有" as separate words), Su Zhe (highly regarded, emphasizes "复性" - returning to nature), Cheng Ju, Ye Mengde, Cheng Dachang (whose claim that Laozi derives entirely from the Yijing is deemed an overstatement), Yuan Xingzong, Lü Zuqian, Ge Changgeng (mixes Buddhist views), Zhao Bingwen, Dong Sijing (especially good on chapter 36), Li Jiamou, Lin Xiyi, Fan Yingyuan (a valuable critical edition citing 30 commentators), Liu Chenweng, Zhang Sicheng, Chen Guanwu, Wu Cheng (highly praised for precision), He Daoquan, and Jiang Rongan.

**Part 7 - Ming Dynasty:** Evaluates: Xue Hui (薛蕙《老子集解》)—who famously abandoned his youthful pursuit of immortality/方士 practices after studying Laozi, and provides important clarifications including refuting interpretations that chapter 36 contains trickery/statecraft (using the example of Chen Ping's confession that Daoist practice forbids plotting) and distinguishing Laozi from the Jin Dynasty's "pure conversation" (清谈) culture, plus criticizing both Zhu Xi's equation of Laozi with Yang Zhu and Sima Qian's conflating of Shen Buhai/Han Fei with Laozi. Thus the lines mean: letting external sensory attention disperse while keeping spirit unified, and focusing on breathing like a newborn infant—i.e., basic meditation instructions (靜修入門要訣). 2. **Chapter 15 restoration**: Through comparison of 郭店楚簡 and other versions, the author reconstructs "孰能濁以靜諸？將徐淸。孰能牝以重諸？將徐生" (Who can quiet turbid water? It will settle and become clear. This is an academic paper titled "The Taoism in Master Han-Shan's Commentary on the Laozi" (憨山大師《老子解》之道論研究) by Kao Ling-Fen (高齡芬), published in the Journal of the College of Chinese Literature, National Chung Hsing University (興大中文學報), Volume 27, June 2010. The paper explores Master Han-Shan's (1546-1623, a prominent Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk) interpretation of the Laozi (Daodejing) from a Taoist doctrinal perspective, rather than the typical Buddhist angle.

The paper is structured in four chapters: introduction, interpreting Laozi's "Wu" (無, nothingness) through Mahayana Buddhist "Emptiness" (空/Kong), interpreting Laozi's Tao through the Shurangama Sutra (楞嚴經), and conclusion.

Key arguments and findings:

1. **Fundamental differences between Buddhist "Kong" (emptiness) and Taoist "Wu" (nothingness)**: Buddhist emptiness refers to all phenomena lacking self-nature (based on dependent origination/緣起法), while Laozi's "Wu" is a metaphysical designation for the Tao - formless and nameless yet capable of generating all things. The author argues these are fundamentally different concepts.

2. **Master Han-Shan's use of Buddhist concepts to interpret the Laozi**: In interpreting Laozi Chapter 16 (致虛極，守靜篤), Master Han-Shan interprets it through Buddhist concepts of "all external things are originally non-existent" (外物本來不有) and mind-body being originally unmoving, which the author argues goes beyond the original Taoist meaning.

3. **Evolution of Master Han-Shan's interpretation**: The paper traces a development in Han-Shan's view of the Tao from initially classifying it as the "consciousness aggregate" (識蘊) - still within unenlightened consciousness (未離識性) - to later elevating it to the highest level of "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom" (大圓鏡智), equivalent to the Buddhist "true constant mind" (真常心).

4. **Key interpretive framework**: Master Han-Shan's hermeneutic is based on "the mind-only consciousness contemplation" (唯心識觀), influenced by his deep study of the Shurangama Sutra and the Avatamsaka Sutra (華嚴經).

5. **Master Han-Shan's three-tier classification of teachings**: He ranked Confucius as a "human vehicle saint" (人乘之聖), Laozi as a "heavenly vehicle saint" (天乘之聖), and Buddhism as the ultimate teaching.

6. **Master Han-Shan's metaphysical methods**: The paper identifies two methods - "fusion/merging" (融通為一), such as interpreting "Tao and name as one unity" in Laozi Chapter 1, and "transcendental distinction" (超越的區分), such as distinguishing "the speakable Tao" from "the eternal Tao."

The paper concludes that while Master Han-Shan's commentary on the Laozi provides brilliant and illuminating insights, it ultimately approaches Taoism from a Buddhist missionary perspective that may not fully align with orthodox Taoist doctrine. The author suggests Master Han-Shan's interpretation is closer to the "state/realm metaphysics" (境界型態) school of Taoist interpretation. The conclusion also discusses legitimate differences between Taoist "true persons" (真人) and Buddhist "Buddhas," noting fundamental differences in their respective worldviews despite formal similarities.

He uses the concepts of 理事無礙 (non-obstruction of principle and phenomena) and connects the "玄之又玄" (mystery of mysteries) to the Huayan school's Ten Mysteries (十玄) and Six Aspects (六相), calling it the "重玄法門" (double mystery dharma gate). He compares this chapter's use of "mu" (having/non-having) to the Heart Sutra's use of "form and emptiness" (色空).

2. The "谷神不死" (Valley Spirit Never Dies) chapter: Yang equates "谷" (valley) with true emptiness (真空) and "神" with wonderful existence (妙有), likening this to the Buddhist "如來藏" (Tathāgatagarbha). He equates "玄牝" with "阿賴耶" (ālaya-vijñāna, storehouse consciousness), noting this matches the Buddha's teaching on the Tathāgatagarbha and ālaya transformation.

3. The "出生入死" (birth and death) chapter: Yang uses the Huayan school's Ten Generations (十世法門) doctrine to explain the three sets of "ten of three" (十有三). He explains that "生之徒十有三" refers to three future generations, "死之徒十有三" refers to three past generations, and "人之生動之死地者亦十有三" refers to three present generations, with the single thought (一念) constituting the tenth. He also states that the rhino, tiger, and weapons imagery is literal (實際效果), not metaphorical, arguing that one who has broken the delusion of arising phenomena (生相無明) achieves unity of inner and outer, and of self and other.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic journal article (published in 中國學術年刊 2015, NTNU) by Shen Ming-qian analyzing Shi Dé-qīng's (釋德清, Han-shan, 1546-1623), a famous Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk's, intertextual interpretive methods in his two works: 《老子道德經解》(Commentary on Laozi's Daodejing) and 《莊子內篇註》(Commentary on the Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi). Shi Dé-qīng was the only eminent Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk to annotate both Laozi and Zhuangzi.

**Core Argument:**
The paper challenges previous research that interpreted Shi Dé-qīng's proposition "《莊子》一書，乃《老子》之注疏" (The Zhuangzi is a commentary on the Laozi) as merely positioning Zhuangzi as a subordinate doctrinal inheritor of Laozi. The author argues this interpretation misreads the statement by:
1. Applying modern understanding of "註疏" (commentary) rather than its Ming Dynasty meaning
2. Not recognizing that the "註疏" term carried implications of reading strategy, not just historical succession
3. Not accounting for Shi Dé-qīng's own stated reading experience

**Key Points:**
- Shi Dé-qīng's own reading experience revealed he first understood the Laozi THROUGH studying the Zhuangzi, so reading must go from Zhuangzi to understand Laozi, then back again
- The proposition drew on earlier thinkers including Lu Xixing (陸西星, 1520-1601), Jiao Hong (焦竑, 1540-1620), and echoed Tang-era views of Lu Deming and Cheng Xuanying
- Shi Dé-qīng elevated Zhuangzi's status while placing both within a Buddhist soteriological framework (判定 system) where Buddhism ultimately encompasses Daoism, positioning Zhuangzi as a "前矛" (vanguard) for Buddhism's goal of breaking attachments
- Shi Dé-qīng considered the Inner Seven chapters the core of Zhuangzi, viewing outer/miscellaneous chapters as supplementary elaboration

**Three Main Intertextual Interpretation Dimensions Identified:**
1. **Original text—Original text mode**: Based on "Zhuangzi as Laozi's commentary" premise, where Zhuangzi passages elaborate Laozi concepts
2. **Original text—Commentary mode**: Where Shi Dé-qīng's commentary on Laozi incorporates Zhuangzi texts (e.g., using 〈馬蹄〉and〈胠篋〉to comment on the "絕聖棄智" chapter), with the commentary becoming the interpretive key for unannotated Zhuangzi chapters
3. **Commentary—Commentary mode**: Where readers must read two of Shi Dé-qīng's commentaries together (e.g., "善行無轍迹" chapter and 〈養生主〉 commentary) to obtain complete meaning

**Methodology:** The paper defines "互文詮釋" (intertextual interpretation) not based on Julia Kristeva's Western Intertextuality but on traditional Chinese classical hermeneutic concepts of互文/互文見義, drawing on examples from Zhouli, Yili, and Zhouyi commentaries (Zheng Xuan, Hu Xu, Ao Jigong).

The paper critiques scholars like Wang Bang-xiong and Li Yi-chun for misreading the proposition, and provides an extensive literature review of both Taiwanese and Chinese scholarship on Shi Dé-qīng's Lao-Zhuang commentaries, including debates about the dating of his works (觀老莊影響論 completed 1590, 莊子內篇註 after 1590, 老子道德經解 written 1592-1606/1607).
</summary>

CONTENT SUMMARY:
"Laozi Yi" is a three-volume work by the Ming scholar Jiao Hong, with an attached one-volume work called 《老子考異》 (Laozi kaoyi, "A Critical Examination of Laozi"). Jiao Hong is also known for another book, 《易筌》 (Yi Quan). The work compiles commentaries on the Laozi (Dao De Jing) from 64 scholars dating from Han Fei onward, plus Jiao Hong's own commentary 《筆乘》, totaling 65 commentators.

COMPILATION METHOD:
- For complete, self-contained commentaries, Jiao Hong followed the model of Li Dingzuo's 《周易集解》 (Zhouyi Jijie), listing each commentator's name at the end of the relevant chapter.
- For brief phonetic/semantic glosses on single characters or phrases, he followed Pei Yin's 《史記集解》 (Shiji Jijie), weaving the glosses together and appending them below the final sentence of each chapter.
- The book is divided into upper and lower chapters (上篇/下篇), one volume each, with the appendix and Laozi kaoyi combined into one volume. It does not use the "Dao Jing" and "De Jing" section names, making it closer to the ancient original structure.

SIGNIFICANCE:
- Most commentaries were drawn from the Daoist canon and include versions rarely found elsewhere.
- Jiao Hong selected commentaries carefully, aiming to illuminate the profound (玄言) and clarify the principles of purity and naturalness (清淨自然之理).
- Commentaries mixing Daoist alchemy and Chan Buddhist rhetoric (e.g., by Ge Changgeng) were listed but mostly excluded.
- Jiao Hong's scholarship on Daoism and Buddhism was deeper than on Confucianism; thus his explanations of Confucian principles sometimes contain errors, but his Daoist and Buddhist interpretations show distinctive insight. Laozi Yi is therefore an important reference work for studying the Laozi.

2. 老子翼卷二 (Volume 2)

4. 老子翼卷四 (Volume 4)

6. 老子翼卷六 (Volume 6) - includes 《老子考異》 (Laozi kaoyi) with chapters 2-81 (the 81 chapters of the Laozi text)

《老子翼》為明代學者焦竑所撰，共三卷，附《老子考異》一卷。焦竑另有《易筌》一書，已有著錄。《老子翼》收集了自韓非以下六十四家解《老子》的著作，並附加焦竑的《筆乘》，合計六十五家。該書選取各家精闢之言，編纂成書。 《老子翼》的編纂體例獨具匠心。對於那些首尾完備、自成章段的解說，焦竑仿效李鼎祚《周易集解》，各標舉姓名，列於本章之後；而對於那些僅取一字一句的音義訓詁，則仿效裴駰《史記集解》，聯貫其文，綴於本章末句之下。《老子翼》分為上下兩篇，各為一卷，附錄和《老子考異》合為一卷。該書不設道經、德經的名稱，亦不妄立篇名，體例上更加接近古籍原貌。 焦竑對道家和佛教的研究深於儒學，因此在闡述儒理時多有涉誤，而在解說道家和佛教的理論時，則表現出獨特的見解和裁決。《老子翼》因此成為研究《老子》的重要參考書籍。,該資料已通過字符識別與對應底本相連結。此文本已有對齊的英文翻譯，可與原文並列顯示。

<summary>
This webpage is a thesis record from the Airiti Library platform (華藝線上圖書館) documenting the master's thesis "焦竑《老子翼》的詮釋向度" (The Interpretive Dimensions of Jiao Hong's "Laozi Yi") by 葉騏睿 (Yeh Chi-Jui), submitted to the Department of Chinese Literature, College of Liberal Arts, National Taiwan Normal University (國立臺灣師範大學) in 2021. The thesis focuses on the late Ming dynasty Confucian scholar Jiao Hong's interpretation of the Laozi (Daodejing) through his work "Laozi Yi."

Key research points from the abstract:
- Jiao Hong studied Confucianism under the Taizhou School (泰州學派) figures Geng Dingxiang and Luo Jinxi, eventually mastering the Three Teachings (Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism)
- Jiao Hong's core argument: while the Three Teachings have different methods, they ultimately point toward the same "Dao" (道)
- The central concept is "復性" (restoring one's nature), which Jiao Hong uses to interpret the Laozi
- The thesis is structured in two parts: (1) examining the Dao-Nature discourse in Laozi Yi, focusing on how "Dao" encompasses the Three Teachings; (2) analyzing the cultivation theory (工夫論), exploring why humans lose their nature and how "restoring nature" is possible through the sage as a model and "purifying emotions to return to nature" (滌情歸性) as a method

Keywords: 焦竑 (Jiao Hong), 《老子翼》(Laozi Yi), 詮釋向度 (interpretive dimensions), 三教 (Three Teachings), 道 (Dao), 性 (Nature)

The reference list includes classical Chinese texts such as the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) annotated by Sima Qian, the Heshang Gong commentary on the Laozi, and translations by Kumarajiva of the Diamond Sutra and Lotus Sutra. The DOI is 10.6345/NTNU202100308, and the thesis is available in the NTNU institutional repository.

<key_excerpts>
本論文以晚明儒者焦竑的《老子翼》為考察核心。焦竑年少學儒於泰州學派耿定向與羅近溪，後出入佛、老，故嫻熟三教義理。焦竑認為三教教法殊異，但細究其中思想，最終實是指向相同之「道」。, 焦竑以聖人與眾人之別，在於聖人歸根復性，而眾人則處於離道失性之困境。故「復性」之工夫實是《老子翼》之核心目的。, 第一部分為《老子翼》之道、性論述，「道」之概念作為《老子》思想的核心，其重要性不言而喻; 第二部分為《老子翼》之工夫論述。

## 唐玄宗三經御注〈序〉及其儒道治國理念研究

### A Study on Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's Prefaces to the Imperial Commentaries on the Three Classics and His Governance Ideals of Confucianism and Daoism

[李龢書(LI He-Shu)](javascript:;)

*[《輔仁宗教研究》  Issue 47 (2023/09) Pp. 81-121](javascript:;)*

Download

### Abstracts

---

本文以唐玄宗（685－762，712－756在位）所撰《御注孝經》、《御注道德經》、《御注金剛經》之〈序〉為主要考察對象，試圖結合玄宗朝的歷史背景與文化政策進行分析，以掘發三〈序〉與玄宗治國理念之間的關係。本文考察後發現，玄宗在儒釋道三教當中最為重視儒教和道教的教化作用，對於釋教則採取消極尊重的態度；面對儒道二教時，也有著從獨尊儒教漸而轉向儒道並尊的立場轉變，而在實際施政則呈現出以儒為主，以道為輔的情況。本文在進一步分析參與《御注孝經疏》《御注道德經疏》之撰著、頒布過程的人物和機構後，認為集賢院與集賢院學士在其中扮演著關鍵性角色；而集賢院的成立則與玄宗「孝治天下」的治國理念相關。本文最後指出，在「孝治天下」的原則下，玄宗逐漸形成儒道共治的治國理念，開元末葉以降設置太清宮、崇玄館、道舉等措施，可能不僅只是出自於玄宗的個人信仰，而是其治國理念的具體實現。而此前推動道教五嶽三山祭祀系統的建立，可能是玄宗儒道共治理念的第一步嘗試，對於太清宮、崇玄館的設置應予以某種啟發。

### Keywords

《御注孝經》 ； 《御注道德經》 ； 唐玄宗 ； 集賢院 ； 太清宮

### Parallel abstracts

---

This study focuses on the prefaces to the Imperial Annotations on the Classic of Filial Piety, the Imperial Annotations on the Dao De Jing, and the Imperial Annotations on the Diamond Sutra, all authored by Emperor Xuanzong of Tang (685-762; r.712-756). By situating these texts within the historical and cultural policy context of Xuanzong's reign, this paper seeks to explore their relationship to his broader political philosophy. The findings reveal that among Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism, Xuanzong emphasized the moral and educational functions of Confucianism and Daoism while adopting a more reserved and respectful stance toward Buddhism. His views shifted over time from privileging Confucianism alone to a more balanced appreciation of Confucianism and Daoism. However, Confucianism remained primary in actual governance, with Daoism serving a supplementary role. Further analysis of the figures and institutions involved in the compilation and promulgation of the Imperial Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety and the Imperial Commentary on the Dao De Jing highlights the pivotal role played by the Academy of Scholarly Worthies (Jixianyuan) and its scholars. The establishment of the Academy itself reflects Xuanzong's governing principle of "ruling the empire through filial piety." The study concludes that under this principle, Xuanzong gradually developed a model of governance integrating both Confucian and Daoist thought. Policies such as establishing the Taiqing Palace and the Chongxuan Institute from the late Kaiyuan era onward were likely not merely expressions of personal religious belief but concrete implementations of this dual-governance ideal. Earlier initiatives to institutionalize Daoist rites for the Five Sacred Peaks and the Three Sacred Mountains may be seen as the first step toward realizing this vision and may have served as a conceptual precursor to the creation of the Taiqing Palace and the Chongxuan Institute.

### Parallel keywords

Imperial Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety ； Imperial Commentary on the Daodejing ； Tang Xuanzong ； Jixian Academy ； Taiqing Palace

- Under this principle, Xuanzong developed a governance model integrating both Confucian and Daoist thought. Policies such as establishing the Taiqing Palace (太清宮) and Chongxuan Institute (崇玄館) from the late Kaiyuan era onward were likely concrete implementations of this dual-governance ideal rather than mere personal religious expression.
- Earlier initiatives to institutionalize Daoist rites for the Five Sacred Peaks and Three Sacred Mountains may represent the first step toward realizing this vision and served as a conceptual precursor to the Taiqing Palace and Chongxuan Institute.

The article references classical Chinese texts including the Mencius (孟子章句), Liji (禮記注), Weishu (魏書), Jinshu (晉書), and Liangshu (梁書). The webpage is hosted on Airiti Library, a Chinese-language academic database platform.

| 2 | 修煉一事，只緣人自有身後，氣質拘於前，物欲蔽於後——猶精金良玉，原無瑕疵，因陷於污泥之中，而金之精者不精，玉之良者不良，所以欲複原形，非用淘汰之力，琢磨之功，不能還乎初質也。太上示人下手之功曰：「谷神不死。」何以為谷神？山穴曰谷，言其虛也；變動不拘曰神，言其靈也。不死，即惺惺不昧之謂也。人能養得虛靈不昧之體以為丹頭，則修煉自易；然而無形無影，不可捉摸，必於有聲有色者，而始得其端倪。古云：「要得穀神長不死，須從玄牝立根基。」何以謂之玄？玄即天也。何以謂之牝？牝即地也。天地合而玄牝出，玄牝出而闔闢成，其間一上一下，一往一來，旋循於虛無窟子，即玄牝之門也。孔子曰「乾坤其易之門」，不誠然乎？第此門也，是陰陽往來之路，天地造化之鄉，人物發生之地，得之則生，失之則死。凡人順用之則為死戶，聖人顛倒之則為生門。人欲煉丹以成長生久視之道，舍此玄牝之門，別無他徑也。非天地之根而何？修士垂簾觀照，混沌無知時，死凡心也。忽焉一覺而動，生道心也。所謂靜則為元神，動則為真意。是其中胎息一動，不要死死執著丹田，必於不內不外間，觀其升降往來，悠揚活潑，即得真正胎息矣。古人云「出玄入牝」，是出非我本來面目，入亦非我本來面目，惟此一出一入間，中含妙諦，即虛靈也。所謂真陰真陽，形而為真一之氣是也。天地之根，豈外此乎？要知穀神者，太極之理；玄牝者，陰陽之氣。其在先天，理氣原是合一；其在後天，理氣不可並言。修道之人欲尋此妙竅，著不得一躁切心，起不得一忽略念。惟借空洞之玄牝，養虛靈之谷神，不即不離，勿忘勿助，斯得之矣。故曰「綿綿若存，用之不勤」。 |
| 3 | 大道無形，生育天地。大道無名，發育萬物。聖人以有而形無，實而形虛，顯呈此至隱至微之一物曰谷神。谷神者，空谷之神，問之若答，應焉如響，即不死也。其在人身，總一虛靈不昧之真。自人喪厥天良，穀神之汩沒者久矣！後之修士，欲得穀神長存、虛靈不昧，以為金丹之本、仙道之根，從空際盤旋，無有把柄；惟從無欲有欲、觀妙觀竅下手，有無一立，妙竅齊開，而玄牝立焉。故曰：「此竅非凡竅，乾坤共合成。名為神氣穴，內有坎離精。」總要精氣神三者打成一片，方名得有無竅、生死門；否則為凡竅，而無一元真氣存乎其中——虛則落頑空，實則拘形跡，皆非虛靈不昧之體。惟此玄牝之門，不虛不實，即虛即實，真有不可名言者，靜則無形，動則有象，靜不是天地之根，動亦非人物之本，惟動靜交關處，乃坎離顛倒之所，日月交關之鄉，真所謂天根地窟也。學人到得真玄真牝，一升一降——此間之氣，凝而為性，發而為情——所由虛極靜篤中，生出法象來。知得此竅，神仙大道盡於此矣。其曰「綿綿若存」者，明調養必久，而胎息乃能發動也；曰「用之不勤」者，言抽添有時，而符火不妄加減也。人能順天地自然之道，則金丹得矣。 |

args.summary:
This webpage is from the Chinese Text Project (中國哲學書電子化計劃, ctext.org), specifically the wiki section for a commentary on Chapter 6 ("谷神不死" - The Valley Spirit Never Dies) of the Dao De Jing (道德經注釋). 

The page contains the original text of Chapter 6: "谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之門，是謂天地根。綿綿若存，用之不勤。" (The valley spirit never dies - this is called the dark female. The gate of the dark female is called the root of heaven and earth. Continuous as if existing, yet used without effort.)

The main content consists of two lengthy classical Chinese commentaries on this chapter, focusing on Daoist alchemical/meditation practices. Key themes include:
- The "Valley Spirit" (谷神) represents emptiness and spirituality; "not dying" (不死) means remaining alert and unclouded.
- "Dark Female" (玄牝) relates to the union of heaven (玄) and earth (牝), representing the gateway for achieving immortality.
- The commentaries discuss concepts such as spirit (神), vital energy (氣), essence (精), the "golden elixir" (金丹) practice, embryonic breathing (胎息), and the balance between activity and stillness in meditation.
- Benefits are framed around cultivating the Dao for longevity and immortality, emphasizing avoiding haste and neglect in practice.

The webpage includes navigation for the Chinese Text Project (available in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese via GB encoding, and English) and is identified by URN ctp:ws206549. The site is copyrighted 2006-2026 with content under discussion.

## 老子書中的谷神

93/02/03  瀏覽次數 11391

陳章波｜ 中央研究院動物研究所

筆者鑽研海洋無脊椎動物，尤其是海岸淺灘附近的棘皮動物。由於海納百川，在臺灣高度的經濟開發、填海造地及環境污染情形下，很多海岸無脊椎動物都受到了傷害，不是滅絕就是大量死亡。這個事實迫使我改變研究的範疇：從海洋延伸到陸地水域、保護環境，以及了解人跟環境的關係，並且更進一步推展生物多樣性中，明智使用生態系之一的生態旅遊，也因此有很多的機會走到臺灣的高山野地。為了更加了解人類對大自然的觀念，開始接觸老莊的書藉，尤其是老子的著作。  
   
 **師法大自然的老子**  
   
 對於一個長期受到生態方面訓練且從事生物生態研究者而言，在閱讀老子文章過程中，很自然地會偏從這個角度來思考與欣賞。感覺到老子真的是一個非常用心的觀察者，他觀察到人逐水草而居，發現了水的很多特質，水向下流，水是柔的，水是無堅不摧的。「大道氾溪，幾可左右」，人跟水的關連是非常緊密的。所以對於整個生命的認知和「道」的比喻，很多方面他都用水來闡釋。  
   
 任何人都能體會水的重要性，「不喝水，很快就會渴死」，沙漠地區就是因為缺水，所以沒有豐富的生物、生命。希臘首位哲學家泰利斯，也以「水為萬物本原」而提出了自然生成變化原理。但要像老子那樣，能將水引伸到為人處世之道的就不多了。  
   
 老子延伸出很多向水學習的為人處事之道，在《老子他說》這本書中，老子對「上善若水」的解釋為：一個人若要效法自然之道的無私善行，便要做到如水一樣至柔之中的至剛、至淨、能容、能大的胸襟和器度。同時老子也觀察到很多的生命延續都要有雌雄兩性的參與，且以雌為重，所以才有所謂的「知其雄，守其雌」等。也認為小個體是最重要的，所以都是復歸於嬰兒。  
   
 老子同時也觀察到人的生命非常的柔弱，隨時會受到自然淘汰，因此有「天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗」的說法，以現今的演化學角度來看，就是天擇。也就是說，凡是不能順應的就被淘汰掉了，其實也沒有所謂的仁不仁、慈不慈，生存之道就是要順應天。因此老子的生存策略是「柔弱生之徒」、「戒剛強」，也就是不要跟大自然抗拒。  
   
 簡單地說，老子從南方的楚到北方的周去做事，看了很多的地理環境，看了很多生命的存亡，所以發展出「人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然」的生存之道，寫成五千字的道德經，從個人的生存到整個國家的生存，都是一樣可以應用的。老子可以說是一個生態學者，而且是生存謀略的專家。  
   
 **各家對谷神的認識**  
   
 來到合歡山，站在立霧溪上游，向下看著河谷，山頭一帶矮箭竹，谷裡大樹林立；嘴裡唸著老子第五章：「谷神不死，是謂玄牝。」一時之間，現今的我與老子做了心靈的交流。古今學者專家對這句話有很多不同的解讀，玄之又玄，對我造成極大的困惑。實際上，把它當做山谷的「谷」就自然清楚了，因為山谷是比較遮蔽、比較溫熱、比較有水，所以母性的動植物大量在此繁衍下一代，因此谷的神貌一直存續著，不會死。由形而下的具像再延伸到形而上的「道」就好懂了。有感於此，查閱了一些手頭上的書籍，將相關重點抄錄如下：  
   
 在《老子新釋》中，對有關「谷神」的「谷」字做了很多有趣的解法。章句異同：畢沅說這個「谷」字本是「浴」；俞樾說「浴」是「谷」的異字，「谷」是「穀」的借字；洪頤火宣說「谷」、「浴」，都是「欲」的借字。「谷神」當作谷中空虛解，是借來喻道的；「不死」喻變化的不停竭。「玄牝」就是大自然生殖萬物的所在，牝牡二字是代表陰陽的基本字。將其譯為白話文：谷神，空靈虛無，無形，無象；自容納一切，永遠長存，所以不死。道之為物，也像谷神一樣，無所不容，無微不入，所有萬物都是由他而生，所以叫做「玄牝」。  
   
 在《老子的智慧》這本書解釋是：虛無而神妙的道，變化是永不窮竭的。它能產生天地萬物，所以稱做「玄牝」。  
   
 在《老子他說》這本書中，認為「谷神」的谷，當然是一般所謂山谷的簡稱。但神的意涵就由自然的聲響現象延伸到宗教神話了。山谷大致可以歸納成兩種型態：一是如袋形的山谷，有進路而無出口；二是兩山夾峙，上仄中空而較隱蔽或者曲折的狹長形通道。  
   
 第一類型的山谷，大多空氣不能對流，凡有聲響動靜，必然會有迴聲。但在某些宗教的觀念看來，便認為這樣的空谷，必是神靈的宅窟，因此而有迴聲。其實迴聲是一種物理作用，並非神靈的顯赫威靈；可是在迷信者的心目中，往往因此形成宗教式的神話，塑造了多少莫須有的傳說，認為其中有神。更有甚者，便套用了道家代表人物，「該老子」的名詞，稱它為「谷神」。  
   
 第二類型的山谷，是隱晦曲折，兩頭相通的狹長通道，空氣對流，由這一頭的傳呼，便很迅速的暢達遙遠的那一頭。因此，也成為被人編織成神話的題材，認為其中如有神助。將它譯成白話文為，「谷神」即空洞虛無而生妙有的功能，便是天地萬物生命泉源的根本，取一個代名詞，便叫它是「玄牝」。  
   
 至於邱少華著《智慧之窗看老子》及孟東籬著《老子的生態觀－道法自然》這二本書，就都沒有引述谷神一節。  
   
 **老子書中其它的「谷」**  
   
 一時好奇，上網到「上古漢語語料庫」查閱老子道德經，發現其中共有八段文字出現「谷」字，茲抄錄如下：

* 道經／六章    谷神不死，是謂玄牝。
* 道經／十五章    敦若朴，混若濁，曠若谷。
* 道經／二十八章  知其榮，守其辱，為天下谷．為天下谷，常得乃足，復歸於朴。
* 道經／三十二章   譬道在天下，猶川谷與江海。
* 德經／三十九章  昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，萬物得一以生，神無以靈，將恐歇；谷無以盈，將恐竭；萬物無以生，將恐滅；侯王無以貴高，將恐……
* 德經／四十一章  明道若昧，進道若退，夷道若類，上德若谷，大白若辱，
* 德經／六十六章   江海所以能為百谷王，以其善下之，故能為百谷王。是以聖人欲上人，必以言下之；欲先人，必以身後之。

  
 這八段中大部分谷字都是「山谷」的涵義，少部分才推廣到「空虛」等其它方面的意涵。「谷」有寬廣的意思，也就是說從山谷上方往下一看的時候，谷地非常的開闊。它能夠讓河川順流而下，所以它能夠接納天下。「谷得一以盈」實際上是谷要有水把它充滿，才有谷的內涵。在臺灣常常可以看到山谷之間有水塘，植物非常茂盛；有的山谷沒有水，生物多樣性就比較差。至於「上德若谷」是指一個有德的人，應該像山谷那樣地虛懷若谷，這是一種形容用法。  
   
 **師法自然永續之道**  
   
 現代學術界研究「老子」的趨向，歸納起來大致可分為三個路線：第一類是純粹走哲學思想的研究路線；第二類是把「老子」單純地歸到個人修養；第三類是把「老子」歸到謀略學的主流（南懷瑾，一九九○）。至於筆者則是從生態學的角度加以呼應。  
   
 地球的存在已有五十億年，自有人類以來也歷經四百萬年。數以萬代的人類在這個地方生活，看到了這些自然景象所傳遞的周而復始訊息，所以老子所看到的一些自然特徵。到了現在，我們用科學的角度來重新詮釋，實際上也沒有什麼不同，所謂事理本是一致的。  
   
 只是因為工業革命，人類使用自然的能力增強了，以致自然環境受到嚴重的破壞。我們還是應該認同人類的渺小，應該以尊重自然的方式來生存。老子從適應自然以及由此所延伸出來的人類生存之道，至今仍然非常實用並且有效，因為人終究屬於生物的一類，還是受制於大自然，「師法大自然」才是人類永續之道！

資料來源

args.key_excerpts: "老子從南方的楚到北方的周去做事，看了很多的地理環境，看了很多生命的存亡，所以發展出「人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然」的生存之道，寫成五千字的道德經，從個人的生存到整個國家的生存，都是一樣可以應用的。","「谷神不死，是謂玄牝。」","上善若水","天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗","師法大自然」才是人類永續之道！","江海所以能為百谷王，以其善下之，故能為百谷王。是以聖人欲上人，必以言下之；欲先人，必以身後之。"
args.summary:
This article, published on the Taiwanese science website 科技大觀園 (Science Vista), is authored by 陳章波 (Chen Chang-po) of Academia Sinica's Institute of Zoology. It explores the interpretation of "谷神" (Valley Spirit) found in Laozi's (老子) Tao Te Ching from an ecological and biological perspective.

**Author's Ecological Background:** Chen, originally a marine invertebrate researcher focusing on echinoderms near coastal shallows, shifted his research scope to terrestrial waters, environmental protection, and understanding human-environment relationships due to Taiwan's economic development, land reclamation, and pollution damaging coastal wildlife. This led him to study the ecological dimensions of Laozi and Zhuangzi's writings.

**Laozi as an Ecologist:** The author argues Laozi was a keen observer of nature who learned from water—its downward flow, softness, and indestructibility. Key ecological insights attributed to Laozi include:
- "上善若水" (supreme goodness is like water)—embodying the softness, cleanliness, capacity, and tolerance of water
- "知其雄，守其雌" (know the male, keep to the female)—observing that both sexes participate in life continuation with emphasis on the female
- "天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗" (Heaven and Earth are not benevolent; they treat all things as straw dogs)—interpreted as modern natural selection (天擇)
- His survival strategy was "柔弱生之徒" (weakness/softness is the companion of life) and "戒剛強" (avoid rigidity), meaning not to resist nature
- He developed the path of "人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然" (man follows earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, the Way follows nature)

**Interpretations of 谷神 (from Tao Te Ching chapter 6):** The author recounts various scholarly interpretations of "谷神不死，是謂玄牝" (The Valley Spirit never dies; this is called the Mysterious Female):
- 《老子新釋》: Notes textual variants where 谷 could be 浴 or 欲; the valley emptiness symbolizes the Way, "不死" (not dying) symbolizes unceasing change, and "玄牝" is where nature reproduces all things
- 《老子的智慧》: The empty, mysterious Way never exhausts its transformations and produces heaven and earth, hence called "玄牝"
- 《老子他說» (Nan Huaijin): Distinguishes two types of valleys—bag-shaped ones with echoes (which gave rise to religious myths about spiritual beings) and narrow winding passages where air flows through; the "Valley Spirit" represents the function of empty, formless nothingness that gives rise to the mysterious—the fundamental source of life for all things

**All "谷" Occurrences in the Tao Te Ching:** The author searched the "上古漢語語料庫" (Ancient Chinese Corpus) and found eight passages containing "谷":
1. Chapter 6: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝
2. Chapter 15: 敦若朴，混若濁，曠若谷
3. Chapter 28: 知其榮，守其辱，為天下谷
4. Chapter 32: 譬道在天下，猶川谷與江海
5. Chapter 39: 谷得一以盈 (the valley becomes full by attaining the One)
6. Chapter 41: 上德若谷 (highest virtue is like a valley)
7. Chapter 66: 江海所以能為百谷王，以其善下之 (rivers and seas become king of a hundred valleys by being lower)

Most of these "谷" mean "valley" (山谷), with some extended meanings of "emptiness" (空虛). A valley is wide, open, lets rivers flow through, and can accept all things. "谷得一以盈" means a valley must be filled with water to have substance—the author notes in Taiwan, valleys with ponds have lush vegetation while dry valleys have poorer biodiversity. "上德若谷" describes a virtuous person as being open-minded like a valley (虛懷若谷).

**Modern Scholarship and Conclusion:** Modern academic research on Laozi follows three approaches: (1) pure philosophical thought, (2) personal cultivation, and (3) strategic/military science (per Nan Huaijin, 1990). The author adds an ecological perspective. The article concludes that Earth has existed for five billion years and humanity for four million years; natural cycles Laozi observed still hold true scientifically today. Since the Industrial Revolution, humans have gained greater power to use nature but have severely damaged the environment. The author argues humans should recognize their smallness, respect nature, and that "師法大自然" (learning from nature) is humanity's path to sustainability. The article was sourced from 《科學發展》 (Science Development), February 2004, issue 374, pages 76-79, and was published on 93/02/03 with 11,391 views.

## 《经典释文》[[查看正文](wiki.pl?if=gb&res=138421&remap=gb)] [[修改](instructions/wiki/zhs#editing)] [[查看历史](instructions/wiki/zhs#editing)]

* 该资料已通过[字符识别](instructions/ocr/zhs#matched)与对应底本相连结。请参考[字符识别相关使用说明](instructions/ocr/zhs#corrections)，以了解如何纠正该资料中的错字。

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| 作者 | [陆德明](searchbooks.pl?if=gb&author=陆德明&remap=gb) |
| 成书年代 | 唐 |
| 版本 | [《钦定四库全书》本](http://ctext.org/library.pl?if=gb&res=4878&remap=gb) |
| 数据项目 | [ctext:368919](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=368919&remap=gb) |
| 检索: |  |

[![](static/wikilogo.png)](https://ctext.org/faq/zhs#copyright "Content based on the corresponding Wikipedia article") 《**经典释文**》成书于[隋朝](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=630334&remap=gb)[开皇](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=708035&remap=gb)三年（583年），是唐代经学家[陆德明](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=809098&remap=gb)的著作，解释经书与《[老子](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=577989&remap=gb)》、《[庄子](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=985466&remap=gb)》音义的专著。他鉴于当时经典旧音太简，微言久绝，大义愈乖，后人攻乎异端，竟生穿凿的现象，于是在癸卯之岁（[陈后主](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=55214&remap=gb)至德元年）在校理群书的基础上，「精研六典，采纳九流，搜访异同，校之《苍》、《[雅](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=969421&remap=gb)》」，著《经典释文》30卷。《经典释文》为经文和注文皆注上反切等注音方法，统一魏晋以来混乱的注音，方便读者了解其句解，唐代以降与《十三经注疏》并行为阅读经籍的依据。《经典释文》还引用了一些今已不存的古书。

其列举徐邈、[李轨](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=969017&remap=gb)、刘昌宗、[郭璞](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=876170&remap=gb)、[郭象](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=466052&remap=gb)、[韦昭](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=307793&remap=gb)、[向秀](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=739980&remap=gb)、[王元规](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=243165&remap=gb)、崔撰、[吕忱](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=931629&remap=gb)、沈重、[戚衮](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=837043&remap=gb)、沈旋、谢峤、[顾野王](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=748180&remap=gb)、[孙炎](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=1640236&remap=gb)、[郑玄](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=384835&remap=gb)、王肃、[何胤](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=410478&remap=gb)、施乾等[汉](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=981499&remap=gb)六朝二十家音切考证，基于230家诸说分析字音字义。

高本汉称《经典释文》和《切韵》(601)是构拟中古汉语两个主要的根据。许多汉语音韵学研究(如参考文献所列)都使用了《经典释文》。

[显示更多...](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=368919&remap=gb#wp_top_zh)

## 版本

《经典释文》各卷头均有「唐国子博士兼太子中允赠齐州刺史吴县开国男陆德明撰」字样，但实际上不是唐代的著作，而是自陈[至德](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=181305&remap=gb)元年（583）开始编篡的6世纪末著作。

《经典释文》共30卷，共有序录、周易音义、尚书音义2卷、毛诗音义3卷、周礼音义2卷、仪礼音义、[礼记](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=503581&remap=gb)音义4卷、春秋左氏音义6卷、[春秋公羊](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=394561&remap=gb)音义、春秋[谷梁传](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=914729&remap=gb)音义、孝经音义、[论语](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=603461&remap=gb)音义、老子道经・德经音义、[庄子](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=985466&remap=gb)音义3卷、[尔雅](datawiki.pl?if=gb&res=969421&remap=gb)音义2卷。

在汉语音韵史上，《经典释文》是比《切韵》略早的南方标准音代表著作，以极多的**异读**为重要特徵。

《经典释文》最早陆德明的原稿是双色抄写，黑色写经文，红色写释文（《经典释文卷一叙录·条例》），唐后期的写本已经简省成一色墨书而在经文上面点朱砂的方法，再往后就变成单色写，彻底没有双色的规矩了。

现存最早的版本是宋刻宋元递修本，此后元明两代没有再刻。到了清康熙年间才有徐乾学主持的《通志堂经解》本，该本是以明末叶林宗根据钱谦益绛云楼藏宋刊本（此本已焚）影抄的本子为底本重刻的。到清乾隆年间，卢文弨以叶林宗影宋抄本为底本，广采各家校勘成果，著成《考证》30卷，与已经精校的《经典释文》原书一并刻入《抱经堂丛书》。此后讫于20世纪80年代通行的都是徐乾学本和卢文弨本以及根据这两个本子翻刻的本子。而宋刻宋元递修本直到1985年才由上海古籍出版社影印出版。

这三个版本相比较，通志堂本最劣，抱经堂本虽胜于通志堂本，也不是很好，主要还是校勘的问题。宋本的宋刻原叶质量很高，但是这个本子中有元朝的修补书叶，这些元修书叶错字特别多，因此宋本的不同部分要区别对待。另外，2006年，中华书局排印出版了黄焯的《经典释文汇校》。这个本子以通志堂本为底本，以包括宋刻宋元递修本在内的各种30卷刻本、30卷影抄本以及元明两代各种《附释音十三经注疏》所附的释文进行通校，并参合清代以来诸家校勘成果写定校勘记，每页分两栏写定，上栏为通志堂本正文，下栏为校语。

这部作品最大的特色是全书十二部分的释文都充分运用可以见到的旧钞残卷（尤其敦煌写本）、单刻本以及30卷残本进行校勘。所以单以参校之富与参校版本之精一项，《汇校》之作就已远超乾嘉以来诸家。而且黄先生在出校方面，只要有版本出现与底本相异的文字则为之出校，不避繁琐务以存真，且并不妄下断语，可谓「天下至慎」，所以堪称目前值得信赖的版本。

现存最早的版本是宋刻宋元递修本，此后元明两代没有再刻。到了清康熙年间才有徐乾学主持的《通志堂经解》本，该本是以明末叶林宗根据钱谦益绛云楼藏宋刊本（此本已焚）影抄的本子为底本重刻的。到清乾隆年间，卢文弨以叶林宗影宋抄本为底本，广采各家校勘成果，著成《考证》30卷，与已经精校的《经典释文》原书一并刻入《抱经堂丛书》。此后讫于20世纪80年代通行的都是徐乾学本和卢文弨本以及根据这两个本子翻刻的本子。而宋刻宋元递修本直到1985年才由上海古籍出版社影印出版。 这三个版本相比较，通志堂本最劣，抱经堂本虽胜于通志堂本，也不是很好，主要还是校勘的问题。宋本的宋刻原叶质量很高，但是这个本子中有元朝的修补书叶，这些元修书叶错字特别多，因此宋本的不同部分要区别对待。另外，2006年，中华书局排印出版了黄焯的《经典释文汇校》。这个本子以通志堂本为底本，以包括宋刻宋元递修本在内的各种30卷刻本、30卷影抄本以及元明两代各种《附释音十三经注疏》所附的释文进行通校，并参合清代以来诸家校勘成果写定校勘记，每页分两栏写定，上栏为通志堂本正文，下栏为校语。 这部作品最大的特色是全书十二部分的释文都充分运用可以见到的旧钞残卷（尤其敦煌写本）、单刻本以及30卷残本进行校勘。所以单以参校之富与参校版本之精一项，《汇校》之作就已远超乾嘉以来诸家。而且黄先生在出校方面，只要有版本出现与底本相异的文字则为之出校，不避繁琐务以存真，且并不妄下断语，可谓「天下至慎」，所以堪称目前值得信赖的版本。 == 总目 == \* 卷一　序录 \* 卷二　周易音义 \*
