This is an academic paper (published in *Studies in Sinology* / 《中國學術年刊》, Volume 36, Autumn issue, September 2014, pp. 19-42, ISSN 1021-7851) by Chiang Shu-chun (National Taiwan Normal University, Department of Chinese) examining the theory of mind-nature (心性論述, xinxing) in Cheng Xuan-ying's (成玄英) commentary on the Daodejing, titled 《道德經開題序訣義疏》 (Dao Der Jing Kai Ti Xu Jue Yi Shu).

CORE ARGUMENT: The paper analyzes the theoretical structure of Cheng Xuan-ying's discussions of mind (心), nature (性), emotions (情), and desire (欲) in his Daodejing commentary, and explores their deep relationship with Buddhist thought. In the early Tang dynasty, Buddhist mind-nature theory had matured, and Daoist Chongxuan (double mystery, 重玄) studies required development of mind-nature theory, leading Daoist commentators on the Laozi to focus on "mind" and "nature" topics while integrating Buddhist thought.

THREE OBSERVATIONAL APPROACHES (the paper's structure):
1. "Dao-Nature Continuity" (道、性一貫) as the ideological premise: Cheng holds that "Dao" and "nature" are one — the innate natural nature/true nature of all beings derives from the transcendent Dao. He explains "Dao" as "void and penetrating" (虛通), and states "所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也" (the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings). He uses "principle" (理) to characterize Dao, marking a major breakthrough in his Laozi scholarship. Dao's subtle principle, when internalized in humans and things, becomes their nature; hence to "preserve and return to true nature" is the path of self-cultivation.
2. "Forgetting Emotions to Complete Nature" (忘情全性) as the master thesis: In commenting on "道可道，非常道," Cheng details the relations among Dao, nature, emotions, form (形), qi (炁), and spirit (神). Since "性動為情" (nature stirring becomes emotion) and emotions contaminate, nature is damaged and distances from Dao. The key statement: "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性" (Dao gives me life, emotions destroy me; if one forgets emotions, nature is made complete). The dialectical process runs: Dao-Nature originally one → Dao-Nature separated (through stirring emotions, deluded mind chasing external objects) → Dao-Nature re-united through cultivation ("復性歸道" / returning nature to Dao as ultimate aim).
3. "Deluded Mind," "Emotional Contamination," and "Attachment to Objects" (妄心、情染、滯境) and the path of cultivation: Cheng identifies deluded mind, emotional contamination, and attachment to sensory objects as the root causes of losing true nature. His cultivation approach incorporates extensive Buddhist concepts — "empty" (空), "mind abiding nowhere" (無所住心), "three karmas clean" (三業清靜), "liberation of six sense faculties" (六根解脫), the bodhisattva ideal, "three poisons" (貪嗔痴), "dependent arising and emptiness" (緣起性空), etc. He reframes the Daoist sage as a bodhisattva-like figure; explains "returning to root/stillness/mandate" (歸根復命); and advocates for "復於真性，反於惠命" (returning to true nature and inherent mandate).

CONCLUSIONS (two observations):
1. The mind-nature discourse of early Tang Chongxuan studies may have independently influenced the mid-Tang Confucian revival (e.g., Li Ao's (李翱) 《復性書》/ "Essay on Restoring Nature," which also advocates "滅情復性" / extinguishing emotions to restore nature). The paper argues the theory of "restoring nature" (復性) was initiated by Cheng Xuan-ying well before Li Ao, challenging the view that Laozi mind-nature interpretation only fully developed in the Song dynasty.
2. The paper highlights the distinctive features of Cheng Xuan-ying's mind-nature discourse in the 《義疏》 and evaluates his value and status in the history of Laozi scholarship — characterizing the early Tang Chongxuan mind-nature theory as marked by Buddhist-Daoist mutual influence, whereas Song Confucian-Laozi interpretation turned toward Confucian-Daoist convergence.

KEY SCHOLARS CITED: Li Gang (李剛) argues Cheng's theory of restoring nature is richer than Li Ao's and scattered across his Laozi/Zhuangzi commentaries; Tang Yi-jie (湯一介) sees Chongxuan philosophy moving from ontology to mind-nature philosophy, similar to Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism (especially Cheng-Zhu), urging attention to the Chongxuan-Song Neo-Confucianism relationship; Dong En-lin divides Tang Laozi studies into three stages (early: Chongxuan with Buddhist coloring; middle: Tang Xuanzong's politicization; late: compilations by Qiang Siqi and Du Guangting). The paper used the Yan Ling-feng (嚴靈峯) edition of the reconstructed 《義疏》 as primary text.
</summary>

This webpage is the full text of the "唐玄宗御注道德真经" (Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's Annotated Commentary on the Daodejing) hosted on Chinese Wikisource (zh.wikisource.org). The work is authored by Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Li Longji (李隆基), and is collected in the "正统道藏" (Zhengtong Daoist Canon). The page provides complete annotations for all 81 chapters of the Daodejing, organized into four volumes (卷): Volume 1 (道经上, Chapters 1-19), Volume 2 (道经下, Chapters 20-37), Volume 3 (德经上, Chapters 38-59), and Volume 4 (德经下, Chapters 60-81). The work begins with a preface (序) by Emperor Xuanzong.

The annotations provide the emperor's commentary on each chapter of the classic Taoist text, explaining key concepts in the imperial interpretation. Notable commentary themes include: the nature of Dao (道) as formless, nameless, and paradoxical; the value of non-action (无为) in governance; the importance of weakness over strength, and humility over pride; warnings against excessive desire, luxury, and warfare; the ideal of the sage-ruler who governs through moral integrity rather than force. The text emphasizes concepts such as 清静 (purity and stillness), 柔弱 (softness and weakness), 冲和 (harmony), and 玄德 (mysterious virtue).

The work is categorized under 李隆基 (Li Longji), 正统道藏 (Zhengtong Daoist Canon), and 唐朝 (Tang Dynasty). The page also includes a list of other Daodejing commentaries for reference, including those by Wang Bi, Heshang Gong, Emperor Huizong of Song, Zhu Yuanzhang, Zhang Daoling, and others. The work is in the public domain as an ancient text. The page also notes that Wikisource has reached 3 million articles.
</summary>

It provided fǎnqiè (反切) phonetic annotations for both the original texts and their commentaries, unifying the chaotic phonetic notations since the Wei-Jin period. Alongside the Shisanjing Zhushu (Thirteen Classics with Commentaries and Sub-commentaries), it served as a standard basis for reading the classics from the Tang dynasty onward. The work cited examples from twenty Han and Six Dynasties phonologists (including Xu Miao, Li Gui, Liu Changzong, Guo Pu, Guo Xiang, Wei Zhao, Xiang Xiu, Wang Yuangui, Cui Zhuan, Lü Chen, Shen Zhong, Qi Gun, Shen Xuan, Xie Qiao, Gu Yewang, Sun Yan, Zheng Xuan, Wang Su, He Yin, and Shi Qian) and analyzed pronunciations based on 230 schools of thought. According to Swedish sinologist Bernhard Karlgren (高本汉), the Jingdian Shiwen and the Qieyun (601 CE) are the two principal sources for reconstructing Middle Chinese. In Chinese phonological history, it is a representative work of the southern standard pronunciation slightly earlier than the Qieyun, characterized by its numerous "variant readings" (异读).

VERSIONS: Though each volume's header states "Composed by Tang Guozibo...Lu Deming," it was actually compiled beginning in 583 CE (late 6th century), not the Tang dynasty. Its 30 volumes cover: Xulu (preface/register), Zhouyi Yinyi, Shangshu Yinyi (2 vols), Maoshi Yinyi (3 vols), Zhouli Yinyi (2 vols), Yili Yinyi, Liji Yinyi (4 vols), Chunqiu Zuoshi Yinyi (6 vols), Chunqiu Gongyang Yinyi, Chunqiu Guliangzhuan Yinyi, Xiaojing Yinyi, Lunyu Yinyi, Laozi Yinyi, Zhuangzi Yinyi (3 vols), and Erya Yinyi (2 vols). Lu Deming's original manuscript was copied in two colors: black for the classic text and red for the glosses (per the Xulü in Volume 1), but later manuscripts simplified this to single-color ink with red vermillion dots over the text, and eventually to entirely single-color writing.

PRINTING HISTORY: The earliest extant edition is the Song-dynasty printing with Song-Yuan successive repairs (宋刻宋元递修本); no further printings occurred during the Yuan and Ming dynasties. In the Qing Kangxi reign, Xu Qianxue supervised the Tongzhitang Jingjie (通志堂经解) edition, based on a Yuan-era manuscript copy made by Ye Linzong from the (now-burned) Song edition in Qian Qianyi's Jiangyunlou collection. 《经典释文》是唐代陆德明（约550-630年，名元朗，字德明，以字行，苏州吴县人）所撰的一部30卷字典，是古人读经书时的必备工具书。它以考证古音为主，兼辨训义，引用了《周易》、《尚书》、《毛诗》、《周礼》、《仪礼》、《礼记》、《春秋左传》、《公羊传》、《榖梁传》、《孝经》、《论语》、《老子》、《庄子》、《尔雅》等十四部文献，保存了唐代当时较早的音训，为历代学人所推崇。

【著书背景】陆德明是隋季唐初著名的音韵学和训诂学家。他鉴于当时经典旧音太简、后人竞生穿凿的现象，在校理群书的基础上"精研六典，采纳九流，搜访异同，校之《苍》、《雅》"，著成《经典释文》30卷，于陈后主至德元年（公元583年）开始编纂。

【主要内容】全书首为《序录》，说明本书的内容安排和经学的传授源流。各卷分别为：《周易》一卷、《古文尚书》二卷、《毛诗》三卷、《周礼》二卷、《仪礼》一卷、《礼记》四卷、《春秋左氏传》六卷、《公羊传》一卷、《谷梁传》一卷、《孝经》一卷、《论语》一卷、《老子》一卷、《庄子》三卷、《尔雅》二卷。因唐代《孟子》尚不为经书，故未收入；而《老子》、《庄子》因魏晋以后玄学影响很大，故也收入。

【价值影响】陆德明以"典籍常用，会理合时"为基本原则统一注音，合原则者为正音，不合原则者则为参考。书中对所注之书均标明书名和章节，然后摘录字句注释音义，绝大多数都标明反切或直音。作者不仅为经典本文注音，还为注文注音，全书共收录汉魏六朝二百三十余家的各种音切和诸家训诂。因绝大多数音训原书都已失传，本书保存的资料弥足珍贵，后世治文字、音韵、训诂之学者均崇此书。

This webpage is from the Chinese Text Project (ctext.org), specifically its Data Wiki entry (ctext:766397) for the person 成玄英 (Cheng Xuanying), a Tang dynasty Taoist monk. The page presents structured data and bilingual (Chinese/English) biographical content.

Key structured data:
- Name: 成玄英 (Cheng Xuanying), courtesy name Zishi (子實)
- Born/died: 700 (in the data fields, though the prose gives approximate dates)
- Associated dynasty: Tang (唐)
- Authority links: VIAF 13197603, Wikidata Q1069899
- Works he created: 流演窮寂圖 (Diagram on Circulation of Changes), 莊子疏 (Subcommentary to Zhuangzi), 道德經開題序訣義疏 (Commentary on Daodejing)

Biographical details (Chinese section):
- From Shan Prefecture (陝州), modern-day Henan province
- A Taoist monk known as a "Double Mystery" (Chongxuan/重玄派) school representative
- Lived in seclusion in Donghai until summoned to Chang'an by Emperor Taizong in 631; participated in Buddhist-Taoist debates in 636 and won, leading Emperor Taizong to declare Taoism supreme and order repair of Laozi's temple; became head of Xihua Abbey in 643
- Works include Subcommentary to the Nanhua Zhenjing (Zhuangzi), Zhouyi Liuyan (on the I Ching), Daodejing commentary, and commentary on the Lingbao scripture

English section details:
- Fl. 631–655; born around first decade of 7th century in Shan Prefecture (modern Henan)
- Summoned to Chang'an in 631, appointed head monk of Xihua Abbey; title "Master of Doctrines" (法師) possibly a later Song-period fabrication
- Participated in Daoist-Buddhist debates in 636 and 638
- In 647 participated in translation of Daodejing into Sanskrit under Xuanzang; wanted to translate "Dao" as "bodhi" but Xuanzang rejected it in favor of "mārga"
- In 647 commissioned with Zhang Huiyuan to investigate the Sanhuangjing; deemed it a forgery and Emperor Taizong ordered all copies burned
- Banished to Yuzhou around 653 after a drought; died sometime between 685 and 690
- His Subcommentary to the Zhuangzi is a sub-commentary to Guo Xiang's commentary, handed down together in the Daozang as the Nanhua Zhenjing Zhushu in 30 juan
- Wrote 2 juan commentary on Daodejing and 7 juan on Laozi kaiti xujue (fragments survive in quotations)
- His commentary on the Lingbao Scripture of Universal Salvation (度人經疏義) was extremely popular, preserved in Daozang
- Authored 5 juan work on the Classic of Changes, the Diagram on the Circulation and Development of the Changes of Zhou (周易流演窮寂圖), now lost

Citation counts from other texts: 四庫全書總目提要 (1), 郡齋讀書志 (4), 資治通鑑 (2), 直齋書錄解題 (1), 宋史 (4). The page content is based on Wikipedia under CC BY-SA 4.0 license. URI: https://data.ctext.org/entity/766397.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from 漢典古籍 (Han Dian Ancient Books), presenting Chapter 6 (第六章) of the 老子道德經校釋 (Annotated Edition of Laozi's Tao Te Ching) by Laozi (老子). The website organizes classical Chinese texts into the traditional four-part classification (經部 Jing, 史部 Shi, 子部 Zi, 集部 Ji), and this text falls under 子部/道家 (Zi section/Daoist).

The chapter text is: "谷神不死，是謂玄牝" (The valley spirit never dies; it is called the mysterious female), followed by "玄牝門，天地根" and "綿綿若存，用之不勤" (Although it remains continuously, its use cannot be exhausted).

The page presents extensive historical textual criticism (校釋) from various scholars debating variant characters. Key scholarly discussions include:
- The character "谷" vs. "浴": 畢沅 (Bi Yuan), 俞樾 (Yu Yue), 洪頤烜 (Hong Yixuan), 徐鼒 (Xu Zi), and 馬敘倫 (under 謙之案) debate whether the original text uses "谷" (valley) or "浴" (bath), with some arguing these are phonetic loan characters. CORE ARGUMENT: The paper analyzes the theoretical structure of Cheng Xuan-ying's discussions of mind (心), nature (性), emotions (情), and desire (欲) in his Daodejing commentary, and explores their deep relationship with Buddhist thought. In the early Tang dynasty, Buddhist mind-nature theory had matured, and Daoist Chongxuan (double mystery, 重玄) studies required development of mind-nature theory, leading Daoist commentators on the Laozi to focus on "mind" and "nature" topics while integrating Buddhist thought.

THREE OBSERVATIONAL APPROACHES (the paper's structure):
1. "Dao-Nature Continuity" (道、性一貫) as the ideological premise: Cheng holds that "Dao" and "nature" are one — the innate natural nature/true nature of all beings derives from the transcendent Dao. He explains "Dao" as "void and penetrating" (虛通), and states "所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也" (the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings). He uses "principle" (理) to characterize Dao, marking a major breakthrough in his Laozi scholarship. Dao's subtle principle, when internalized in humans and things, becomes their nature; hence to "preserve and return to true nature" is the path of self-cultivation.
2. "Forgetting Emotions to Complete Nature" (忘情全性) as the master thesis: In commenting on "道可道，非常道," Cheng details the relations among Dao, nature, emotions, form (形), qi (炁), and spirit (神). Since "性動為情" (nature stirring becomes emotion) and emotions contaminate, nature is damaged and distances from Dao. The key statement: "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性" (Dao gives me life, emotions destroy me; if one forgets emotions, nature is made complete). The dialectical process runs: Dao-Nature originally one → Dao-Nature separated (through stirring emotions, deluded mind chasing external objects) → Dao-Nature re-united through cultivation ("復性歸道" / returning nature to Dao as ultimate aim).
3. "Deluded Mind," "Emotional Contamination," and "Attachment to Objects" (妄心、情染、滯境) and the path of cultivation: Cheng identifies deluded mind, emotional contamination, and attachment to sensory objects as the root causes of losing true nature. His cultivation approach incorporates extensive Buddhist concepts — "empty" (空), "mind abiding nowhere" (無所住心), "three karmas clean" (三業清靜), "liberation of six sense faculties" (六根解脫), the bodhisattva ideal, "three poisons" (貪嗔痴), "dependent arising and emptiness" (緣起性空), etc. He reframes the Daoist sage as a bodhisattva-like figure; explains "returning to root/stillness/mandate" (歸根復命); and advocates for "復於真性，反於惠命" (returning to true nature and inherent mandate).

1. The mind-nature discourse of early Tang Chongxuan studies may have independently influenced the mid-Tang Confucian revival (e.g., Li Ao's (李翱) 《復性書》/ "Essay on Restoring Nature," which also advocates "滅情復性" / extinguishing emotions to restore nature). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic paper (by scholar Jiang Shujun, published in 《東亞漢學研究》第13號) examining the differences between the Daoist commentaries on the Laozi (道德經) by the Tang dynasty Daoist scholars Li Rong (李榮, in his 《道德真經注》) and Cheng Xuanying (成玄英, in his 《老子義疏》). Both are considered leading figures of the Tang dynasty "Chongxuan" (重玄, double mystery) school of Daoism. The paper challenges the traditional view (originating with scholar Meng Wentong) that Li Rong was merely Cheng Xuanying's disciple and follower whose interpretations were essentially identical, arguing instead that Li Rong had distinctive approaches.

The paper identifies two main points of divergence:

1. **"常道" (Constant Way) as "人間常俗之道" (the Way of ordinary human worldly customs)**: In interpreting the opening line of Chapter 1 ("道可道，非常道"), Cheng Xuanying follows the traditional interpretation that the Dao IS the "constant/true Way" — a transcendent, ineffable "真常凝寂之道" that cannot be captured in language or concepts. By contrast, Li Rong interprets "常道" as "the ordinary human way of worldly customs" — characterized by valuing ritual propriety (禮義), superficiality (浮華), fame-seeking, and profit-chasing. For Li Rong, the Dao is precisely NOT this "常道," but rather the opposite of it, advocating "去仁義之華，取道德之實" (discarding the superficial flowers of benevolence and righteousness, taking the substance of Dao and virtue). Similarly, he interprets "常名" as "常俗榮華之虛名" (the empty fame of ordinary worldly glory). This reflects Li Rong's core value proposition of "道與俗反" (the Dao opposes the vulgar/worldly), evidenced throughout the commentary in passages contrasting 道 (Dao) with 俗 (worldliness), advocating "捐俗禮、歸真道" (discarding worldly ritual, returning to true Dao) and "反俗修德" (reversing worldliness, cultivating virtue).

2. **Emphasizing "以道德為宗" (making Dao and Virtue/De the fundamental core)**: In interpreting Chapter 1's "此兩者同出而異名" (These two come from the same source but have different names), Li Rong interprets "兩者" (the two) as referring to 道 (Dao) and 德 (De/Virtue), presenting them as a dialectical unity — "道生德畜" (Dao generates, De nurtures), "道靜德動," "從體起用" (from substance to function), where Dao and De are "混沌理一" (undifferentiated in principle) yet "異名" (differently named). The paper notes that no earlier commentary interpreted "兩者" this way. Throughout the commentary, Li Rong frequently pairs Dao and De (道德連言), establishing them as the theoretical bedrock of Laozi's thought. In contrast, Cheng Xuanying's commentary on Chapter 1 never pairs Dao and De in this manner, suggesting Cheng valued the moral/Dao-De dimension far less strongly than Li Rong. This "以道德為宗" approach influenced later scholars including Tang Xuanzong's imperial commentary and particularly Du Guangting's 《道德真經廣聖義》, who developed the "道生德畜" ti-yong (substance-function) concept extensively.

The paper further illustrates the divergence using the interpretation of Chapter 2's "有無相生" (Being and Non-being generate each other): Li Rong reads it through the lens of cosmogony (天下萬物生於有，有生於無), understanding You/Wu as dual characteristics of the Dao ("從無出有，自有歸無"), while Cheng Xuanying reads it as the mutual dependence of relative concepts, using Buddhist ideas to critique dualistic conceptualization of the phenomenal world. --- SOURCE 13: [PDF] 李榮《道德經注》心性思想研究 - 國文學系- 國立臺灣師範大學 ---
URL: https://www.ch.ntnu.edu.tw/SIS/downloadfile.php?periodicalsPage=2&issue_id=12&paper_id=55

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article, "Study of mind thinking from Li Rong's (李榮) note for TaoDeJing (道德經注)" (published in Studies in Sinology, Vol. 37, Spring 2015, pp. 97-116, by Hsieh, Wan-hsin), examines the mind-nature theory (心性論) in Li Rong's commentary on the Tao Te Ching. Li Rong (號任真子) was a prominent early Tang dynasty Taoist of the Chongxuan (重玄, "Double Mystery") school, equally famous as Cheng Xuanying, and considered a representative figure of Chongxuan learning. The article argues that while Li Rong's academic importance parallels Cheng Xuanying's, he has not received commensurate scholarly attention.

The paper is organized into four main sections. First, on theory of nature (性論), Li Rong distinguishes two levels of nature: the "natural nature" (自然之性), which is innate, pure, self-sufficient, and perfectly complete (本乎自然, 樸，本也), and the "emotional nature" (情性), which derives from yin-yang qi and is subject to desires, deceptions, and sensory attractions. Li Rong advocates "以性制情" (controlling emotions with nature) and returning to one's original nature. His view of nature as the highest moral value aligns with the Cheng-Zhu school's "性即理" (nature is principle) approach.

Second, on theory of mind (心論), Li Rong attributes three functions to the mind: activity (活動義), cognition (認知義), and grasping/clinging (執取義). He calls the mind a "靈臺" (spirit tower) and "玄鏡" (mysterious mirror), which can illuminate and perceive the world, but once the mind stirs and clings to external phenomena, it covers the original nature. The mind can move toward either Dao-action (undirected) or non-Dao-action; cultivation work must therefore begin from the mind itself.

Third, on cultivation practices (心性修養工夫), Li Rong proposes three methods: (1) "制之未動，持心守心" (controlling before movement begins, guarding and keeping the mind), using the analogy of upper, middle, and lower scholars to describe levels of prevention; (2) "虛心復性" (emptying the mind and restoring nature), including "灰心" (ash-heart, extinguishing desires) and "混心" (mixing the mind, eliminating discriminations); and (3) "不滯兩邊，遣之又遣" (not adhering to either extreme, dispelling again and again), a double-dispelling Chongxuan method that transcends all dualities and even forgets the dispelling itself.

The conclusion highlights that Li Rong inherited and developed Cheng Xuanying's ideas—Cheng emphasized "復性" (restoring nature) while Li emphasized "修心" (cultivating the mind)—both predating Li Ao's famous "復性說" in the mid-Tang. Li Rong's philosophy notably shifted away from traditional Daoist immortality-seeking toward spiritual cultivation, even asserting that "心為死地" (the mind is the place of death), meaning that once the mind dies, even a living physical body is as good as a walking corpse. The article includes an abstract in English and extensive bibliographic references in Chinese and English on Chongxuan studies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

This webpage is from the Chinese Text Project (ctext.org), specifically the wiki section of the Chinese Philosophy Digital Project, presenting the text "道德真經玄德纂疏卷一" (Volume 1 of the Moral Classic's Dark Virtue Compilation Commentary). This is a Daoist commentary on the Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) compiled by Xiqiang Si (濛陽強思齊), featuring annotations from Tang Emperor Xuanzong (唐玄宗, imperial commentary), He Shang Gong (河上公), Yan Junping (嚴君平), Li Rong (李榮), and Cheng Xuanying (成玄英).

The text opens with an introduction describing the Daodejing as the crown of the three teachings and leader of all scriptures. The first chapter (道可道章第一) is divided into four sections: (1) marking the principle and teaching, (2) broadly clarifying root and traces, (3) distinguishing the two contemplations (of Existence and Non-existence), and (4) unifying the "double mystery" (重玄) principle.

Key content includes extensive commentary on the opening lines: "道可道，非常道" (The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao) and "名可名，非常名" (The name that can be named is not the eternal name). The commentary explores the concept of the Three Ones (三一: essence, spirit, and qi) as the body of Laozi, discusses creation from primordial qi (元氣), and explains that the eternal Dao transcends speech, form, sound, and thought.

The second chapter (天下皆知章第二) addresses how "when all under heaven know beauty as beauty, ugliness arises" and "when all know goodness as goodness, non-goodness arises." Commentators discuss how relative concepts (existence/non-existence, difficulty/ease, long/short, high/low, sound/voice) are all empty of inherent reality, citing Zhuangzi and other sources. The text concludes with the "double mystery" concept (玄之又玄), where one must abandon attachment not only to existence and non-existence but also to the mystery itself as the gate to all wonders (眾妙之門).

The page uses Traditional Chinese and is part of the wiki-based collaborative editing system of the Chinese Text Project, with the URN identifier ctp:ws822537.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Wikisource page for 卷第二十五 (Volume 25) of the 《經典釋文》(Classic of Exegesis/Interpretation of Classics), specifically the 四部叢刊本 (Sibu Congkan edition) version. The page contains two main sections:

1. **《老子道經音義》(Phonological/Glossarial Commentary on the Dao Jing of Laozi)** – attributed to 陸德明 (Lu Deming), a 唐代 (Tang Dynasty) 國子博士 (National University Erudite). The page opens with biographical notes on 老子 (Laozi), describing him as surnamed 李 (Li), named 耳 (Er), with alternate names 重耳 (Chong'er) and 伯陽 (Boyang), from 陳國苦縣厲鄉 (Li Village, Ku County, Chen State). It notes that he was born with white hair at birth, served as 周柱下史 (Zhou Zhou's official under the pillar/historian), and seeing the decline of Zhou, traveled west through the pass where he was received by the Pass Official 尹喜 (Yin Xi), to whom he wrote the 道德二篇 (two-chapter work on Dao and De) advocating emptiness and non-action, totaling some 5,000 words. The text mentions 河上公 (Heshang Gong) who wrote a chapter-and-verse commentary in four volumes, and recounts an anecdote about 漢文帝 (Emperor Wen of Han) summoning Heshang Gong, who levitated into mid-air, prompting the emperor to apologize and receive the 漢文老子章句四篇. The commentary follows 王弼's (Wang Bi, 王輔嗣) version while collating various schools. The body of this section lists numerous glosses on characters and terms from chapters of the Dao Jing, providing phonetic (反切) readings and variant readings across editions (河上本, 簡文, 顧本, 鍾會, 梁武, etc.).

2. **《老子德經音義》(Commentary on the De Jing of Laozi)** – introduces the De Jing as "德者得也" (De means obtaining), noting that the Dao gives life to all things which obtain it, hence "德經," containing 44 chapters (some editions have 43). This section likewise provides extensive phonetic glosses and variant readings for characters throughout the De Jing.

The volume closes with a note that it was 挍訂 (proofread/collated) by 後學成德 (Later Scholar Chengde). The page is part of the larger 《經典釋文》 work in the 四部叢刊 (Sibu Congkan) edition, with navigation links to the preceding (卷第二十四) and following (卷第二十六) volumes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: 經典釋文 - 中國哲學書電子化計劃 ---
URL: https://ctext.org/wiki.pl?if=gb&res=610679

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Chinese Text Project (ctext.org) wiki page about the "經典釋文" (Jingdian Shiwen / "Exegesis of the Classics"), a Chinese philological work by Lu Deming (陸德明), a Tang dynasty classical scholar. The work was completed in 583 CE (Sui dynasty, Kaihuang 3rd year; also referenced as Chen dynasty Zhide 1st year), comprising 30 volumes providing phonetic annotations (fanqie 反切) for the pronunciation and meaning of classical texts, including the classics and the Laozi and Zhuangzi. It systematized the chaotic phonetic notations of the Wei-Jin period and was used alongside the "Shisan Jing Zhushu" (Thirteen Classics with Commentaries) as a standard for reading classics. The work cites approximately 230 schools of thought and draws on 20 scholars of the Han and Six Dynasties periods (including Xu Miao, Li Gui, Guo Pu, Guo Xiang, Wei Zhao, Xiang Xiu, Zheng Xuan, Wang Su, and others). Swedish sinologist Bernhard Karlgren identified the Jingdian Shiwen and the Qieyun (601 CE) as the two principal sources for reconstructing Middle Chinese. On the phonological history, it is a representative of the Southern standard pronunciation, slightly earlier than Qieyun, notable for its abundant "different readings" (異讀).

The edition section describes: the original manuscript was written in two colors (black for text, red for annotations); the earliest extant version is the Song print with Song-Yuan later repairs (宋刻宋元遞修本). Versions include Xu Qianxue's Tongzhitang Jingjie edition (Qing Kangxi era), Lu Wenchao's Baoyingtang Congshu edition (Qing Qianlong era) with 30 volumes of textual criticism, and the 1985 Shanghai Classics Publishing House photolithographic edition of the Song print. In 2006, Zhonghua Book Company published Huang Zhuo's "Jingdian Shiwen Huijiao" (匯校), which used the Tongzhitang edition as base text and collated against Song prints, Dunhuang manuscripts, and various other editions; it is praised as the most trustworthy current version, surpassing even Qianlong-Jiaqing era scholarship. The full table of contents lists all 30 volumes: Preface, Zhouyi phonetic annotations, Shangshu (2 vols), Maoshi (3 vols), Zhouli (2 vols), Yili, Liji (4 vols), Chunqiu Zuoshi (6 vols), Gongyang, Guliang, Xiaojing, Lunyu, Laozi, Zhuangzi (3 vols), and Erya (2 vols). The page also provides a detailed chapter-by-chapter outline of the text. Further reading citations include works by Kishima Fumio (2001, in Japanese), Du Qirong (1965), and Wang Kuan-to (Journal of the Institute of Chinese Studies, CUHK). The page notes it is based on Wikipedia content under CC BY-SA 4.0 license, and warns the text was generated via OCR (character recognition) and may contain errors.

The work is included in the Zheng Tong Dao Zang (正统道藏) canon under the Dong Shen Bu Yu Jue category (洞神部玉诀类), and appears at sutra number 680 in the Dao Zang Ti Yao index, located in volume 368 of the Hanfenlou edition, volume 20 of the Xinwenfeng edition, and volume 12 of the Sanjia edition. He argues that Yang Zhu (杨朱) adhered to Laozi's substance but fell short by excessively valuing the body and despising material things; Zhuangzi (庄周) mastered Laozi's function but went too far by seeking to abandon sageliness and discard wisdom; Shen Buhai and Han Feizi (申韩) lost Laozi's reputation through harsh and punitive governance; and Wang Bi and He Yan (王何) lost Laozi's way by falling into empty nihilism and indolence. Lu considered Sima Qian (司马迁) to be the closest approximation of true Laozi philosophy among ancient writers.

Lu Xisheng further develops his core thesis by connecting Laozi with three sages: he claims Laozi shares the same origin (同原) as Fu Xi, who drew the Eight Trigrams, depicted all phenomena, explored the principles of life, and followed the harmony of virtue; that Laozi shares the overarching lineage (通其宗) with King Wen, who observed the I Ching's yin-yang movements, valued strength and change while emphasizing moderation; and that Laozi's views align in power/application (与其合其权) with Confucius, who emulated Yao and Shun, modeled the Zhou founders Wen and Wu, and guided the people through benevolence and righteousness. Lu concludes that Laozi "transformed and connected with, turned back and merged with" all three sages, making him "utterly divine" (至神). The entire work combines Confucian and Taoist thought to present a political philosophy, making it an important source for late Tang intellectual and ideological history.

Li Rong (號任真子) was a prominent early Tang dynasty Taoist of the Chongxuan (重玄, "Double Mystery") school, equally famous as Cheng Xuanying, and considered a representative figure of Chongxuan learning. The article argues that while Li Rong's academic importance parallels Cheng Xuanying's, he has not received commensurate scholarly attention.

The paper is organized into four main sections. First, on theory of nature (性論), Li Rong distinguishes two levels of nature: the "natural nature" (自然之性), which is innate, pure, self-sufficient, and perfectly complete (本乎自然, 樸，本也), and the "emotional nature" (情性), which derives from yin-yang qi and is subject to desires, deceptions, and sensory attractions. Li Rong advocates "以性制情" (controlling emotions with nature) and returning to one's original nature. His view of nature as the highest moral value aligns with the Cheng-Zhu school's "性即理" (nature is principle) approach.

Second, on theory of mind (心論), Li Rong attributes three functions to the mind: activity (活動義), cognition (認知義), and grasping/clinging (執取義). He calls the mind a "靈臺" (spirit tower) and "玄鏡" (mysterious mirror), which can illuminate and perceive the world, but once the mind stirs and clings to external phenomena, it covers the original nature. The mind can move toward either Dao-action (undirected) or non-Dao-action; cultivation work must therefore begin from the mind itself.

Third, on cultivation practices (心性修養工夫), Li Rong proposes three methods: (1) "制之未動，持心守心" (controlling before movement begins, guarding and keeping the mind), using the analogy of upper, middle, and lower scholars to describe levels of prevention; (2) "虛心復性" (emptying the mind and restoring nature), including "灰心" (ash-heart, extinguishing desires) and "混心" (mixing the mind, eliminating discriminations); and (3) "不滯兩邊，遣之又遣" (not adhering to either extreme, dispelling again and again), a double-dispelling Chongxuan method that transcends all dualities and even forgets the dispelling itself.

The conclusion highlights that Li Rong inherited and developed Cheng Xuanying's ideas—Cheng emphasized "復性" (restoring nature) while Li emphasized "修心" (cultivating the mind)—both predating Li Ao's famous "復性說" in the mid-Tang. Li Rong's philosophy notably shifted away from traditional Daoist immortality-seeking toward spiritual cultivation, even asserting that "心為死地" (the mind is the place of death), meaning that once the mind dies, even a living physical body is as good as a walking corpse. The article includes an abstract in English and extensive bibliographic references in Chinese and English on Chongxuan studies.

Key sections and arguments:

1. **Early Daoist foundations**: The article examines the views of Western Han scholar 嚴遵 (Yan Zun), who distinguished between 常道 (constant Dao, the natural state of non-action) and 可道之道 (expressible Dao, marked by human artifice). Yan Zun argued for "以無為為治" (governing through non-action) for both body and state, and proposed the analogy of body and state: "我身者，彼身之尺寸也…我國者彼國之準繩也" (my body is the measure of other bodies... my state is the standard for other states).

2. **河上公 (Heshang Gong)**: Added the concept that 常道 is "自然長生之道" (the Dao of natural longevity) while 可道之道 is "經術政教之道" (the Dao of statecraft and education). He connected governing the state to inner alchemy (內丹) cultivation, stating "國身同也，母，道也" (state and body are the same; their mother is the Dao).

3. **《太平經》(Scripture of Great Peace, Eastern Han)**: Extended the interpretation from the perspective of primordial qi (元氣), holding that governing the body nourishes the balanced qi and can serve as a model for governing the state: "先學其身，以知吉凶…故能太平也" (first learn to govern the body to know fortune and misfortune... thus peace can be achieved).

4. **葛洪 (Ge Hong, Wei-Jin period)**: Held that "道" can "內以治身，外以為國" (internally govern the body, externally govern the state). For Ge Hong, governing the body focused on "修命" (cultivating longevity/immortality) while still emphasizing 忠孝仁義 (loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, righteousness) as "the foundation" — though he saw these as secondary manifestations of the Dao. He offered a detailed body-state analogy: "胸腹之位，猶宮室也。四肢之列，猶郊境也。骨節之分，猶百官也。神猶君也，血猶臣也，氣猶民也" (the chest and abdomen are like palaces, the limbs like border regions, the bones like officials, spirit like the ruler, blood like ministers, qi like the people).

5. **Tang Dynasty characteristics**: The article stresses that "唐老子" (Tang commentaries on the Laozi) emphasized the "理身理國" dimension, influenced by Buddhism's flourishing in the Tang period. Key figures discussed:
   - **司馬承禎 (Sima Chengzhen)**: In dialogue with Emperor Ruizong, he insisted "國猶身也" (the state is like the body), reinterpreting "無為" through Buddhist concepts like 斷緣 (cutting ties), 收心 (collecting the mind), and 泰定 (calm stability). He transformed Daoist governing into a religious approach grounded in karma ("業由我造，命由天賦" — karma is created by me, fate is given by heaven).
   - **唐玄宗 (Emperor Xuanzong)**: His commentary on the Daodejing summarized its core as "理身理國," holding that governing the body is the foundation of governing the state: "聖人理國，理身以為教本" (the sage governs the state with body-governing as the teaching's foundation). His "理國無為" meant not burdening or disturbing the people ("有為則政煩").
   - **杜光庭 (Du Guangting, late Tang/Five Dynasties)**: Cataloged 38 teachings from the Daodejing, of which many directly concern "理身理國." He championed 重玄 (Twofold Mystery) philosophy, arguing one must transcend both 有為 (action) and 無為 (non-action) — "心跡俱無為" (non-action in both mind and traces). He refined the analysis into four combinations of mind/traces being active or non-active, with true non-action being "心無為跡無為" (mind non-active, traces non-active).

6. **Conclusion**: The "身國共理(治)" (joint governance of body and state) concept establishes an ontological basis connecting individual life with social existence, where ontology (what is) and ethics (what ought to be) are isomorphic. The article concludes that even today, the ideal that leaders should cultivate personal moral character and refrain from using concern for the people as an excuse to disturb them ("治之無為") retains theoretical relevance.

Note at the end: The original publication in 《宗教學研究》2000, issue 2, omitted several passages and had typographical errors in the print edition.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"我身者，彼身之尺寸也……我國者彼國之準繩也；人主者，天下之腹心也；天下者，人主之身形也。故天下者與人主俱利俱病，俱邪俱正，主民俱全，天下俱然。" (Yan Zun, 老子指歸)

"國身同也，母，道也。人能保身中之道，使精氣不勞，五神不苦，則可以長久。" (Heshang Gong)

"故一人之身，一國之象也。胸腹之位，猶宮室也。四肢之列，猶郊境也。骨節之分，猶百官也。神猶君也，血猶臣也，氣猶民也。故知治身，則能治國也。" (Ge Hong)

URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E5%94%90%E7%8E%84%E5%AE%97%E5%BE%A1%E8%A8%BB%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%9C%9F%E7%B6%93

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikisource page containing the complete text of the "唐玄宗御註道德真經" (Tang Xuanzong's Imperial Commentary on the Daodejing), a classical Chinese Daoist text with annotations by Emperor Li Longji (李隆基) of the Tang Dynasty. The work is preserved in the 正統道藏 (Zhengtong Daoist Canon).

The page is organized into four volumes (卷):
- 卷之一 道經上 (Volume 1, Dao Jing Part 1): Chapters 1-19
- 卷之二 道經下 (Volume 2, Dao Jing Part 2): Chapters 20-37
- 卷之三 德經上 (Volume 3, De Jing Part 1): Chapters 38-59
- 卷之四 德經下 (Volume 4, De Jing Part 2): Chapters 60-81

Each chapter contains the original Daodejing text followed by Li Longji's commentary in parentheses (〈〉), providing imperial interpretations of Daoist philosophy, governance, and self-cultivation principles. The commentary emphasizes themes of non-action (無為), simplicity (樸), humility, governing through moral virtue rather than force, and the balance between Dao (道) and De (德).

The work is categorized as a Tang Dynasty text, attributed to author Li Longji, and it is referenced alongside other famous Daodejing commentaries including Wang Bi's version, the Heshang Gong commentary, and imperial commentaries by Song Huizong and Ming Taizu. The page notes the work is in the public domain as the author died over 100 years ago and the work was published before January 1, 1931.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
「唐玄宗御註道德真經」作者：李隆基，本作品收錄於《正統道藏》, 此唐朝作品在全世界都屬於公有領域, 因為作者逝世已經超過100年，且作品於1931年1月1日之前出版。, 道可道章第一: 道者，虛極之妙用。名者，物得之所稱。用可於物，故云可道。無名者，妙本也。有名者，應用也。, 太上章第十七: 太上者，淳古之君也。功成而不執，事遂而無為，百姓日用而不知，謂我自然而成遂

URL: https://zh.daoinfo.org/index.php?title=%E5%94%90%E7%8E%84%E5%AE%97%E5%BE%A1%E5%88%B6%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%9C%9F%E7%B6%93%E7%96%8F&variant=zh-hant

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides an entry on the "唐玄宗御製道德真經疏" (Commentary on the Daodejing, Imperially Composed by Tang Emperor Xuanzong), a Taoist classical text. Key details include:

**Authorship and Date**: The work is traditionally attributed to Tang Emperor Xuanzong (李隆基), but was actually co-authored with Taoist priests and officials proficient in the Daodejing. It was completed in the 23rd year of the Kaiyuan reign (開元二十三年, 735 CE).

**Publication Details**: Originally six volumes, the Zhengtong Daozang (正統道藏) edition comprises ten volumes. It is cataloged in the 洞神部玉訣類 (Dongshen Section, Jade Instructions Category) of the Zhengtong Daozang. It can be found in the Hanfenlou edition at volumes 356-357, the Xinwenfeng edition at volume 19, and the Sanjia edition at volume 11. Its Daozang index number is 673, and it appears in the Zhonghua Daozang (中華道藏) at volume 9. Fragments of Dunhuang manuscripts also exist.

**Content and Method**: The work expounds upon Emperor Xuanzong's own "道德真經注" (Commentary on the Daodejing), also incorporating older interpretations and contemporary discussions (termed "又解"). It reflects debates between Buddhism and Taoism in the early Tang period regarding the philosophical meaning of the Daodejing. It is a continuation of Xuanzong's earlier commentary with a similar purpose.

**Structure**: It follows the "重玄學" (Chongxuan/Twofold Mystery) scholastic format of "開題釋義" (opening topics and explaining meanings), placing a "釋題" (explanation of the title/topic) before each chapter that explicates the chapter structure of the Daodejing and the layered meanings of each chapter - the same format used in Cheng Xuanying's (成玄英) "道德經開題序訣義疏".

**Reference**: The entry cites 胡孚琛主編《中華道教大辭典》(Beijing: 中國社會科學出版社, 1995), p. 316.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

The paper explores the primary philosophical ideas found in Emperor Tang Xuanzong's annotations (注疏) on the Daoist classic the Daodejing (道德真经). The author employs a "体用哲学" (tiyong philosophy, or substance-function philosophy) framework to organize and analyze the commentary's discussions into four sections: "道体" (the substance/essence of the Dao), "道用" (the function/operation of the Dao), and the "体" (substance) and "用" (function) of "人" (human beings). The document notes that the commentary emphasizes two central concepts: "清淨虚静" (purity, tranquility, and emptiness/stillness) and "无为" (wuwei, or non-action/effortless action). --- SOURCE 5: 唐玄宗《道德真經》注疏的幾點觀察 - 國立臺灣師範大學 ---
URL: https://scholar.lib.ntnu.edu.tw/zh/projects/%E5%94%90%E7%8E%84%E5%AE%97%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%9C%9F%E7%B6%93%E6%B3%A8%E7%96%8F%E7%9A%84%E5%B9%BE%E9%BB%9E%E8%A7%80%E5%AF%9F-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research project page from National Taiwan Normal University (國立臺灣師範大學) describing a Ministry of Science and Technology (科技部計畫) funded government research project titled "唐玄宗《道德真經》注疏的幾點觀察" (Several Observations on Emperor Xuanzong's Annotation and Commentary on the Daodejing). The project is led by Principal Investigator Chiang Shu-Chun (Chiang, Shu-Chun) from the Department of Chinese (國文學系).

The project examines Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's (唐玄宗) imperial annotations and commentary on the Daodejing, specifically his 《唐玄宗御註道德真經》(imperial annotation) and 《唐玄宗御製道德真經疏》(imperial commentary). The research notes that among the four surviving complete imperial annotations, Xuanzong's works have received relatively high academic and philosophical evaluation. The annotation (註) was completed before the commentary (疏), with the commentary serving to supplement gaps in the annotation, though Xuanzong's views remained dominant in both.

Three core research questions are addressed:
1. Analyzing the ideological connections between Xuanzong's annotation and commentary, and determining whether the commentary team upheld the principle of "疏不破注" (commentary not contradicting the annotation) or exhibited "以疏破注" (commentary breaking with the annotation).
2. Clarifying the relationship between Xuanzong's Laozi scholarship and the early Tang "Chongxuan" (重玄學, Twofold Mystery) school, focusing on the "遣之又遣" (dispelling again and again) way of thinking, "去執去滯" (removing attachments and obstructions) cultivation practices, the inner logic of heart-mind discourse (心性論述), and Buddhist-influenced interpretive perspectives.
3. Comprehensive reading and analysis of the late Tang Daoist priest Du Guangting's (杜光庭) work 《道德真經廣聖義》, which promoted and elaborated upon Xuanzong's annotations.

The project highlights how Xuanzong, as an emperor and political figure, necessarily interpreted the Laozi text through the lens of political thought and ruling-class perspectives, offering insights into how a monarch practiced Laozi's political philosophy among the people. The project also notes that later scholars including Wang Zhen, Li Yue, Lu Xisheng, Qiang Siqi, and Du Guangting cited or followed Xuanzong's interpretations, demonstrating his influence on contemporary Laozi scholarship.

Project status: Completed (已完成). Effective start/end dates: 2018/08/01 to 2020/07/31.

Keywords: 《唐玄宗御註道德真經》, 《唐玄宗御製道德真經疏》, 重玄學 (Twofold Mystery school), 心性論述 (heart-mind discourse), 佛教思想 (Buddhist thought).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
針對目前存留完整的四家御注而言，以學術眼光與哲學的理論高度而言，《唐玄宗御註道德真經》、《唐玄宗御製道德真經疏》一向獲得較高評價。玄宗的《註》蓋先成於《疏》，《疏》乃所以補充《註》之不足。 ("Among the four surviving complete imperial annotations, Xuanzong's works have consistently received higher evaluation from an academic and philosophical standpoint. His annotation was completed before the commentary, which served to supplement the annotation's shortcomings."), 因此，考察《御注》、《御疏》之間的思想聯繫，將兩者視為一個有機整體的架構，發明其間思維理路的脈絡與理論宗趣的旨歸，當是構織玄宗老學思想的重要進路。 ("Therefore, examining the intellectual connections between the annotation and commentary, treating them as an organic whole structure, is an important approach to constructing Xuanzong's Laozi scholarship."), 其後王真、李約、陸希聲、強思齊、杜光庭等皆援引其說或從其說，說明其注、疏對當朝老子學的影響。 ("Later figures such as Wang Zhen, Li Yue, Lu Xisheng, Qiang Siqi, and Du Guangting all cited or followed his interpretations, demonstrating the influence of his annotation and commentary on contemporary Laozi scholarship."), 就玄宗而言，從現實的政治條件、存在處境出發的新視域，對於《老子》文本的解讀，蓋能得到一番嶄新的發揮與應用 ("For Xuanzong, a new interpretive horizon starting from his actual political conditions and existential situation yielded fresh developments and applications in reading the Laozi text.")
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikisource (Chinese-language wiki) page containing the full text of "道德真经传卷之一" (Volume 1 of the "Commentary on the True Classic of the Dao and Virtue") by 陆希声 (Lu Xisheng) from 吴郡 (Wu Commandery). The work is a Tang-dynasty commentary on the Daodejing (道德经 / Tao Te Ching) attributed to Laozi (老子).

The document presents a series of chapters from the Daodejing (the 道可道 first chapter, 天下皆知美之为美, 不尚贤, 道冲而用之, 天地不仁, 谷神不死, 天长地久, 上善若水, 持而盈之, 载营魄抱一, 三十辐共一毂, 五色令人目盲, 宠辱若惊, 视之不见, and several others), each followed by Lu Xisheng's commentary (传). The commentary interprets the Daodejing through the lens of the distinction between "体" (substance/essence) and "用" (function/application), discussing concepts such as 无名/有名 (the nameless/the named), emperors (帝) vs. kings (皇), 无为 (non-action), and guarding the center (守中).

A key feature of the commentary is its explicit defense of Laozi against the claim that his teachings contradict those of Confucius (仲尼). Lu Xisheng argues over the final chapters that Laozi's doctrine, including passages about abandoning wisdom (绝圣弃智), is fully compatible with Confucian teachings, explaining that such statements address specific historical conditions of moral decline rather than rejecting Confucian values outright. He draws parallels between Laozi and Confucius, citing the Spring and Autumn Annals, and argues that when properly understood, "孔老之术不相悖" (the methods of Confucius and Laozi do not contradict each other).

The text includes one editorial note: "克念作圣" - the character 克 was originally written as 兄, corrected according to the 指海 edition. The Wikisource page also contains navigation metadata indicating this is Volume 1 of the work, with Volume 2 accessible via a "下一卷" (next volume) link.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"夫道者，体也。名者，用也。夫用因体生，而体本无用；名因道立，而道本无名。" (The Way is substance; names are function. Function arises from substance, but substance is originally without function; names are established by the Way, but the Way is originally without names.)

"所谓无名者，道之体，动静之先也；有名者，道之用，善恶之元也。体为名本，故能离动静，原之则天地之始也。" (The nameless is the substance of the Way; the named is its function... The body is the root of the name, the beginning of heaven and earth.)

"学者能统会其旨，则孔老之术不相悖矣。" (If scholars can comprehend the unified meaning, then the methods of Confucius and Laozi do not contradict each other.)

"且此章之末在少私寡欲耳，然则绝仁弃义，岂老氏之指哉。" (Moreover, the end of this chapter lies in reducing selfishness and desire; could abandoning benevolence and righteousness truly be Laozi's intention?)

"於乎老氏之受诬久矣，吾今乃阐而明之。" (Alas! Laozi has been slandered for a long time; I now clarify and illuminate his teachings.)
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikisource (维基文库) page hosting the complete text of 《道德真经传》(Commentary on the True Classic of the Way and Virtue) by Tang dynasty author 陆希声 (Lu Xisheng). The work is an annotated commentary on the 《道德经》(Daodejing/Tao Te Ching) and is included in the 《正统道藏》(Zhengtong Daozang, the Daoist Canon of the Zhengtong period). The page presents the author's preface (道德真经传序) in full, in which Lu Xisheng argues that Laozi's teachings are fundamentally compatible with Confucius's, treating them as two complementary approaches: Confucius's method governing through culture/literature (文) which manages the emotions, and Laozi's method grounded in simplicity/essence (质) which restores one's fundamental nature. The preface critiques followers of Laozi—including Yang Zhu, Zhuangzi, Shen Buhai/Han Feizi, and Wang Bi/He Yan—as "罪人" (sinners/wrongdoers) of the Laozi school for their excesses, and defends Laozi against accusations that his teachings are incompatible with Confucianism. Lu also draws parallels between Laozi and the sages Fuxi, King Wen, and Confucius, and criticizes Ban Gu for placing Laozi in the third rank of his ancient figures table. The main body of the work is divided into four scrolls (卷之一 through 卷之四), each linked to a separate subpage. The page also lists other Daodejing commentaries (e.g., Wang Bi's, Heshang Gong's, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's, etc.) and notes that this Tang dynasty work is in the public domain (author deceased over 100 years, published before 1931). Categories: 陆希声, 正统道藏, 唐朝.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published April 21, 2010 in Guangming Daily by scholar Zeng Zaozhuang (曾枣庄), examines the historical status and achievements of the Three Su (三苏) - father Su Xun (苏洵, 1009-1066) and his sons Su Shi (苏轼) and Su Zhe (苏辙) - in Chinese culture. The essay is organized around several themes:

**Contrasting careers:** Su Xun was a late bloomer who did not begin studying seriously until age 27, failed the imperial examinations twice, and only became famous near age 50. He held only low official posts (equivalent to a section-level cadre). In contrast, his sons achieved fame young - Su Shi at 22 and Su Zhe at 19 upon passing the jinshi examination. Su Shi governed eight prefectures and reached the rank of Minister of Rites (礼部尚书), while Su Zhe rose from county magistrate to Vice Chancellor (副相), outranking his brother. Su Zhe's political abilities flourished mainly during the Yuanyou era (元祐年间).

**Political roles before and after the Wang Anshi reforms:** Su Xun was primarily a political commentator (政论家) known as "talent of a king's advisor" (王佐才), while the sons were both commentators and active politicians. Su Xun emphasized administrative reform over legal reform, arguing "政之失，非法之罪" (political failures are not the fault of the law). The sons opposed Wang Anshi's New Policies; Su Zhe opposed them four months before Su Shi and left the capital two years earlier. Su Shi criticized Emperor Shenzong for being "too hasty in governance, too broad in listening, too sharp in advancing people" (求治太急，听言太广，进人太锐). During the Yuanyou era, Su Zhe submitted 74 memorials in ten months as Right Remonstrance Official, including eight calling for punishment of Han Zhen and three for executing Lü Huiqing.

**Literary achievements:** All three are among the "Eight Great Prose Masters of Tang and Song" (唐宋八大家). Su Xun's prose was praised by Ouyang Xiu as "辞辩闳伟" and by Zhu Xi as "雄浑". Su Shi was a pioneering figure across genres - known as Ou-Su with Ouyang Xiu in prose, Su-Huang with Huang Tingjian in poetry, and Su-Xin with Xin Qiji in ci poetry (founding the heroic school). Su Zhe's poetry was praised by Su Shi as superior to his own ("子由诗过吾远甚") and by Lu You as "温雅高妙，如佳人独立".

**Artistic accomplishments:** All three understood music (Su Xun owned a Lei qin), played chess modestly, excelled in calligraphy (Su Shi ranked first among the four great Song calligraphers), and appreciated painting. Su Shi established the "painting with a complete bamboo in one's chest" (胸有成竹) theory and founded the Huzhou school of literati painting.

**Historical scholarship:** Su Xun wrote the three-part Shilun (史论), praised as showing "true historical talent" and "the brush of Sima Qian". Su Zhe wrote the Gushi (古史) to correct errors in Sima Qian's Shiji, plus Longchuan Luezhi and Longchuan Biezhi documenting contemporary history, works that Zhu Xi frequently cited.

**Unorthodox thought:** Su Xun rejected the Confucian principle of righteousness over profit, arguing "利之所在，天下趋之" (where profit lies, the world rushes there). All three interpreted the Six Classics through human emotion (人情). Su Xun viewed the I Ching as a means of divine deception. The sons opposed Wang Anshi and Cheng Yi for being "inhumane" (不近人情). Su Zhe was particularly eclectic, integrating Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism, and famously argued that "老聃、庄周之言不可以周、孔辩" (the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi cannot be debated using Zhou and Confucius) and that one must evaluate ideas without invoking Confucius or Laozi as authorities.

**Conclusion:** The author argues that while Su Shi is generally most celebrated, Su Xun deserves greater recognition for educating and cultivating his two famous sons, achieving greatness without any teacher through his own efforts - "上继韩、欧，下开长公兄弟" (succeeding Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu above, and opening the way for his son Su Shi below).
</summary>

Zheng Tianxi's 2020 article deepened this from a yili (義理) perspective, focusing on "道器不離" (Dao and tools are inseparable), which effectively harmonized the two traditions.

2. **Mind-Study (心學) Tendency**: Lin Xiyi showed tendencies toward mind-study, emphasizing self-attainment (自得) and inner realization rather than book learning. Liu Sihe (2013) first noted this, arguing Lin was closer to Zhuangzi and Chan Buddhism than to either Zhu Xi or Lu Jiuyuan. Huang Yun further developed this, analyzing Lin's concept of "無容心" (non-attachment of mind), distinguishing two stages of mind, and linking it to Cheng Hao's views. The article notes there is as yet no dedicated study on Lin's relationship to mind-study, suggesting this as a fruitful research avenue for understanding the continuity of mind-study between Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming.

3. **Using Buddhism to Interpret the Laozi (借佛解老)**: Liu Sihe (2013) argued Lin maintained his Neo-Confucian position, using Chan concepts only as tools (e.g., using "悟"/enlightenment merely as a means to grasp 天理), with Buddhism in a subordinate position. Huang Yun disagreed, arguing Lin engaged in an equal dialogue between Buddhism and Daoism, focusing on experiential understanding (體悟) rather than subordinating one to the other; this blurred distinctions between the two traditions. Zhang Miao (2019) held that Lin was rooted in Confucianism but acknowledged the inherent commonalities between Buddhism and Daoism and adopted multi-angled, flexible approaches to integrating them. Several scholars, including Huang Yun and Zheng Tianxi, noted Lin's misreadings of Buddhist concepts but did not determine whether these were intentional or unintentional distortions. Zheng Tianxi also analyzed Lin's views on the "無心" (no-mind) state of those who attain the Dao, influenced by both Mencius's "不動心" and Chan's "無念," and Lin's cultivation practices emphasizing self-realization and the idea that "道體在我" (the Dao substance is within oneself).

4. **Literary/Language Commentary (文章學點評)**: Wang Weiqian's 2012 article first discussed the characteristics of the commentary - Lin used simple, colloquial language (口義 style) with clear explanations, rhetorical devices like metaphor, strong overall coherence, and cross-referential interpretation of chapters. Huang Yun's thesis more deeply analyzed Lin's popularization of difficult language, clarification of metaphors, and pointing out both strengths and weaknesses (verbosity where explanation was unnecessary, and overextending metaphors - e.g., interpreting literally factual statements as figurative). Sun Mingjun's 2017 article analyzed this from a rhetorical perspective, identifying three literary features Lin highlighted: 借物明道 (using objects to illuminate the Dao through metaphor), exquisite conclusions (結語精妙, similar to "煞尾" in storytelling), and direct commentary on writing style. Zheng Tianxi argued Lin's sometimes forced "借喻" analysis aimed to counter Zhu Xi's negative evaluations of the Laozi.

The article concludes that existing research remains insufficiently deep across all four areas, and suggests future research directions: exploring alternative angles beyond harmonization for the Dao-Confucianism relationship, studying Lin's influence on mind-study's development, deeper investigation of Lin's complex relationship with the vast Buddhist tradition, and examining how Lin handled passages in the Laozi that are difficult to connect coherently.

2. **The "Dao equals Li" (道理合一) interpretation**: Wu Cheng equated the Daoist "Dao" (道) with Neo-Confucian "Principle" (理/天理), infusing the Dao with Confucian moral attributes (仁義禮智 - benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom). He used the "Li Yi Fen Shu" (理一分殊, one principle, many manifestations) concept to interpret the Dao-De relationship as "Dao producing myriad virtue" (道一分殊). He viewed "Dao" as metaphysical principle and "De" as its manifestation in all things.

3. **Mind-nature theory (心性論)**: Wu Cheng drew on Lu Xiangshan's (陸九淵) concept that "mind is principle" (心即是理), arguing that all principles of things are inherent in the mind (萬事萬物之理皆備於我). He emphasized "inner contemplation" (內觀) over external seeking, distinguishing "virtue-knowledge" (德性之知) from "hearing-seeing knowledge" (聞見之知). Wu Cheng's philosophy reconciles Zhu Xi and Lu Xiangshan, though leaning toward Lu's "revering virtue" (尊德性).

He advocated returning to the infant-like (嬰兒/赤子) state of simplicity and true purity (真樸), achieving unity with the Dao.

5. **Cultivation practices (工夫修養)**: Wu Cheng proposed principles for nurturing form, qi, and spirit (形、氣、神). For recluses (出世之人): preserving form, qi, and spirit (存形、存氣、存神); for those in the world (住世之人): nourishing them (養形、養氣、養神). 1. **The interpretive foundation**: Wu Cheng understood the Laozi's "道" (Dao) through the Neo-Confucian "縱貫縱講" (vertical/creative) interpretive framework rather than the "縱貫橫講" (horizontal/subjective) framework that Mou Zongsan later applied to Daoism. In Wu's commentary, Dao is not merely a state/boundary (境界形態) but possesses real creative ontological status, generating the universe ("無名者，道也，天地亦由此道而生"). Wu interprets the creation sequence as 道→一(沖虛一氣) →二(陰陽) →三, incorporating "德" (virtue/de) as the "一" into the cosmic generation scheme, thereby bridging the gap that Han dynasty 氣化宇宙論 (qi-based cosmology) had created between Dao and all things.

2. **A critical reassessment**: The paper challenges scholars like Huang Zhao and Liu Yijun who equate Wu's interpretation of the Dao with the Neo-Confucian "天理" (Heavenly Principle). The author argues against this for two reasons:
   - **First**, in Wu's commentary, 無為 (non-action) serves as the ultimate value, while 仁義 (benevolence and righteousness) remain secondary virtues. This places Wu's interpretation firmly within the Daoist system, differentiating it from Neo-Confucian thought where 仁義 constitutes the Heavenly Principle itself. Wu's commentary on chapters 16/18 emphasizes that filial piety and loyalty should be practiced naturally as "常分" (ordinary duty), not through external promotion.
   - **Second**, Wu's purpose in commenting on the Laozi was to distinguish (分判) rather than reconcile Confucianism and Daoism. In the 《吳文正集》, Wu explicitly criticizes the Laoist view of "自無而有" ("有生於無") as implying 理氣二分 (division of li and qi) and 理先氣後 (li prior to qi), which Wu rejects in favor of the Neo-Confucian position that 理氣 are inseparable and without priority. Wu regarded the Laozi's teaching as "異端似是之非" (heterodox doctrine resembling the truth).

**Conclusion**: While Wu's commentary does grant the Dao real creative ontological status similar to the Neo-Confucian 天理 (justifying the "以理釋《老》" characterization), the author argues that Wu maintained a clear distinction between the Daoist interpretation of 道/理 and the Neo-Confucian 理. Wu never equated the Dao of the Laozi with the 天理, as the ultimate values differ (無為 vs. 仁義) and their respective relationships with qi differ fundamentally (理氣二分 vs. 理氣不二). Thus, prior scholars' claims of full identity between Wu's Dao and the Neo-Confucian 理 constitute over-interpretation.
</summary>

- Scholars have generally characterized Wu Cheng's (吳澄, 1249-1333) interpretation of the Daodejing Commentary as "interpreting the Laozi through principle (li)" (以理釋《老》), based on Wu's status as a Neo-Confucian (理學家).
- Wu Cheng applied the Song Confucian "vertical-preaching" interpretive horizon of "Heavenly Principle" (天理) to Laozi's discussion of "moral/way and virtue" (道德), transforming the Laozi from a contemplative, aesthetic metaphysics into one with genuinely creative (generative) significance—giving Laozi's "moral" an ontological-cosmological creative meaning, making it highly consistent with Confucian "Heavenly Principle."
- Because "principle" (理) and "Way" (道) share similar metaphysical implications and can be compared, Wu Cheng integrated the li-qi (理氣, principle-energy) theories of Zhang Zai (張載) and Zhu Xi (朱熹) into his annotations, giving the Commentary a strong flavor of Confucian-Daoist convergence.

HOWEVER, the thesis argues that "principle" and "Way" cannot be fully equated, for two reasons:
1. Throughout the Commentary, Wu Cheng took "non-action" (無為) as the ultimate value with "benevolence and righteousness" (仁義) as secondary virtues, showing his interpretation remained within the Daoist framework.
2. The core meaning of "Way" is "spontaneity/naturalness" (自然): applied to the self it is "natural human nature" (人性自然), and applied to politics it is "governance through non-action" (無為之治). From "natural human nature" unfolds cultivation of spirit and regimen from having no self (無身) to having self (有身); from "governance through non-action" is traced the "non-action–self-transformation" (無為－自化) structure of "governing the Way–being governed by the Way" (治道－道治) between sage and the people, thereby outlining an ideal political vision.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the text of "道德真经注" (Commentary on the Daodejing) by Su Zhe (苏辙) of the Song Dynasty, also known as "老子解" (Explanation of Laozi). The text is preserved in the "正统道藏" (Orthodox Daoist Canon) in the "洞神部玉诀类" (Dong Shen section, Yu Jue category), consisting of four volumes (卷). The source text is based on the Orthodox Daoist Canon edition, with a reference edition from the Wuqiu Beizhai (无求备斋) reprint of the Baoyan Tang (宝颜堂) edition.

The content provides Su Zhe's philosophical commentary on the first fourteen chapters (章) of the Daodejing. Key commentaries include:
- Chapter 1 (道可道): Distinguishes between the "道" (Way) that can be spoken and the eternal, unspoken Way. While Confucian virtues (仁仁义礼智 - benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom) are "speakable Ways" and therefore changeable, the true Way is unchanging and undefinable.
- Chapter 2 (天下皆知): Discusses how distinctions like beauty/ugliness, good/evil, being/non-being, and long/short are relative and interdependent; the sage practices non-action (无为) and wordless teaching.
- Chapter 3 (不尚贤): Argues against elevating worthies, valuing rare goods, or displaying desires; the sage governs by emptying the mind, filling the belly, weakening ambition, and strengthening bones.
- Chapter 4 (道冲): The Way is empty yet inexhaustible, the ancestor of all things, preceding even the Emperor (帝).
- Chapter 5 (天地不仁): Heaven and Earth treat all things like straw dogs - without favor or disfavor; the bellows (橐钥) analogy shows how emptiness produces movement.
- Chapter 6 (谷神不死): The valley spirit (谷神) is formless, deathless, and is the "玄牝" (mysterious female), root of Heaven and Earth.
- Chapter 7 (天长地久): Heaven and Earth endure because they do not live for themselves; likewise the sage places himself after others and outside himself.
- Chapter 8 (上善若水): The highest good is like water, which benefits all without contending and dwells where others dislike.
- Chapter 9 (持而盈之): Warns against excess, fullness, and arrogance; advocates retiring after success, following the Way of Heaven.
- Chapter 10 (载营魄): Discusses the soul (魂) and bodily spirit (魄), cultivating unity of spirit and body, and reaching the state of an infant; includes commentary on the "six entrances" (六入) citing the Buddhist Śūraṅgama Sūtra (《首楞严》).
- Chapters 11-14: Cover the utility of emptiness in wheels, vessels, and rooms; the dangers of sensual indulgence (five colors, five sounds, five flavors); understanding favor and disgrace; and the invisible, inaudible, intangible nature of the Way that unifies into the One (性 - nature).

Su Zhe's commentary frequently draws on the Book of Changes (《易》) and engages with the concept of "性" (innate nature) and "神" (spirit), reflecting Song Dynasty Neo-Confucian and Chan Buddhist influences in interpreting the Daodejing.
</summary>

"莫非道也。而可道者不可常，惟不可道，而后可常耳。今夫仁义礼智，此道之可道者也。然而仁不可以为义，而礼不可以为智，可道之不可常如此。" (Chapter 1 - distinguishing the speakable from the eternal Way)

The work is a major Daoist commentary on the Tao Te Ching, divided into two volumes (卷上 covering the 道經/Book of the Way, and 卷下 covering 德經/Book of Virtue).

The introductory 提要 (preface) notes the work was edited in October 1775 (乾隆四十年) under imperial auspices by 紀昀, 陸錫熊, 孫士毅 and 陸費墀. This is an academic paper titled "The Taoism in Master Han-Shan's Commentary on the Laozi" (憨山大師《老子解》之道論研究) by Kao Ling-Fen (高齡芬), published in the Journal of the College of Chinese Literature, National Chung Hsing University (興大中文學報), Volume 27, June 2010. The paper explores Master Han-Shan's (1546-1623, a prominent Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk) interpretation of the Laozi (Daodejing) from a Taoist doctrinal perspective, rather than the typical Buddhist angle.

The paper is structured in four chapters: introduction, interpreting Laozi's "Wu" (無, nothingness) through Mahayana Buddhist "Emptiness" (空/Kong), interpreting Laozi's Tao through the Shurangama Sutra (楞嚴經), and conclusion.

Key arguments and findings:

1. **Fundamental differences between Buddhist "Kong" (emptiness) and Taoist "Wu" (nothingness)**: Buddhist emptiness refers to all phenomena lacking self-nature (based on dependent origination/緣起法), while Laozi's "Wu" is a metaphysical designation for the Tao - formless and nameless yet capable of generating all things. The author argues these are fundamentally different concepts.

2. **Master Han-Shan's use of Buddhist concepts to interpret the Laozi**: In interpreting Laozi Chapter 16 (致虛極，守靜篤), Master Han-Shan interprets it through Buddhist concepts of "all external things are originally non-existent" (外物本來不有) and mind-body being originally unmoving, which the author argues goes beyond the original Taoist meaning.

3. **Evolution of Master Han-Shan's interpretation**: The paper traces a development in Han-Shan's view of the Tao from initially classifying it as the "consciousness aggregate" (識蘊) - still within unenlightened consciousness (未離識性) - to later elevating it to the highest level of "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom" (大圓鏡智), equivalent to the Buddhist "true constant mind" (真常心).

4. **Key interpretive framework**: Master Han-Shan's hermeneutic is based on "the mind-only consciousness contemplation" (唯心識觀), influenced by his deep study of the Shurangama Sutra and the Avatamsaka Sutra (華嚴經).

5. **Master Han-Shan's three-tier classification of teachings**: He ranked Confucius as a "human vehicle saint" (人乘之聖), Laozi as a "heavenly vehicle saint" (天乘之聖), and Buddhism as the ultimate teaching.

6. **Master Han-Shan's metaphysical methods**: The paper identifies two methods - "fusion/merging" (融通為一), such as interpreting "Tao and name as one unity" in Laozi Chapter 1, and "transcendental distinction" (超越的區分), such as distinguishing "the speakable Tao" from "the eternal Tao."

The paper concludes that while Master Han-Shan's commentary on the Laozi provides brilliant and illuminating insights, it ultimately approaches Taoism from a Buddhist missionary perspective that may not fully align with orthodox Taoist doctrine. The author suggests Master Han-Shan's interpretation is closer to the "state/realm metaphysics" (境界型態) school of Taoist interpretation. The conclusion also discusses legitimate differences between Taoist "true persons" (真人) and Buddhist "Buddhas," noting fundamental differences in their respective worldviews despite formal similarities.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic journal article (published in 中國學術年刊 2015, NTNU) by Shen Ming-qian analyzing Shi Dé-qīng's (釋德清, Han-shan, 1546-1623), a famous Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk's, intertextual interpretive methods in his two works: 《老子道德經解》(Commentary on Laozi's Daodejing) and 《莊子內篇註》(Commentary on the Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi). Shi Dé-qīng was the only eminent Ming Dynasty Buddhist monk to annotate both Laozi and Zhuangzi.

**Core Argument:**
The paper challenges previous research that interpreted Shi Dé-qīng's proposition "《莊子》一書，乃《老子》之注疏" (The Zhuangzi is a commentary on the Laozi) as merely positioning Zhuangzi as a subordinate doctrinal inheritor of Laozi. The author argues this interpretation misreads the statement by:
1. Applying modern understanding of "註疏" (commentary) rather than its Ming Dynasty meaning
2. Not recognizing that the "註疏" term carried implications of reading strategy, not just historical succession
3. Not accounting for Shi Dé-qīng's own stated reading experience

**Key Points:**
- Shi Dé-qīng's own reading experience revealed he first understood the Laozi THROUGH studying the Zhuangzi, so reading must go from Zhuangzi to understand Laozi, then back again
- The proposition drew on earlier thinkers including Lu Xixing (陸西星, 1520-1601), Jiao Hong (焦竑, 1540-1620), and echoed Tang-era views of Lu Deming and Cheng Xuanying
- Shi Dé-qīng elevated Zhuangzi's status while placing both within a Buddhist soteriological framework (判定 system) where Buddhism ultimately encompasses Daoism, positioning Zhuangzi as a "前矛" (vanguard) for Buddhism's goal of breaking attachments
- Shi Dé-qīng considered the Inner Seven chapters the core of Zhuangzi, viewing outer/miscellaneous chapters as supplementary elaboration

**Three Main Intertextual Interpretation Dimensions Identified:**
1. **Original text—Original text mode**: Based on "Zhuangzi as Laozi's commentary" premise, where Zhuangzi passages elaborate Laozi concepts
2. **Original text—Commentary mode**: Where Shi Dé-qīng's commentary on Laozi incorporates Zhuangzi texts (e.g., using 〈馬蹄〉and〈胠篋〉to comment on the "絕聖棄智" chapter), with the commentary becoming the interpretive key for unannotated Zhuangzi chapters
3. **Commentary—Commentary mode**: Where readers must read two of Shi Dé-qīng's commentaries together (e.g., "善行無轍迹" chapter and 〈養生主〉 commentary) to obtain complete meaning

**Methodology:** The paper defines "互文詮釋" (intertextual interpretation) not based on Julia Kristeva's Western Intertextuality but on traditional Chinese classical hermeneutic concepts of互文/互文見義, drawing on examples from Zhouli, Yili, and Zhouyi commentaries (Zheng Xuan, Hu Xu, Ao Jigong).

The paper critiques scholars like Wang Bang-xiong and Li Yi-chun for misreading the proposition, and provides an extensive literature review of both Taiwanese and Chinese scholarship on Shi Dé-qīng's Lao-Zhuang commentaries, including debates about the dating of his works (觀老莊影響論 completed 1590, 莊子內篇註 after 1590, 老子道德經解 written 1592-1606/1607).
</summary>

CONTENT SUMMARY:
"Laozi Yi" is a three-volume work by the Ming scholar Jiao Hong, with an attached one-volume work called 《老子考異》 (Laozi kaoyi, "A Critical Examination of Laozi"). Jiao Hong is also known for another book, 《易筌》 (Yi Quan). The work compiles commentaries on the Laozi (Dao De Jing) from 64 scholars dating from Han Fei onward, plus Jiao Hong's own commentary 《筆乘》, totaling 65 commentators.

COMPILATION METHOD:
- For complete, self-contained commentaries, Jiao Hong followed the model of Li Dingzuo's 《周易集解》 (Zhouyi Jijie), listing each commentator's name at the end of the relevant chapter.
- For brief phonetic/semantic glosses on single characters or phrases, he followed Pei Yin's 《史記集解》 (Shiji Jijie), weaving the glosses together and appending them below the final sentence of each chapter.
- The book is divided into upper and lower chapters (上篇/下篇), one volume each, with the appendix and Laozi kaoyi combined into one volume. It does not use the "Dao Jing" and "De Jing" section names, making it closer to the ancient original structure.

SIGNIFICANCE:
- Most commentaries were drawn from the Daoist canon and include versions rarely found elsewhere.
- Jiao Hong selected commentaries carefully, aiming to illuminate the profound (玄言) and clarify the principles of purity and naturalness (清淨自然之理).
- Commentaries mixing Daoist alchemy and Chan Buddhist rhetoric (e.g., by Ge Changgeng) were listed but mostly excluded.
- Jiao Hong's scholarship on Daoism and Buddhism was deeper than on Confucianism; thus his explanations of Confucian principles sometimes contain errors, but his Daoist and Buddhist interpretations show distinctive insight. Laozi Yi is therefore an important reference work for studying the Laozi.

Key research points from the abstract:

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Wikisource document containing the complete text of "老子衍" (Laozi Yǎn, "An Exegesis of the Laozi"), a philosophical commentary on the Tao Te Ching written by the Ming dynasty scholar 王夫之 (Wang Fuzhi), and published as part of the 船山遗书 (Chuanshan Yishu, "Posthumous Works of Chuanshan"). The page includes Wang Fuzhi's dated preface and a chapter-by-chapter commentary on the Laozi text, annotated by his son Wang Yu (王敔).

The preface criticizes earlier commentators on the Laozi, including Wang Bi (王辅嗣), He Yan (何平叔), Kumarajiva, Emperor Wu of Liang, Lu Xisheng (陆希声), Su Che (苏子繇), Jiao Hong (焦竑), and Li Zhi (李贽), for improperly mixing the text with Confucian and Chan Buddhist interpretations. Wang Fuzhi argues that forcing Confucianism to align with Daoism misrepresents Confucianism, and forcing Daoism to align with Buddhism misrepresents Daoism. He identifies three failures in discourse on the Dao: opposing popular customs without fairness (不公), upholding incidental insights without constancy (不经), and ostentatious cleverness without auspiciousness (不祥), all of which he says the Laozi exhibits. He nevertheless values the text's utility, citing the Han dynasty emperors Wen and Jing, Zhang Zifang (Zhang Liang), and Sun Zhonghe as successful practitioners of its principles, and approving of Sima Qian's assessment that "Lao Dan (Laozi) governed through non-action and self-transformation, and was pure and self-correcting."

The main body presents Wang Fuzhi's exegesis of chapters 1-68 of the Laozi, organized into two sections: 上篇道篇 (Upper Section on the Way, chapters 1-37) and 下篇德篇 (Lower Section on Virtue, chapters 38-68), with the text ending mid-chapter at chapter 68. The commentary draws on many earlier scholars, including Wang Bi, Lü Jifu (吕吉甫), Li Yue (李约), Wang Yuanze (王元泽), Li Xizhai (李息斋), Wang Anshi (王介甫), Han Feizi, Su Che (苏子繇), Wu Youqing (吴幼清), Xue Juncai (薛君采), Ye Mengde (叶梦得), Zhong Shiji (锺士季), Lu Xisheng (陆希声), Yan Junping (严君平), Zhao Zhijian (赵志坚), Liu Zhongping (刘仲平), and Shao Ruoyu (邵若愚). The preface is dated to the year of 旃蒙协洽 (a cyclical year, generally identified with 1615 or 1655 depending on reckoning) in the month of Zhuangyue (the sixth lunar month), signed "南公王夫之序" (Preface by Lord Nan, Wang Fuzhi).
</summary>

URL: https://rc019.ndhu.edu.tw/var/file/56/1056/img/2548/315885094.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic article published in 《東華漢學》(Dong Hwa Journal of Chinese Studies), Issue 32 (December 2020), pages 213-254, titled "成純與貞勝：王夫之天人思想與處世實踐析論" ("Achieving Simplicity and Continually Prevailing: A Look at Wang Fuzhi's Philosophy of Heaven-Human Relationship and his Way of Being in the World") by 林書漢 (Shu-Han Lin), a doctoral candidate at National Taiwan University's Department of Chinese Literature and part-time lecturer at Cardinal Tien Junior College of Healthcare and Management.

**Main Thesis:** The article examines Wang Fuzhi (王夫之, 1619-1692), also known as Chuanshan (船山), a thinker who lived during the Ming-Qing transition. Facing the turmoil of dynastic change, Wang developed a coherent system of Heavenly-human philosophy and practical ethics. The author combines three concepts to analyze Wang Fuzhi's thought:

1. **成純 (Chengchun, "Achieving Simplicity")** - Derived from Zhuangzi's "Discussion on Making All Things Equal" (齊物論): "參萬歲而一成純" (takes part in ten thousand ages and achieves simplicity in oneness). This serves as the foundation of Wang's worldview, built on the Qi (氣) theory where all things emerge from the interaction of yin-yang forces. Wang integrated this with Zhang Zai's 張載《正蒙》concepts of 太虛 (Great Void) and 太和 (Great Harmony), establishing a harmonious, cyclical cosmic order. Key elements include the 天均 (Heavenly Balance) as the great foundation of all things, the 環中 (Center of the Ring) as a method for transcending disputation, and 純氣之守 (guarding the pure Qi) as a practice of concentrating the will and calming the spirit to achieve union between Heaven and humans.

2. **貞勝 (Zhensheng, "Continually Prevailing")** - Derived from the Book of Changes (周易·繫辭下傳): "吉凶者，貞勝者也" (Good fortune and ill are continually prevailing each against the other by an exact rule). This serves as Wang's principle of conduct—observing shifts in affairs, finding the principle of the exact rule (貞一之理) and the moment of multiplication (相乘之幾), then acting accordingly. Wang emphasized three "great constants" (大貞): the separation of Chinese and barbarians (華夷), of gentleman and petty persons (君子小人), and of male/female roles.
