播报

编辑

### 综述

《道德经》主要论述“道”与“德”：“道”不仅是宇宙之道、自然之道，也是个体修行即修道的方法；“德”不是通常以为的道德或德行，而是修道者所应必备的特殊的世界观、方法论以及为人处世之方法。

老子的本意，是要教给人修道的方法，德是基础，道是德的升华。没有德的基础，为人处世、治家、治国，很可能都失败，就没有能力去“修道”。所以修“德”是为修道创造良好的外部环境，这可能也是人所共需的；修道者更需要拥有宁静的心境、超脱的人生，这也缺“德”不可。《道德经》德经部分，在经文中占了很大部分，这是修道的基础。

“道”是浑全之朴，“众妙之门”。“道”生成了万物，又内涵于万物之中，“道”在物中，物在“道”中，万事万物殊途而同归，都通向了“道”。

“道”不只是有形的“物质”、思虑的“精神”、理性的“规律”，而是造成这一切的无形无象、至虚至灵的宇宙本根。“物质”、“精神”、“规律”皆是“道”的派生物。 “道”是先天一炁，混元无极，“道”是其大无外、其小无内、至简至易、至精至微、至玄至妙的自然之始祖、万殊之大宗，是造成宇宙万物的源头根本。 [4-5]

### 主题思想

《道德经》主题思想为“[道法自然](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E9%81%93%E6%B3%95%E8%87%AA%E7%84%B6/64671?fromModule=lemma_inlink)”。

“道法自然”是《道德经》中老子思想的精华。“道”作为《道德经》中最抽象的概念范畴，是天地万物生成的动力源。“德”是“道”在伦常领域的发展与表现。“道”与“法”在规则、常理层面有相通点，但不同于西方自然法。“法”应效法自然之道，在辨证的反向转化之中发挥其作用。

哲学上，“道”是天地万物之始之母，阴阳对立与统一是万物的本质体现，物极必反是万物演化的规律。伦理上，老子之道主张纯朴、无私、清静、谦让、贵柔、守弱、淡泊等因循自然的德性。政治上，老子主张对内无为而治，不生事扰民，对外和平共处，反对战争与暴力。这三个层面构成了《道德经》的主题，同时也使得《道德经》一书在结构上经由“物理至哲学至伦理至政治”的逻辑层层递进，由自然之道进入到伦理之德，最终归宿于对理想政治的设想与治理之道。也就是从自然秩序中找出通向理想社会秩序的光明正道。 [6]

一、“道”与“德”之内涵界定

1、“道”

老子在《道德经》开篇阐明：“道，可道，非常道。名，可名，非常名。无，名天地之始；有，名万物之母。故常无，欲以观其妙；常有，欲以观其徼。此两者同出而异名，同谓之玄。玄之又玄，众妙之门。”这是老子对于“道”这个概念的总括性的描述：道，非当时社会一般的道， 即人伦、常理之道，也非当时时人所能命名之道。“道”在老子那里已经超越了世俗社会生活，更加接近于自然法则之道，因为天地万物的始基与母源在于“道”，由道开始，“道生一，一生二，二生三，三生万物”。由此，老子用“玄之又玄”来描述道的特殊性与深奥性，而其实这个“道”虽然“视之而弗见”、“听之而弗闻”、“捪之而弗得”，但老子所言之道并不远人，这里只是老子用“玄”来强调他所言之道与当时社会所言之道的差异性，并且阐述他所言之道的超然性与根基性。

所以老子在后面的论述中又坦言，“吾言，甚易知也，甚易行也，而人莫之能知也，而莫之能行也。”老子感慨道：“知我者希，则我贵矣。是以圣人被褐而怀玉。”

老子所言之“道”即“有物混成，先天地生。萧呵，潦呵，独立而不垓，可以为天地母。吾未知其名，字之曰道。强为之名曰大。”这句话意思是，在天地生成之前，宇宙中就有混沌的物体存在，它幽静无声，广阔无边，无依无靠又长存不改，它就是化育万物的慈母。“我”——老子不知道它的名字，就勉强称它为“道”，命名为“大”。

由此得知，老子所言之道首先具有物质性，是天地万物生成的原始动力源，并且它的存在独立而不可丈量，具有无限性。对于“道”这种力量，老子自己是无法给予它确切的描述的，所以他认为，道只是权宜之称。

道的特性：老子说，“道冲，而用之，有弗盈也。”道体似虚而实，所以体内蕴含用之不竭的物质和能量，但不会因自满而溢出。老子认为，道体柔而不刚，内部单纯，外部朴素无华，且清澈透明，长存于天地之间。所以道无处不在，不管是个人，还是人类社会，包括天地万物都应该效法道而运行，而道法自然，[返璞归真](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E8%BF%94%E7%92%9E%E5%BD%92%E7%9C%9F/5105?fromModule=lemma_inlink)。这里的“自然”字面解为本来如此，但是道与自然规律是同一的，也即“国中四大”皆应效法自然无为而无不为的特性，从而保持自身“天长地久”。

老子所处当时[东周](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E4%B8%9C%E5%91%A8/507892?fromModule=lemma_inlink)社会，诸侯各国穷兵黩武，战乱频仍，社会之礼仪伦理已无法恢复，所以老子看透人类社会之所以会纷争不已，都是由于圣人、礼仪、法令、欲望、智慧等有为措施所引起的，正是因为社会看中名利、实力、好胜等荣誉，所以天下才会出现资源有限性的占有之争。老子因此提出回归自然，顺应无为而治、清净绝智的自然世界的规律，从而才能守弱胜强，达到小国寡民的平静生活，“民至老死而不相往来。” [6]

2、“德”

“德”是“道”在伦常领域的发展与表现，因此由道进入德是由自然秩序同向社会秩序的一道屏障，即转而论述人的行为规范。德与法都是规范社会与人的行为的约束力量，但在老子那里两者有不同的地位。老子认为，上德的本质与道之德的本质同于一，因此上德源自于“道” 。老子所言之德也不同于常人所言之德。第三十八章载：“上德不德，是以有德；下德不失德，是以无德。上德无为而无不为，下德为之而有以为；上仁为之而无以为；上义为之而有以为；上礼为之而莫之应，则攘臂而扔之。故失道而后失德，失德而后失仁，失仁而后失义，失义而后失礼。”

[老子](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E8%80%81%E5%AD%90/5448?fromModule=lemma_inlink)认为，上德主张无所事事，一切顺应自然，带有明显的“无为”特征，可理解为因循自然的行为规范。这种因循自然的德重生命，轻名利，持守清静，戒除贪欲，息心止行，悟道四达， 自然无为，同时以百姓之心为心，将自身与自然融为一体，最后归于道。下德由上仁、上义及上礼组成，需要人实际去实行与推广，带有明显的“有为”特征，注重人为的行为规范。从这里可以看出，在老子眼里，[孔子](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%AD%94%E5%AD%90/1584?fromModule=lemma_inlink)推行的仁义礼智信只是人为教化的结果，没有达致真正无为超脱的上德境界，所以贬之为下德。上德的无为境界与法本身需要国家制定、国家干预以及公之于世的特性相违背，所以法律不过是下德的范畴而已。但是下德之中，法律与仁、义、礼又有所不同，老子并没有把法纳入到下德的探讨范围之内，似乎可以得出，老子认为，仁义礼是高于法律的，而法律不过是一种治国之器物。

老子之德与孔子之德有区别，同时也不同于“礼”，但是世俗之法与礼法有着千丝万缕的联系，从某种程度来讲，春秋战国时期，礼法之间是合为一体的。孔子之德在老子看来是属于“下德”范畴，是属于人为规范的领域，而老子认为，上德表现为无为，即不去考虑德与不德的问题， 反而是最大的德。 [6]

二、“道法自然”的本体论意义

1、人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然

[河上公](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E6%B2%B3%E4%B8%8A%E5%85%AC/0?fromModule=lemma_inlink)注：“人当法地安静柔和也，种之得五谷，掘之得甘泉，劳而不怨也，有功而不制也。天湛泊不动，施而不求报，生长万物，无所收取。道清静不言，阴行精气，万物自成也。道性自然，无所法也。”王弼注：“法，法则也。人不违地，乃得全安；法地也。地不违天，乃得全载；法天也。天不违道，乃得全覆也；法道也。道不违自然，乃得其性；法自然者，在方而法方，在圆而法圆，于自然无所违也。自然者，无称之言，穷极之辞也。用智不及无知，而形魄不及精象，精象不及无形，有仪不及无仪，故转相法也。道顺自然，无故资焉；地法于天，人故象焉，所以为主，其一之者，主也。”可见，“法”此处并非法令制度，而作动词“效法”之意。《道德经》第25节中，老子第一次提到“法”字，据帛书记载，即“人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然。”通俗理解为，道是创造天地万物的原始之母，因此人要效法地，地效法天，天效法道，道效法自然。“道法自然”并不是把道与自然对立起来，道是终极的、绝对的，没有“外”，所以“道”就是“自然”。“自然”这一概念在老子的学说中一般有三方面构成，即一是不干预，自由发展，二是不勉强，三是出于天然，不假人工造作者。

由此可以看见，老子所言之道，即因循自然之规律达致“无为而无不为”之境。此处，“法”一词在句中作为动词，即效法、因循、遵守之意，而无法则、法律之意。

当然，法“道”也有超越世俗法律之上的自然法则之意，即遵循社会常理、常识、常情，而这些既是“道”的引申义，从而也可作为世俗法律之根基与合理性之评判。

老子认为，“国中有四大”即“道大、天大、地大、君王大”。天、地、王三者都要依循道来成就，他们之间的关系就在于道是根基、母体之所在。而王作为国家的统治者要治理国家，也应遵循老子所言之道，而此道运用到政治治理之中，也即法律、伦理、政策、规则等都应顺应道的发展规律。 [6]

2、王法地地，法天天，法道道，法自然

由于古书一般没有标点与分段，所以后人在加注的时候，囿于不同的学识，从而对此句话产生不同的意义理解。这种划分是由唐代[李约](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E6%9D%8E%E7%BA%A6/7101?fromModule=lemma_inlink)在《道德真经新注》断句而成，他将“人”改为“王”而衔接上句国中四大之君王大。

李约注：“道大，天大，地大，王亦大”，是谓“域中四大”。王者“法地”“法天”“法道”之三自然而理天下也。天下得之而安，故谓之“德”。凡言人属者耳，其义云“法地地”如地之无私载。“法天天”，如天之无私覆。“法道道”，如道之无私生成而已。如君君、臣臣、父父、子子这例也。后之字者谬妄相传，皆云“人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然”。则域中有五大非四大矣。岂王者只得“法地”，而不得“法天”，“法道”乎？天地无心，而亦可转相法乎？又况“地法天，天法道，道法自然”之道为天地之父，自然之子，支离决裂，义理疏远矣。高明也在《帛书老子校注》中认为，李说虽辨，而历代学者多弃之不用或谓“乃小儿牙牙学语”单词重叠，非老子之。虽说不词，但确为古之一说，况且如今尚有信从者。按“人法地，地法天，天法道”所言非王者只得“法地”而不得“法天”“法道”，而谓人，地，天皆法于道也。若此句法如四十二章“道生一，一生二，二生三，三生万物”，此虽谓“三生万物”不言而喻，生万物者当为“道”绝不会理解为生万物者“三”耳。

古棣在《老子校诂》中解释此四句说：“法地地”，是说以地之所以为地者，为法，地之所以为地，即地无私载；“法天天”，是说以天之所以为天者，为法，天之所以为天，即天无私覆；“法道道”，是说以道之所以为道者，为法。

道之所以为道者的特质，即“道法自然” 。“自然”便是自己如此，即自因、自成、自本、自根，“道法自然”，即道以自己如此，自成、自因为法，而不横加干预，亦即“无为”。这里“法”字有法则之意，君王要以大地的无私载、谦卑无争为法，以天之无私藏为法，以道之自然为法，从而道与自然归一。

此处之法乃道之法，对道的遵循可以使得天、地、人三界秩序井然，得以理治。高定彝认为，此句表达了古人的系统论的观点， 宇宙万物是一个整体，人、天、地、自然等构成了一个有层次、结构、整体的系统，相互联系，相互制约。

当然由王到地、天，最后到道、自然，[叶海烟](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%8F%B6%E6%B5%B7%E7%83%9F/0?fromModule=lemma_inlink)认为，这一层层递进之中也有超越之意在其中，也即“法”可以扩充为“归向”、“超越”的意蕴，而不止于“依循”、“效仿” 。 [6]

三、“道法自然”的法哲学意义

1、“道”与“法”的关系

一是老子之道是一种特殊之物，看不见，听不见，摸不着，人们无法确定其名，以“道”相称。这种特殊之物有具体与抽象之分，道不仅指“道路”、“路程”、“途经”等，还指代“方法”、“技艺”、“事理”、“规则”、“常理”、“思想体系”等。而特殊之物主要是从具体之道层面而言。如第二十五节，“吾未知其名，字之曰道。强为之名曰大。”

二是精神性范畴之道，主要指老子将道对自然界的作用抽象化，演化为“无为而治”的治国之道。

三是规则或常理层面之道。如第九节，“功遂身退，天之道也” 。

四是方法层面之道。如第五十九节，“是谓深根固柢，长生久视之道也。”

上述四层关于“道”义的阐述中，第三层规则或常理层面之道与法律之法是相通的。法是对常理常识常情的一种规范化，通过国家强制力保证这种刚性规则得以实施。而作为规则或常理之道更多的是一种自然法层面的东西，或者道之规则为自然规律，不以人的主观意志为转移，否则将受到自然规律的惩罚。常理之道是社会生活之道，主要体现在人与人、人与社会的关系之中，是一种普遍认同的社会规律或习俗习惯，受到伦常关系的制约。

从这两个层面来说，道之规则与常理是法形成的环境与基础，法不过是以正式的形式规范化了的自然规律与常理，因此法与道是两个不同层次的问题，法来源于道，且反过来要顺应道的运动。 [6]

2、“道法自然”思想异于西方自然法

《老子》中体现的就是中国自然法思想，可以看做是中国道家法律学说的肇始。在中国古代，老子第一个提出“道法自然”的自然法思想观点。老子的“道法自然”与西方自然法思想在本质上不一样。西方自然法思想发源于古希腊古罗马的自由主义和理性主义传统，正义、善、民主等理念是其基础，并且作为评价实在法或人定法的应然性依据。而老子的“道法自然”思想立足于万物的本原，即“道”，试图通过认知“道”来达到对自然世界和人类社会的终极把握，从而依“道”而生。这种“道”不是自由、理性、民主或正义等理念和评价标准，而是一种“不可名”之特殊物，一种“天长地久”的规律性东西，兼具物质和精神层面，存于天地之间自我循环。

总而言之，老子认为，统治者治理国家贵在“无为”、“无事”等圣人之治，而圣人之治的手段并不是通过制定刑法等国家制度来对老百姓加以规制，圣人以合乎自然、不行强制来推行其统治。而法律制度是治国者统治人民的工具，是统治者为了保障自身的利益与维持社会秩序建构的国家机器，老子认为这些法律制度以及国家机器的存在都是统治者的有为措施，而这些有为措施又体现了统治者雄心、私欲、智慧等产生争战、贫富、盗贼等祸害的缘由的因素，往往滋扰人民按自然之道来生活，所以老子极力反对这些措施与法令制度。因此，从老子“道法自然”思想中可以得出结论，法需要顺应“道”与“德”的运动，效法自然之律，在辩证的反向转化之中发挥其治理作用。 [6]

君子文化

《道德经》中的君子文化尽管不是体现在“君子”一词使用的频率和含义上，但其一系列主张和思想内容恰好契合了温、良、恭、俭、让的君子人格，包括：主张温和、虚、静、柔弱，反对暴烈；主张上善若水及对善与不善的辩证肯定；主张自然无为、道法自然，反对乱作为、粗暴干预；主张俭朴，反对奢靡；主张谦虚、忍让、不争、低调、涵容，反对显摆、张扬和高调等。同时，《道德经》对《易经》中坤卦系列多所继承且受谦卦影响较大，也深化了其中的君子文化内涵。 [52]

消极思想

当然，老子的思想也有问题：一是退化。不同于近代史上的“进化”，老子的历史观是“退化”。他把整个文明都拿来批判，“大道废，有仁义；智慧出，有大伪；六亲不和，有孝慈；国家昏乱，有忠臣”。《老子》似乎在满怀恐惧和慨叹地总结着历史上的“成败、存亡、祸福、古今之道”。面对“金玉满堂，莫之能守”的困局，如何才能“长治久安”呢？老子向往的是比孔墨理想更为久远的“小国寡民”时期。在那个时期，一切任其“自然”， “祸莫大于不知足，咎莫大于欲得”。因此，对于文字、技术等方面的人类进步他是否定的，庄子更是继承和发扬了这种社会理想。在这个意义上，“无为而治”在政治层意义上是积极的，在社会层意义上却是消极的。他反对贪欲，进而反对智慧，主张回到没有文明的时代，这显然是消极的。在小国寡民中，虽然“甘其食，美其服，安其居，乐其俗”仍然有正价值，代表了人民对美好生活的向往，但“鸡犬之声相闻，民至老死，不相往来”，却是今天的我们无论如何也难以接受的。二是愚民。这既表现在绝圣弃智上，也表现在绝仁弃义上。他反对以智治国：“古之善为道者，非以明民，将以愚之。民之难治，以其智多。故以智治国，国之贼；不以智治国，国之福。”他还看到了大道之废与仁义兴起之间的关系：“故失道而后德，失德而后仁，失仁而后义，失义而后礼。夫礼者，忠信之薄，而乱之首。”他说：“圣人之治，虚其心，实其腹，弱其志，强其骨。常使民无知无欲，使夫智者不敢为也。为无为，则无不治。”圣人要保证老百姓的基本生活，但要求百姓不要追求过多的欲望。追求五色、五音、五味，都是指代过度的物质需求，而不是基本的需求。其实人类社会的冲突都是由于过度的欲望引起的，如对物质的欲望，对名誉的欲望和对权力的欲望。然而，老子对于愚、智的理解又是十分独特的。他说自己，“众人皆有余，而我独若遗，我愚人之心也哉！俗人昭昭，我独昏昏；俗人察察，我独闷闷”。这也是讲君主茫然无知，而臣属却工于算计，正如《吕氏春秋》所言，“得道者必静”。“治大国如烹小鲜”，君要愚世要智，可能也有其积极意义。在他看来，小国寡民的社会图景和无为而治原则，只有具备圣人品格的统治者才能担当和组织实施。三是循环。老子充满了“反本”思想，他认为，循环运行是道运动的必然结果，任何事物运动都会复归，回到原初状态和原来的出发点。“大曰‘逝’，逝曰‘远’，远曰‘反’”。“致虚极，守静笃。万物并作，吾以观复”。四是无为。与庄子的无为不同，老子的无为是“无不为”。如果把无为理解为遵守规律的为，才能求得正解。 [53]

### 文学特色

音韵之美

《道德经》句式整齐，大致押韵，为诗歌体之经文。读之朗朗上口，易诵易记。体现了中国文字的音韵之美。如“有无相生，难易相成，长短相形，高下相倾”（二章）、“虚其心，实其腹，弱其志，强其骨”（三章）、“挫其锐，解其纷，和其光，同其尘”（四章）、“其政闷闷，其民淳淳”（五十八章）。这些词句，不仅押韵，而且平仄相扣，有音韵美，也有旋律美。朗诵经文，是一种美的享受，在音韵之美中体味深刻的哲理。 [7]

[](https://baike.baidu.com/pic/%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%BB%8F/327138/0/8694a4c27d1ed21b87bb585baa6eddc451da3f19?fr=lemma&fromModule=lemma_content-image "《道德经》")《道德经》

讲究修辞

《道德经》的语言非常讲究艺术性，运用了多种修辞方式，使词句准确、鲜明、生动，富有说理性和感染力。 [7]

1、对偶

如：“道，可道，非常道；名，可名，非常名”、“无，名天地之始，有，名万物之母”（一章）、“贵以贱为本，高以下为基”（三十九章）、“祸兮，福之所倚；福兮，祸之所伏”（五十八章）、“天下难事，必作于易；天下大事，必作于细”（六十三章）。对偶句子看起来整齐醒目，听起来铿锵悦耳，便于记忆、便于传诵。

2、排比

排比可以增强语言的气势、鼓动力。《道德经》中排比句较多。如：“五色，令人目盲；五音，令人耳聋；五味，令人口爽；驰骋畋猎，令人心发狂；难得之货，令人心妨”（十二章）、“曲则全，枉则直，洼则盈，敝则新，少则得，多则惑”（二十二章）、“自见者不明，自是者不彰。自伐者无功，自矜者不长”（二十四章）、“大方无隅，大器晚成，大音希声，大象无形”（四十一章）。

3、比喻

《道德经》中比喻亦多。如：“谷神不死，是谓玄牝。玄牝之门，是谓天地根。绵绵若存，用之不勤”（六章），以玄牝喻“道”，生养万物。又如：“上善若水，水善利万物而不争”（八章），通篇以水喻人，把水拟人化，赞颂得道者的高贵品质。再如：“专气致柔，能婴儿乎”（十章）、“我独泊兮其未兆，如婴儿之未孩”（二十章）、“复归于婴儿”（二十八章），皆以婴儿喻道者的纯洁、天真、朴实无华。又如：“合抱之木，生于毫末；九层之塔，起于累土；千里之行，始于足下”（六十四章），连用三个比喻，讲明从小做起的道理。这些比喻，增强了语言的形象性，加深了读者的印象。

4、设问和反问

如：“何谓宠辱若惊？宠为下，得之若惊，失之若惊，是谓宠辱若惊”、“何谓贵大患若身？吾所以有大患者，为吾有身，及吾无身，吾有何患”（十三章）、“民不畏死，奈何以死惧之”（七十四章），这些设问与反问，增加了语言波澜，扣人心弦，起到了引人注意、思索的效果。

5、联珠

联珠又叫顶真，是把前一句后边的词语作为后一句开头的词语，把语言连续说下去的一种修辞手法。如：“人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然”（二十五章），又如“道生一，一生二，二生三，三生万物”（四十二章），联珠使语气连贯，结构严密，更好地反映事物的有机联系。 [7]

语言精辟

《道德经》语言极为精辟，是至理名言，形成诸多成语、格言、座右铭。如：“天长地久”（七章）、“上善若水”（八章）、“少私寡欲”（十九章）、“弱之胜强，柔之胜刚”（七十八章）、“祸莫大于不知足，咎莫大于欲得”（四十六章）。有的原句，今已演变为警句，广泛流传。如：“功成，名遂，身退”（九章），现为“功成身退”；“知其白，守其黑”（二十八章），现为“知白守黑”；“大巧若拙，大辩若讷”（四十五章），现演变出“大智若愚”；“天网恢恢，疏而不失”（七十三章），现为“[天网恢恢，疏而不漏](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%A4%A9%E7%BD%91%E6%81%A2%E6%81%A2%EF%BC%8C%E7%96%8F%E8%80%8C%E4%B8%8D%E6%BC%8F/6347516?fromModule=lemma_inlink)”；“知足之足，常足矣”（四十六章），现为“知足常乐”；“宠辱若惊”（十三章），现为“宠辱不惊”。 [7]

### 中国影响

《道德经》内容涵盖哲学、[伦理学](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E4%BC%A6%E7%90%86%E5%AD%A6/3712?fromModule=lemma_inlink)、政治学、[军事学](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%86%9B%E4%BA%8B%E5%AD%A6/0?fromModule=lemma_inlink)等诸多学科，被后人尊奉为[治国](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E6%B2%BB%E5%9B%BD/569882?fromModule=lemma_inlink)、[齐家](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E9%BD%90%E5%AE%B6/8566244?fromModule=lemma_inlink)、[修身](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E4%BF%AE%E8%BA%AB/3400276?fromModule=lemma_inlink)、为学的宝典。它对中国的哲学、[科学](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E7%A7%91%E5%AD%A6/10406?fromModule=lemma_inlink)、政治、[宗教](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%AE%97%E6%95%99/81929?fromModule=lemma_inlink)等产生了深远的影响，体现了古代中国人的一种世界观和人生观。先秦诸子、中国人的文化思想等没有不受老子影响的，被华夏先辈誉为万经之王 [1]。《道德经》的影响也是多方面的，包括政治、文化、科学、宗教等等方面。据[元朝](https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E5%85%83%E6%9C%9D/266205?fromModule=lemma_inlink)时的不完全统计，先秦以来，研老注老著作至元朝时就超过三千余种，具有代表性的不少于一千种，从侧面说明了《道德经》的巨大影响。 [5]

《道德经》的辩证法为内丹修炼中先天与后天、顺与逆、颠倒等概念提供了理论框架。《道德经》有关生命和理想人格的思想则对内丹生命观和仙真的修炼目标观提供了思想源头。 [54]

### 国际影响

在世界文化经典文献中，《道德经》有广泛的影响力，就被翻译的次数和语种而言，《道德经》仅次于《圣经》，成为《圣经》以外流传最广的外文著作。 [57]

据美国学者邰谧侠（Misha Tadd）于2019年发表的《<老子>译本总目》显示，《老子》译本的总目共涉及73种语言，1500余种译本。其中，在西方世界传播的《道德经》译本语种主要集中于英语、德语、西班牙语与法语。 [58]

鸦片战争之后，英国的传教士和汉学家们开始将《道德经》翻译成英语介绍给西方世界。此后的一百多年，西方逐渐认可和重视老子的思想。 [50]

1988年时任美国总统里根在国情咨文中引用了老子的名言“治大国若烹小鲜”，使《道德经》风行美国，引得各大出版社争相出版。美国畅销书作家和翻译家史蒂芬•米歇尔（Stephen Mitchell）的《道德经》英译本也由此被带到了聚光灯下。它的版权售价高达13万美元，在出版后8年间共计发行55万余册。 [56]

args.summary:
This is a Baidu Baike (Baidu Encyclopedia) entry on the "道德经" (Dao De Jing / Tao Te Ching), the classic philosophical work attributed to Laozi (老子), written during the Spring and Autumn Period. 

KEY FACTS:
- The Dao De Jing is also known as 《德道经》 (De Dao Jing), 《道德真经》, 《老子》, 《五千言》, and 《老子五千文》.
- It is an important source of Daoist philosophical thought, considered a pre-Qin work.
- The text is divided into two sections: originally the upper section was 《德经》 (De Jing) and lower 《道经》 (Dao Jing), without chapters. Later it was reorganized with the Dao Jing's 37 chapters first, followed by the De Jing, totaling 81 chapters.
- Word counts vary by version: Mawangdui silk manuscripts have ~5,344 characters (Version A) and ~5,342 characters (Version B); Heshanggong version ~5,201 characters; Wang Bi's commentary version 5,162 characters (the modern standard text); Fu Yi's ancient edition ~5,450 characters.
- The text uses philosophical "道德" (dao/de) as its guiding principle, discussing self-cultivation, governance, military affairs, and health/nourishment of life, with politics as the ultimate aim - the "内圣外王" (inner sage, outer king) philosophy.
- Known as the "King of All Classics" (万经之王).

TEXTUAL HISTORY:
- In December 1973, Western Han silk manuscripts of the Dao De Jing were excavated from Mawangdui in Hunan, dated to the Gaodi and Wendi periods.
- In October 1993, bamboo-slip versions were excavated from Tomb No. 1 at Guodian, Jingmen, Hubei (a Warring States Chu tomb), yielding three versions (Groups A, B, C) totaling 2,046 characters with significant differences from the modern text.
- The Guodian discovery proved the text was compiled no later than the mid-Warring States period, refuting the "late compilation" theory of scholars like Liang Qichao, Feng Youlan, Gu Jiegang, and Qian Mu.

PHILOSOPHY:
- Core theme is "道法自然" (Dao follows its own nature / Naturalness).
- "Dao" is the origin and mother of all things in heaven and earth; yin-yang opposition and unity is the essence of all things; things reverse at their extremes.
- Ethically, Laozi advocates purity, selflessness, tranquility, humility, gentleness, and restraint.
- Politically, Laozi advocates "无为而治" (governing by non-action/non-interference), opposing war and violence.
- "De" (virtue) is the development and expression of Dao in ethics; the upper virtue (上德) is characterized by wu wei (non-action).
- The text is noted for critical discussion of its "negative" ideas including historical regression, opposition to wisdom/civilization, and the doctrine of "愚民" (keeping people simple/ignorant).

LITERARY FEATURES:
- Poetic style with parallel structure, rhyme, and rhythmic beauty.
- Rich rhetorical devices: antithesis (对偶), parallelism (排比), metaphor (比喻), rhetorical questions, and chain/enchainment (联珠).
- Sources of numerous idioms and maxims still used today, including: 功成身退 (retire after success), 上善若水 (highest good is like water), 大智若愚 (great wisdom appears foolish), 天网恢恢疏而不漏 (Heaven's net is vast and nothing escapes), 知足常乐 (contentment brings happiness), 宠辱不惊 (unmoved by favor or disgrace).

INFLUENCE:
- Deep influence on traditional Chinese philosophy, science, politics, and religion.
- Per UNESCO statistics, it is the most translated cultural classic after the Bible.
- Per American scholar Misha Tadd's 2019 bibliography, there are over 1,500 translations in 73 languages.
- After the Opium War, British missionaries and sinologists began translating it into English.
- In 1988, US President Reagan quoted "治大国若烹小鲜" (governing a great nation is like cooking a small fish) in his State of the Union address, making the book popular in America; Stephen Mitchell's English translation sold over 550,000 copies in 8 years with a copyright price of $130,000.

The page includes comprehensive historical evaluations from Chinese figures (Sima Tan, Sima Qian, Wang Bi, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Ouyang Xiu, Su Zhe, Lu Xun, Mao Zedong, etc.) and international figures (Joseph Needham, Nietzsche, Kant, Hegel, Tolstoy, Bohr, etc.), as well as extensive lists of historical commentaries/annotations spanning from the pre-Qin to modern eras.

## 《第三十九章》[[查看正文](wiki.pl?if=gb&chapter=987130)] [[修改](instructions/wiki/zh#editing)] [[查看歷史](instructions/wiki/zh#editing)]

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧， |
| 2 | 謙之案：「寧」字，績語堂碑錄因避清帝諱改為「寧」，今據原碑文改正，下同。 |
| 3 | 神得一以靈，穀得一以盈，萬物得一以生， |
| 4 | 嚴可均曰：「萬物」，各本作「萬物」。 |
| 5 | 羅振玉曰：敦煌戊本無此句。 |
| 6 | 謙之案：景福本、範本「萬」亦作「萬」。又陳碧虛曰：「嚴君平本無『萬物得之以生』，並下文『萬物無以生將恐滅』十四字。」 |
| 7 | 侯王得一以為天下正。 |
| 8 | 嚴可均曰：「天下正」，御注、王弼作「下貞」。 |
| 9 | 範應元曰：貞，正也。王弼、郭云同古本。一本「貞」作「正」，亦後人避諱也。河上本作「侯王」。 |
| 10 | 謙之案：傅、範本、柰卷作「王侯」，群書治要、孫盛老子疑問反訊、晉書裴楷傳、書鈔一四九引並作「貞」，嚴遵、河上、顧歡、景福、樓正、慶陽、磻溪、室町及玉篇「一」字下引均作「正」，遂州本作「政」。中都四子本此句作「以天下為正」。 |
| 11 | 王念孫曰：河上本「貞」作「正」，注云：「為天下平正。」念孫案：爾雅曰：「正，長也。」呂氏春秋君守篇「可以為天下正」，高注曰：「正，主也。」「為天下正」，猶洪範言「為天下主」耳。下文「天無以清」，「地無以寧」，即承上文「天得一以清，地得一以寧」言之。又云「侯王無以貴高」，「貴高」二字正承「為天下正」言之，是「正」為君長之義，非平正之義也。王弼本「正」作「貞」，借字耳。 |
| 12 | 東條一堂曰：「為天下貞」，按「貞」一本作「正」，與注乖。下同。貞觀政要刑法第三十一引亦作「正」。 |
| 13 | 彭耜曰：「諸本貞作正，避廟諱。」 |
| 14 | 易順鼎曰：「貞」或作「正」，古字通用。王氏讀書雜志謂此「貞」為借字，似未盡然。易「貞勝者也」，韓注引老子曰：「王侯得一以為天下貞。」王弼周易略例：「制天下之動者，貞夫一者也。」邢注引老子亦作「貞」。文選王元長曲水詩序注引亦作「貞」。是「貞」為本字。 |
| 15 | 勞健曰：「侯王得一以為天下貞」，「貞」字景龍、景福作「正」，開元、傅、範與諸王本皆作「貞」。範注：「貞，正也。一本作正，後人避諱也。」按道藏御注、御疏本原作「正」，疏云：「本或作貞字，貞即正也。」開元石刻乃改從「貞」，範云「後人避諱」，非也。又此章凡「侯王」字，傅、範亦作「王侯」，非也。諸唐本、諸王本、河上本皆作「侯王」，與「貞」字自諧句中韻。 |
| 16 | 謙之案：作「貞」是也。易系辭曰：「天下之動，貞夫一者也。」又曰：「言致其一也。」老子此章言「侯王得一以為天下貞」下，傅、範及釋文下有「其致之一也」，與易義均合。又柰卷及大阪圖書館舊鈔本，均作「天下貞」，狩野直喜謂：「河上公本亦有作『貞』者，蓋自宋刻避帝諱改『貞』作『正』。」今證之以景龍碑文，知「貞」「正」二字古通用，而避諱之說亦非。 |
| 17 | 天無以清，將恐裂；地無以寧，將恐發； |
| 18 | 謙之案：碑文與羅卷此均作「無」，不作「無」，為變例。武內法京敦乙本作「無」。又莊子至樂篇：「天無為以之清，地無為以之寧。」語意本此。 |
| 19 | 劉師培曰：「發」讀為「廢」。說文：「廢，屋頓也。」淮南子覽冥訓「四極廢」，高注：「廢，頓也。」左傳定三年「廢於爐炭」，杜注：「廢，墜也。」頓墜之義，與傾圮同。恐發者，猶言將崩圮也，即地傾之義。「發」為「廢」字之省形。 |
| 20 | 蔣錫昌曰：劉說是。莊子列禦寇「先生既來，曾不發藥乎」，釋文：「發，司馬本作廢。」列子黃帝篇引作「廢」。又繕性「非藏其智而不發也」，御覽逸民部引作「廢」。左傳哀十一年疏引竹書紀年云：「梁惠王廢逢忌之藪以賜民。」漢書地理志引作「發」。均其證也。「發」「廢」雙聲，故可通用。此言天無以清將恐裂，地無以寧將恐廢也。 |
| 21 | 神無以靈，將恐歇；穀無以盈，將恐竭； |
| 22 | 畢沅曰：「竭」，河上公、王弼並作「歇」，案應作「竭」。 |
| 23 | 謙之案：河上公、王弼並作「竭」，上句作「歇」，畢誤校。「歇」，說文：「息也。一曰氣越洩也。」廣雅釋詁二：「歇，洩也。」七發：「精神越洩，百病咸生。」「竭」借為「渴」，「渴，盡也，從水，曼聲。」爾雅釋詁：「涸，渴也。」經傳多以「竭」為之，是竭有涸盡之義。周語「伊、洛竭而夏亡」，注：「涸也。」淮南說林：「淵泉不能竭。」本經：「竭澤而漁。」河上注此：「言谷當有盈縮虛實，不可但欲盈滿無已時，將恐枯竭不為谷。」「竭」與「渴」同義，不必改字。 |
| 24 | 萬物無以生，將恐滅； |
| 25 | 羅振玉曰：敦煌本無此句。 |
| 26 | 侯王無以貴高，將恐蹶。 |
| 27 | 武內義雄曰：景、遂、敦三本「侯王」與上文合，下又同。景、遂二本「貴高」，敦本無「高」字，然下文「貴高」並稱，有「高」字是。 |
| 28 | 羅振玉曰：敦煌本「貞」下有「而」字。 |
| 29 | 謙之案：此句疑有誤文。諸河、王本、顧歡本、磻溪、景福、樓正、室町、柰卷句同此。範本作「王侯無以為貞，將恐溪」，高翿作「侯王無以貞而貴高，將恐蹶」，傅奕作「王侯無以為貞而貴高，將恐溪」，彭耜，趙孟俯同傅本，惟「王侯」作「侯王」。嚴遵同彭本，惟「無以為貞」作「無以為正」。皆川願老子繹解又與嚴遵同。 |

This webpage is from the Chinese Text Project (ctext.org), a digital library of classical Chinese texts. The specific page is the Wiki (維基) section for Chapter 39 (第三十九章) of the "Laozi Daodejing Collated and Explained" (老子道德經校釋, wiki page 974135). 

The content is a scholarly collation (校釋) of the chapter's text, presenting the main lines of the chapter alongside extensive textual criticism and variant readings from numerous scholars and editions. Key content includes:

**Main Text of Chapter 39:**
- The chapter opens with "昔之得一者" (Those who of old obtained the One), listing how Heaven, Earth, spirits, valleys, the ten thousand things, and feudal lords/kings each obtain the One (清/clarity, 寧/tranquility, 靈/spirituality, 盈/fullness, 生/life, 正/uprightness).
- Warns that if any of these lose the One, they will fall into ruin (裂/crack, 發/quake, 歇/cease, 竭/run dry, 滅/perish, 蹶/stumble).
- Includes the famous passages "故貴以賤為本，高以下為基" (Honor has lowliness as its root; highness has lowliness as its foundation) and "不欲琭琭如玉，落落如石" (Does not desire to be tinkling as jade, nor clanging as stone).

**Key Textual Scholarship and Variants:**
- Numerous scholars are quoted on variants, including: 嚴可均, 羅振玉, 王念孫, 東條一堂, 彭耜, 易順鼎, 勞健, 劉師培, 蔣錫昌, 畢沅, 武內義雄, 洪頤烜, 徐鼒, 高延第, 羅運賢, 章炳麟, and 謙之 (the compiler).
- The word "貞" vs. "正" (uprightness) is extensively discussed — the compiler (謙之) concludes "貞" is correct, citing the Book of Changes (易系辭: "天下之動，貞夫一者也"). Several scholars note "貞" was changed to "正" to avoid imperial name taboos (避諱).
- "侯王" vs. "王侯" ordering is debated; 謙之 notes that 傅, 範 versions use "王侯."
- "谷" vs. "轂"/"穀" (grain) in 不穀: Scholars debate whether it means "wheel hub" (車轂) or is a variant of 穀 meaning "good" — concluding it is a humble self-designation (謙辭) of lords/kings, essentially meaning "I am unworthy," with 章炳麟 suggesting "不穀" is a compound phonetic form of "僕" (servant).
- The phrase "數車無車" (numbering a cart, no cart) is extensively discussed. 謙之 argues both "車" and "輿" (and "與") are corruptions of "譽" (fame/reputation), so the text should read "致數譽無譽" (to count reputation - no reputation). This is supported by quoting the Buddhist text Milindapañha (彌蘭王問經 / 那先比丘經), which contains the famous dialogue about the parts of a chariot not being the chariot — demonstrating Buddhist influence on this interpretation.
- "琭琭如玉，落落如石" variants: 琭/碌/淥/祿/鹿 and 落/珞/硌 are all shown to be phonetic variants; scholars (高延第, 謙之) interpret them as meaning "following along with others" (隨從) versus "aloof/unusual" (落落難合).

**Poetic/Rhyme Analysis:**
The chapter's rhymes are analyzed (江氏韻讀): 清、寧、靈、盈、生、貞 rhyme in the 耕 (geng) group; 裂、發、歇、竭、滅、溪 rhyme in the 祭 (ji) group; 邪、乎、車 rhyme in the 魚 (yu) group; 琭、玉 rhyme in the 侯 group; 落、石 rhyme in the 魚 group.

**Character Counts of Various Editions:**
- 景龍碑 (Jinglong stele): 133 characters, no chapter division
- 敦煌本 (Dunhuang manuscript): 132 characters
- 河上本 (Heshang Gong): 135 characters, titled "法本第三十九"
- 王本 (Wang Bi): 134 characters, titled "三十九章"
- 傅本 (Fu Yi): 139 characters
- 範本 (Fan Yingyuan): 136 characters, titled "昔之得一章第三十九"

## 道德經開題序訣義疏

如内内

有有終，則終不成終；□□□□，則始始不不

成成始。始所以無始，終不成終，是故無終。故

玄妙内篇云：老子不生不㓕，無始無終。序訣

云：老子之号，因玄而出，在天也之先，無衰老

之期，故曰老子。㩀教而言，有此三觧。約理而

辯，只自是一。㩀教即是逗機。故西昇云：智亦

不獨生皆須對因。緣，對緣之義，何止在三。趣

有三機，而作三説。若其得理，既不滯三，亦不

執一。第二名氏者，案文始内傳云：尹憙稽。

首：敢問大人姓字。老子曰：吾姓字眇眇，非可

備説。今姓李名耳，字伯陽，外字老聃。而有胎

經八十一年。曽逍遥李樹之下，思閒清風以

袪塵。或乃剖左腋而生老子，仙童王女，手執

香花，侍衛左右。玄妙即指樹云：𬼘可爲汝姓。

神仙傳云：老子生而能言，目指李樹爲姓。上

元經云：李母晝卧，見五色珠大如彈丸，自天

而下，因而吞之，遂即有胎。陸先生云：老子初

生，却行九步，因即能言。但内外經書説者非

一，今不具載。名耳者，老子耳無輪郭，顯示異

相因以爲名也。字伯陽者，伯，長也。陽，生也。言

聖人應世，利益弘多，方欲長飬黎元，生成庶

品，故經云：生之畜之，長之育之也。外自聃者，

言舌聃聃然，既長且廣，所以字聃也。史記云：

老子之子名宗，仕魏，封於段干宗之子汪，汪

子宫，宫玄孫瑕，瑕子解，仕漢爲膠西王太傅。

第三法體者，案九天生神經云：聖人以玄天

始三氣爲體，言同三天之妙氣也。臧宗道又

用三一爲聖人應身。所言三一者，一精、二神、

三氣也。精者，靈智慧照之心；神者，無方不測

之用。氣者，色象形相之法。經云：視之不見名。

曰夷，精也。聽之不聞，名曰希，神也；博之不得，

名曰微，氣也。總𬼘三法爲一聖體經云：此三

者不可致詰，故混而爲一也。但老君以三一

爲身，身有真應之别，而解者義有三家：

第一云：散一以爲三，是聖人應；混三以歸

一，是聖人真。第二云：三之與一俱是應，非

三非一，乃是真。爲三一俱是數故也。第三

云：豈有離名數之外，别有無名數之真耶？即

𬼘三一非三一是真，非三一而三一是應；非

三一而三一之應，𬼘應是真，應三一而非三

一之真，𬼘真是應應。真真之真，不可定言頁，

真應之應，不可定言應。所以非真非應，而應

而真。伹聖人赴感，逗機應物，或寄人閒，或生

天上，隨方顯見，相好不同，故昇玄經云：於彼

淨土，相好嚴儀，處𬼘多𬊡形，同下斯源。夫能

天能人者，豈天人之所能㢤？必非天非人，故

能天能人耳。且妙體希夷，卒難詳究，今直據

周時一應論。老君容狼者，案葛抱朴引朱韜

玉札云：老子黄色，美眉，廣顙，長耳，大目，疏齒，

方口厚脣，額有叁午達理，日角月玄，鼻有雙

骨，耳有三門，足蹈二五，手挹十文。此是託神

李母，下爲周師之相也，雖復真應，不同而俱。

以自然爲體，故莊云：常因自然而不益生。序

訣云：老子體自然而然，生乎太無之先也。

第四時莭者，案葛洪神仙傳云：老子以伏羲

時爲欎華，神農時爲緣因，祝融時爲傅豫，黄

帝時爲廣成子。而逗機赴感，應變隨時，顯晦

無方，今不詳載。故序訣云：世人謂老子當始

於周代。老子之号，始於無數之刼，甚窈窈冥

𡨋，眇邈久遠。又云：開闢以前，復下爲國師代。

代不休，人，莫能知之。是知老君出世，非止於

周眀矣。但前刼遐曠，存而不論。今且據在周

託生時莭者，案劉向、嵇康、皇甫謐並云生於

殷末，爲文王師。序訣云：老子以上皇元年太

歲丁夘，正月十二日丙午，下爲周師。既爲文

王作師，理當生於殷末，故下爲周師，即殷之

丁夘歲也。案文始内傳、仙公序訣皆云：老子

以無極元年太歲癸丑，五月壬午，去周西度。

而解者多云是幽王時出，開𬼘未可依准。何

者？今檢幽王庚申年立，立十一年，爲犬戎所

滅，十一年内，竟無癸丑。以前七年癸丑乃是

宣王之時。又國語云：幽王二年，三川震，岐山

崩。伯陽父曰：周將亡矣，不過十年。若以宣王

時出關者，則不應見三川震，岐山崩也。尋平

王宜咎東遷洛邑，以辛未歲立，立世三年，方

次癸，丑案：玉緯云：是𬼘時出關也。臧玄静云

西出壟關，猶據幽王在長安之歲，恐當謬也。

既平王時出關，則是西度函谷，故出塞記云：

西出函函谷谷關。關今在陝州桃林縣南十

里，有故關門是也。又尋漢文以前，直云无年

二年，未有别号。漢武之世，方号元鼎元朔。今

序訣云：老子以上皇元年下爲周師，至無極

元年，去周西度者，此兼取人閒世代，配諸天

年号，理非流俗所知，例如經中朱靈、開皇等

号也。出塞記及玄妙内篇，文始内傅並云關

令尹喜預瞻，見紫雲西邁，知有道人當過，即

以其年十二月廿五日，老子乘青牛薄板車，

徐甲爲御，到關也。至廿八日日中，授喜道德

經上下卷。臨去之際，又説西昇事畢，乃示見

通，通，騰空數丈，存亡恍惚，老少無恒，於是適

彼罽賓，逗機行化。故皇甫謐云：老子西之流

沙，作浮屠經以化俗也。文始内傳又云：老

子出關，周流八十一國，後至罽賓，化胡也。自

紫氣浮關，青牛西度，老君覆還東夏，凡有三

時。一者，尋仲尼以周靈王廿一年庚戊歲十

月庚子夜生，仍師於老君，伏膺問道。故史記

云：吾今日見老子，其猶龍乎！又家語云：周之

老聃，吾之師也。二者，𧹞王時，授干室太平經，

并百八十𢦶，治國治身脩飬要訣。三者，漢安

時，於蜀授天師正一眀威之教。于時蕭鼓雲

駕，浮空而下，自稱周之柱史，太上所遣。但神功

不測，應感無方，或見聖容，或示凡迹，千變萬

化，不可思議，豈得以朝菌之齡，語大椿之壽

㢤？尋内外經典，證據極多，皆云西□戎夷，竟

無死迹。唯莊周云：老聃死，秦夫吊之者，斯假

設之辭耳。欲眀死生之道均齊，凡聖之理泯

一，猶如鴻蒙雲將之談，蓋寓言也。今雍州盩

屋縣有樓觀者，即是尹真人之故宅。宅南有

山阜，名老子陵，俗傳云是老君墓，何誣之甚

也！然墓者，埋葬也。老君既無死迹，豈有墓乎？

當是於𬼘山上西昇輕舉，後人追記聖德，因

号曰老子陵。且老君在周，隱身卑位，縱爲陵

墓，理亦不高。今撿𬼘陵，上聳數千尺，周迴數

百步，假使帝王國力，恐未能然。以此推量，固

非嫁墓眀矣。

第五方所者，案玄妙内篇、出塞記，葛稚川、皇

甫謐並云：老君生於陳國苦縣瀨鄉曲仁里

渦水之陰。而説者或云楚國，或云楚縣，或稱

陳群，或稱豫州者，尋楚以熊繹爲始封之君，

其地運楚，故稱楚國。又春秋之日，縣大而郡

小，以郡屬縣，故云楚縣。伹陳則太䁺之墟，都

於菀丘之側，案禹别九州，則豫州之分，故稱。

豫州。又武王伐紂，封舜後胡公滿於陳，以備

三恪，故稱陳國。逯漢高祖滅秦，仍改陳國爲

淮陽郡，則郡大縣小，故有陽夏、寧平、苦柘四

縣，屬淮陽也。至後漢章帝，又改淮陽爲陳郡。

雖復時代遷貿，名号不同，其於處所，祇自是

一。漢桓帝夢見老子，乃詔陳相邊韶，於老君

生處建碑立祠。祠側即有李母廟，虚無堂，左

帶靈溪，右環渦水，前後顯敝，寔惟勝地。唐貞

觀十一年，有詔以皇家宗祏，系自老君，給

廟户廿人修葺。院宇皇甫。謐云：老子，楚之相

人者。今廟北有相城，故知相是地名，非官号

也。

後顯所説正法又開爲五，第道德、第二釋。

經，第三宗體，第四、文數，第五章卷。

第一道德者，道是圓通之妙境，德是至忘之

聖智，非。境無以導智，非智無以昭境。境智

相會，故稱道德。然境智智境，不一不異，而異

而一，故西昇云：道德混沌，玄妙同也。且古來

解道，极有不同，今汎舉大綱，義開五别。所言

五者，第一、依訓釋，第二、依義釋，第三、待

對釋，第四、所表釋，第五、無方釋。

第一、依訓釋者，道，無也，德有也。故輔嗣云：道无。

又解云：道，道也，德，德也。今眀道之爲名，窮理盡

性，不復可加，故非訓釋之所能𥁞。直置道以道

爲義，義自多。合不繁曲碎，更爲他解。故宣尼觧

易須、晉二卦，云：須，須也。晉，晉也。

荑二、依義釋者，道以虚通爲義，德以尅獲受

名爲道能通物，物能得道故也。篤論道物，亦不

一不異，故經云：道之爲物，唯恍惚唯。又莊云：

言而足，則終日言而盡道；言而不足，則終日言

而𥁞物也。

第三待對釋者，道以德爲義，德以道爲義，非

道无以通德，非德无以顯道故也。又解云：道

人物爲義，德以喪爲義，皆相顯對故也。

第四、所表𥼶者，道以不道爲義，德以不德爲

義，所以説道以彰於不道，所以説德以表於

不德。故經云：上德不德，是以有德。莊云：不言

之辯，不道之道。若有能𬼘，之謂天府。嚴君平

云：不道之道，不德之德，正之无也。是知説道

説德，以表於不道不德也。

第五、无方釋者，耶教正言，患應自然，稊稷凡甓，

无非至道。所以道无不在，所在皆通，隨物方

圓，曽无執滯。故莊云：夫道未始有封，言未始

有常也。

第二釋經者，尋三洞尊文七部玄教，討其

題目，僉号曰：經。是知經者，法教之總名，至人

之洪𦳛。經之爲義，大矣㢤，蓋群品之舟𦩃者

也。但經乃多種，大略有三：一者、五德、三元凝

空雲篆，垂芒，八角妙氣之文；二者、空林紫筆，

金蕳玉字，苞以鳳文之緼，藏於七寶玄臺，或

在山洞之中。或在諸天之上。三者，簡策縑紙。

篆𮇬隨時，傳授流通，見行於世。雖復有此三

迹，粗妙不同，而皆是聖言，並詮至理，咸能治

病，悉名良藥。但經之義訓，訓亦多塗，舉其樞

要，略爲四釋。所言四者，一由、二徑，三法、四常。

第一訓由者，言三世天尊，十方太上，莫不因由

此經而得成道。

第二訓俓者，言能開通萬物，導達四生，任學

者之津梁，寔脩真之要俓。

第三訓法者，音趣玄妙，能所精微，可以軌則

蒼生，揩模衆聖也。

第四訓常者，言非但理致深遠，湛寂凝然，抑

亦萬代百王不刊之術。具斯四義，故稱爲經

也。而言序訣者，序，述也。訣，斷也。序述聖人之

旨訣，斷學者之疑也。禮記云：作者之謂聖，述

者之謂眀。仙公有聖眀之德，故作序以述經旨。

第三、宗體者，夫釋義解經，宜識其宗致。然古

今注疏，玄情各别，而嚴君平旨歸以玄虚爲

宗，顧徵君堂詰以无爲爲宗，孟智周、臧玄静

以道德爲宗，鿄武帝以非有非无爲宗。晉世

孫登云託重玄以寄宗。雖復衆家不同，今以

孫氏爲正，宜以重玄爲宗，无爲爲體。所言玄

者，深遠之名，亦是不滯之義。言至深至遠，不

滯不著，既不滯有，又不滯无，豈唯不滯於滯，

亦乃不滯於不滯。百非四句，都无所滯，乃曰

重玄。故經云：玄之又玄，衆妙之門。隱訣頌云：

玄玄至道宗，上德體洪无也。而言无爲者，鏡

像蒼生，蒭狗萬物，雖復揮斥八極，而神氣无

變，故爲則无爲，无爲則爲，豈曰拱默而稱无

爲㢤？故經云：損之又損之，以至於无爲。又云：

道常无。爲而无不爲序。訣云：无爲之文，汗之

不辱，餝之不榮也。

第四文數者，尋青牛發軫，紫氣浮關，真人

尹氏親承聖旨當爾之日，止授五千文，故序。

訣云，於是作道德二篇五千文，上下經焉。是

知五千之文，先有定數，後人流傳，亟生改易。

案河上公本，長五百四十餘字，多是兮乎者

也，蓋逗機應物，故文餝其辭耳。但高士逸人，

多尚其業，好異之徒，例皆添糅，遂使魚目亂

珠，玉石无辨。太極仙公欲崇本抑末，乃示以

本文，止五千字，故序訣云：吾已於諸天校定，得

聖人本文者乎。今所講誦，多依葛本，其葛本

字體，亦有訛濫，事由鈔寫，差錯，豈關仙公。所

爲至。若以愚爲娱以，仚爲喘如。斯之文，愚所

未喻，唯當研尋玄旨，擇善而從，无容膠柱刻

船，域心固執項。諸學者搜蕳定數，云少一字，不

滿五千。解者不同，而罕得厥中。或言關𬼘一字。

因象太一之无，或云少此一字，以眀絶言之理，

斯並苟爲異端，妄生。抑度。竊尋經意，豈其然

乎？只是經中卅輻也。且古者三十分爲二文，

今時卅總爲一字，有𬼘離合，故少一文也。

第五章卷者，此一部妙經，五千奥典，上下二卷，

八十一章，各有表眀，咸資法象，豈徒然㢤！良

有以也。故八十一章，象太陽之極數；上下二

卷，法兩儀之生育。是以上經眀道以法天，下

經眀德以法地。而天數奇，故上經有卅七章；

地數偶，故下經有卌四章。經云：有物混成，先

天地生。莊云：神鬼神帝，生天生地。西昇云：大

曠蕩，无不制圍。是知至道虚通，括囊无外，豈

止陰陽天地而已。今眀立教利物，故寄之兩

明朋明明明五篇。五明前朋

略明五篇。

明五篇者，輕重相形，放名爲篇。又云：篇者，𩔫也。又説抣等名萹益

篇，各具三抣，故名篇。

This webpage presents the full text of "道德經開題序訣義疏" (Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Opening Preface and Secret Formulas of the Daodejing), attributed to Cheng Xuanying (成玄英) of the Tang Dynasty. This is a scholarly annotation of the Daodejing from the Dunhuang manuscript P.Ch.2353, hosted on the Shidianguji (识典古籍) digital library platform.

The text provides a detailed commentary organized into five main sections on the Dao (道):

1. **On the name "Laozi" (老子)**: Explains that Laozi (Old Master) is non-begotten and non-annihilated, without beginning or end, citing the Xuanmiao neipian (玄妙内篇) and Xujue (序訣). The name derives from the Dao (to be "born before heaven"). His surname Li (李), personal name Er (耳), courtesy name Boyang (伯陽), and style Lao Dan (老聃) are explained — Er because his ears lacked proper contours (an auspicious sign), and Dan because his tongue was long and broad. The text provides genealogical details: son Zong served Wei and was enfeoffed at Duangan; descendants through Wang, Gong, and Xia; Jie served Han as Grand Tutor of Jiaoxi.

2. **On the dharma body (法體)**: Laozi's body consists of the Three-Ones (三一): Jing (精/essence, wisdom), Shen (神/spirit, immeasurable function), and Qi (氣/breath, visible form) — corresponding to the three Daoist states of Yi (invisible), Xi (inaudible), and Wei (intangible). Three interpretations of the relationship between the three and the one are discussed.

3. **On the seasons/times (時莭)**: Laozi manifested in different forms across ages (as Yuhua in Fuxi's time, Yuanyin in Shennong's time, Fuyu in Zhurong's time, Guangchengzi in the Yellow Emperor's time). The text argues Laozi was born at the end of the Shang dynasty to serve as King Wen's teacher, citing conflicting dates (玉纬 says the Shang dingmao year; the first year of the Shanghuang era). He went west through Hanggu Pass during King Ping's reign, when Guanling Yin Xi (關令尹喜) received him. Per the Chusai ji (出塞記), on the 25th day of the 12th month Laozi arrived riding an ox pulled cart driven by Xu Jia, and on the 28th day at noon transmitted the Daodejing in two volumes to Yin Xi. Other accounts say Laozi traveled through 81 kingdoms, reaching Kāpiśa (罽賓) to convert the barbarians (化胡). The text ends by refuting claims of Laozi's death — the "Laozi's tomb" in Zhouzhi County, Yongzhou is explained as a commemorative marker because he ascended into the heavens without dying.

4. **On his birthplace (方所)**: Laozi was born at Quren Village, Lixiang, Kuxian, Chen State, on the northern side of the Wo River (渦水之陰). The text explains the various historical names of this region (Chen/Chu/Chu County/Yuzhou). Emperor Huan of Han had a stele and shrine erected at his birthplace; in the 11th year of Zhenguan (637 CE), the Tang Emperor granted 20 households for its maintenance.

5. **The main exposition is then divided into five parts**: On Dao and De (道德), explanation of "Jing" (經), the sect's essence (宗體), the number of characters (文數), and chapter divisions (章卷).

Key arguments include:
- **On Dao (道)**: Five interpretive approaches — 1) by traditional gloss (unable to fully capture its meaning), 2) by meaning (Dao is emptiness/penetration, De is attainment), 3) by contrast (each defined by the other), 4) by reference (speaking of Dao to manifest non-Dao), 5) by unboundedness (Dao is everywhere, adapting without fixed attachment).
- **On "Jing" (經)**: Four meanings — 1) by cause (all achieve enlightenment through it), 2) by path (the essential route to cultivation), 3) by model (pattern for all beings), 4) by constancy (immutable through ages).
- **On sect's essence (宗體)**: Various commentators set different sectarian bases (Yan Junping: mysterious emptiness; Gu: non-action; Meng Zhizhou and Zang Xuanjing: Dao and De; Emperor Wu of Liang: neither being nor non-being). Cheng Xuanying adopts Sun Deng's position: **"以重玄爲宗，无爲爲體"** (Chongxuan/Double Mystery as the sect, non-action as the body) — neither attached to being nor non-being, nor even to non-attachment: "百非四句，都无所滯，乃曰重玄" (beyond all negations and four propositions, unattached to all, this is called Chongxuan).
- **On character count (文數)**: The original was exactly 5,000 characters. Later transmissions added over 540 characters (mostly connective particles like "xi"). The "Shaozi Yi" discrepancy (the text being one character short of 5,000) is explained by the archaic script combining "卅" (thirty) as one character versus two characters ("三十") in modern script.
- **On chapters/scrolls (章卷)**: The text has 2 scrolls and 81 chapters, symbolically matching the extreme number of the sun (太陽之極數); two scrolls model the two instruments (Heaven and Earth); the upper scroll (37 chapters) illuminates Dao, modeling Heaven (odd numbers); the lower scroll (44 chapters) illuminates De, modeling Earth (even numbers).

The text cites numerous classical sources including the Xuanshen jing, Shengxuan jing, Wen Shi neizhuan, Ge Hong's Shenxian zhuan, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), and Zhuangzi, and discusses important geographical references such as the Hanggu Pass in Shanzhou, the Louguantai (Tower Observatory) in Zhouzhi County, and the Laozi shrine in Chen State.

<summary>
This webpage is an academic journal article record from an Airiti Library database (a Chinese academic platform). The article is "成玄英《道德經義疏》重玄思想之探析" (Exploration and Analysis of Cheng Xuan-ying's Twofold Mystery Thoughts in Dao De Jing Yi Shu), written by 林文彬 (Wen-Ping Lin), published in 《興大中文學報》(Journal of the Chinese Department of National Chung Hsing University), Issue 29, June 2011, pages 179-192. DOI: https://doi.org/10.30091/JCDNCHU.201106.0007.

The article examines Cheng Xuan-ying (成玄英), an important representative of the School of Twofold Mystery (重玄學派) in the Early Tang Dynasty. The Dao De Jing Yi Shu is his foundational work, which uses the "Twofold Mystery" (重玄) concept to establish an ontological realm of unobstructed reason (虛通之理) and emphasize cultivation of the mind and nature through wisdom (智悟).

The paper identifies three academic contributions of the work: (1) Regarding Laozi studies, it links academia and religion while summarizing predecessors' theories; (2) In Chinese intellectual history, it represents a third period of Taoist thought development after Wei-Jin Xuanxue, serving as a fusion of Xuanxue (Neo-Taoism) and Buddhist Prajñā (Wisdom); (3) In terms of influence, it is the most philosophically significant school in Taoist history, influencing Song and Yuan dynasty Inner Alchemy (Neidan) and the Science of Mind-Nature, and likely enlightening Neo-Confucianism development.

The historical context notes that Sun Deng of the Eastern Jin Dynasty first annotated Laozi using the Twofold Mystery concept, and from the Southern and Northern Dynasties through the Sui and Tang Dynasties, many Taoists used it to comment on Laozi and Zhuangzi, forming the School of Twofold Mystery.

Keywords: 成玄英 (Cheng Xuan-ying); 重玄 (Twofold Mystery); 道德經 (Dao De Jing); 虛通之理 (unobstructed reason); 眾生之性 (nature of beings).

ABSTRACT (Chinese): Sun Deng of the Eastern Jin Dynasty was the first to annotate the Laozi using the concept of "Twofold Mystery" (重玄). The book's academic status has three aspects: (1) For the study of Laozi, it links academic and religious thought and summarizes previous theories; (2) In the history of Chinese thought, it represents the third period of Taoist thought development after Wei-Jin Xuanxue, serving as a fusion of Neo-Taoism and Buddhist Prajñā; (3) In terms of influence, it represents the most philosophically rich school in Taoist history, influencing Song-Yuan Inner Alchemy (Neidan) and mind-nature studies, and possibly enlightening the development of Neo-Confucianism (Song-Ming lixue).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic paper (published in *Studies in Sinology* / 《中國學術年刊》, Volume 36, Autumn issue, September 2014, pp. 19-42, ISSN 1021-7851) by Chiang Shu-chun (National Taiwan Normal University, Department of Chinese) examining the theory of mind-nature (心性論述, xinxing) in Cheng Xuan-ying's (成玄英) commentary on the Daodejing, titled 《道德經開題序訣義疏》 (Dao Der Jing Kai Ti Xu Jue Yi Shu).

CORE ARGUMENT: The paper analyzes the theoretical structure of Cheng Xuan-ying's discussions of mind (心), nature (性), emotions (情), and desire (欲) in his Daodejing commentary, and explores their deep relationship with Buddhist thought. In the early Tang dynasty, Buddhist mind-nature theory had matured, and Daoist Chongxuan (double mystery, 重玄) studies required development of mind-nature theory, leading Daoist commentators on the Laozi to focus on "mind" and "nature" topics while integrating Buddhist thought.

THREE OBSERVATIONAL APPROACHES (the paper's structure):
1. "Dao-Nature Continuity" (道、性一貫) as the ideological premise: Cheng holds that "Dao" and "nature" are one — the innate natural nature/true nature of all beings derives from the transcendent Dao. He explains "Dao" as "void and penetrating" (虛通), and states "所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也" (the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings). He uses "principle" (理) to characterize Dao, marking a major breakthrough in his Laozi scholarship. Dao's subtle principle, when internalized in humans and things, becomes their nature; hence to "preserve and return to true nature" is the path of self-cultivation.
2. "Forgetting Emotions to Complete Nature" (忘情全性) as the master thesis: In commenting on "道可道，非常道," Cheng details the relations among Dao, nature, emotions, form (形), qi (炁), and spirit (神). Since "性動為情" (nature stirring becomes emotion) and emotions contaminate, nature is damaged and distances from Dao. The key statement: "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性" (Dao gives me life, emotions destroy me; if one forgets emotions, nature is made complete). The dialectical process runs: Dao-Nature originally one → Dao-Nature separated (through stirring emotions, deluded mind chasing external objects) → Dao-Nature re-united through cultivation ("復性歸道" / returning nature to Dao as ultimate aim).
3. "Deluded Mind," "Emotional Contamination," and "Attachment to Objects" (妄心、情染、滯境) and the path of cultivation: Cheng identifies deluded mind, emotional contamination, and attachment to sensory objects as the root causes of losing true nature. His cultivation approach incorporates extensive Buddhist concepts — "empty" (空), "mind abiding nowhere" (無所住心), "three karmas clean" (三業清靜), "liberation of six sense faculties" (六根解脫), the bodhisattva ideal, "three poisons" (貪嗔痴), "dependent arising and emptiness" (緣起性空), etc. He reframes the Daoist sage as a bodhisattva-like figure; explains "returning to root/stillness/mandate" (歸根復命); and advocates for "復於真性，反於惠命" (returning to true nature and inherent mandate).

CONCLUSIONS (two observations):
1. The mind-nature discourse of early Tang Chongxuan studies may have independently influenced the mid-Tang Confucian revival (e.g., Li Ao's (李翱) 《復性書》/ "Essay on Restoring Nature," which also advocates "滅情復性" / extinguishing emotions to restore nature). The paper argues the theory of "restoring nature" (復性) was initiated by Cheng Xuan-ying well before Li Ao, challenging the view that Laozi mind-nature interpretation only fully developed in the Song dynasty.
2. The paper highlights the distinctive features of Cheng Xuan-ying's mind-nature discourse in the 《義疏》 and evaluates his value and status in the history of Laozi scholarship — characterizing the early Tang Chongxuan mind-nature theory as marked by Buddhist-Daoist mutual influence, whereas Song Confucian-Laozi interpretation turned toward Confucian-Daoist convergence.

KEY SCHOLARS CITED: Li Gang (李剛) argues Cheng's theory of restoring nature is richer than Li Ao's and scattered across his Laozi/Zhuangzi commentaries; Tang Yi-jie (湯一介) sees Chongxuan philosophy moving from ontology to mind-nature philosophy, similar to Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism (especially Cheng-Zhu), urging attention to the Chongxuan-Song Neo-Confucianism relationship; Dong En-lin divides Tang Laozi studies into three stages (early: Chongxuan with Buddhist coloring; middle: Tang Xuanzong's politicization; late: compilations by Qiang Siqi and Du Guangting). The paper used the Yan Ling-feng (嚴靈峯) edition of the reconstructed 《義疏》 as primary text.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Chinese Text Project (ctext.org), specifically the wiki section of the Chinese Philosophy Digital Project, presenting the text "道德真經玄德纂疏卷一" (Volume 1 of the Moral Classic's Dark Virtue Compilation Commentary). This is a Daoist commentary on the Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) compiled by Xiqiang Si (濛陽強思齊), featuring annotations from Tang Emperor Xuanzong (唐玄宗, imperial commentary), He Shang Gong (河上公), Yan Junping (嚴君平), Li Rong (李榮), and Cheng Xuanying (成玄英).

The text opens with an introduction describing the Daodejing as the crown of the three teachings and leader of all scriptures. The first chapter (道可道章第一) is divided into four sections: (1) marking the principle and teaching, (2) broadly clarifying root and traces, (3) distinguishing the two contemplations (of Existence and Non-existence), and (4) unifying the "double mystery" (重玄) principle.

Key content includes extensive commentary on the opening lines: "道可道，非常道" (The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao) and "名可名，非常名" (The name that can be named is not the eternal name). The commentary explores the concept of the Three Ones (三一: essence, spirit, and qi) as the body of Laozi, discusses creation from primordial qi (元氣), and explains that the eternal Dao transcends speech, form, sound, and thought.

The second chapter (天下皆知章第二) addresses how "when all under heaven know beauty as beauty, ugliness arises" and "when all know goodness as goodness, non-goodness arises." Commentators discuss how relative concepts (existence/non-existence, difficulty/ease, long/short, high/low, sound/voice) are all empty of inherent reality, citing Zhuangzi and other sources. The text concludes with the "double mystery" concept (玄之又玄), where one must abandon attachment not only to existence and non-existence but also to the mystery itself as the gate to all wonders (眾妙之門).

The page uses Traditional Chinese and is part of the wiki-based collaborative editing system of the Chinese Text Project, with the URN identifier ctp:ws822537.
</summary>

This article, published in the Shanghai Jiao Tong University newspaper's "Siyuan Lake" column (Issue 1700, March 12, 2021, edited by Wang Bingyu), was written by Niu Jinhai of the School of Biomedical Engineering. It discusses the study of the Tao Te Ching (Dao De Jing) and its famous sayings on governance.

The article first examines the textual history of the Tao Te Ching, noting that the original work is lost and surviving versions are copies. It identifies three important versions: the Jin Dynasty Wang Bi commentary edition, the Mawangdui silk manuscripts (甲乙本) from Changsha, Hunan, and the Guodian bamboo slips (甲乙丙 groups) from Hubei. A scholar named "Xu Feng Qingyu" proposed a "dialectical version" synthesizing these sources. The article notes that the original opening line was "道可道，非恒道" (Tao that can be spoken is not eternal Tao), but was changed to "非常道" to avoid the taboo of Emperor Liu Heng of the Han Dynasty. "恒" means eternal while "常" means ordinary or common.

The article discusses the history of commentaries on the Tao Te Ching, beginning with Han Feizi's "解老" and "喻老" (circa 245 BC, about 240 years after the original), followed by Heshang Gong's "老子章句," Yan Zun's "老子注," and Wang Bi's works. The commentaries by Han Fei, Heshang Gong, and Wang Bi are considered closest to the original meaning. The article addresses the philosophical paradox that the Tao Te Ching opens with "道可道，非恒道" (the speakable Tao is not eternal Tao), yet the work itself is written down. 【成书过程】唐玄宗因认为以往各家对《道德经》的注疏"并未精当，有失玄元妙旨"，担心"无为之理将失"，而决定亲自作注。他一生两度注释《道德经》：开元二十三年（735年，时年51岁）首次完成《御注道德经》并颁之全国，诏令天下"士庶家藏一本，劝令习读"，此次采用河上公本《老子》为底本；约二十年后（天宝十四年，755年）进行第二次注疏，称《道德经真经疏》，因对河上公本不满意而改用王弼本为底本，并再次亲自作序颁于天下。

【内容结构】全书共四卷，分《道经》上下、《德经》上下各二卷，总计八十一章，每章以开头三五字为章名，依从古本。唐玄宗改定章句，"凡言道者类之上卷，言德者类之下卷"。流传中存在二卷本（如《新唐书·艺文志》所载）与四卷本（《道藏》本）之别。

【主要思想】御注的根本宗旨在于"理身理国"，核心是阐发老子的无为之理，并发展了这一哲学，具体体现在君德官德思想、民本与教化思想、"国际交往"思想及军事战争哲学中的自然无为、慈爱于人、节俭爱费、谦柔不争、公平无私等主张。

【刊刻与流传】开元二十三年（735年），唐玄宗采纳道门威仪司马秀建议，诏令天下各州在主要大道观设立石台，刊刻勒石此注，以使其"晓谕天下，传之久远"。注本曾在全国多地刻石留存，包括成都、阌乡、荆州、怀州、遂州、易州、邢州、苏州等处。后世主要流传版本有易州本和邢州本。至今在河南鹿邑太清宫、河北易县、邢台市、江苏镇江焦山、陕西周至县等地仍存有唐代留下的道德经碑幢，其中鹿邑太清宫的碑刻即"开元神武皇帝《道德经》注碑"。明人焦竑《老子翼》卷七记载："唐玄宗既注《老子》，始改定章句为《道德经》……刻石涡口老子庙中"。2024年有研究著作《唐玄宗御注〈道德经〉心解》出版。

The work is included in the Zheng Tong Dao Zang (正统道藏) canon under the Dong Shen Bu Yu Jue category (洞神部玉诀类), and appears at sutra number 680 in the Dao Zang Ti Yao index, located in volume 368 of the Hanfenlou edition, volume 20 of the Xinwenfeng edition, and volume 12 of the Sanjia edition. It is also included in volume 9 of the Zhonghua Daozang under the Four Supplementary Scriptures section.

The book begins with a self-authored preface (自序) in which Lu Xisheng critiques various earlier commentators on Laozi's teachings. He argues that Yang Zhu (杨朱) adhered to Laozi's substance but fell short by excessively valuing the body and despising material things; Zhuangzi (庄周) mastered Laozi's function but went too far by seeking to abandon sageliness and discard wisdom; Shen Buhai and Han Feizi (申韩) lost Laozi's reputation through harsh and punitive governance; and Wang Bi and He Yan (王何) lost Laozi's way by falling into empty nihilism and indolence. Lu considered Sima Qian (司马迁) to be the closest approximation of true Laozi philosophy among ancient writers.

Lu Xisheng further develops his core thesis by connecting Laozi with three sages: he claims Laozi shares the same origin (同原) as Fu Xi, who drew the Eight Trigrams, depicted all phenomena, explored the principles of life, and followed the harmony of virtue; that Laozi shares the overarching lineage (通其宗) with King Wen, who observed the I Ching's yin-yang movements, valued strength and change while emphasizing moderation; and that Laozi's views align in power/application (与其合其权) with Confucius, who emulated Yao and Shun, modeled the Zhou founders Wen and Wu, and guided the people through benevolence and righteousness. Lu concludes that Laozi "transformed and connected with, turned back and merged with" all three sages, making him "utterly divine" (至神). The entire work combines Confucian and Taoist thought to present a political philosophy, making it an important source for late Tang intellectual and ideological history.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an annotated analysis of the classical Chinese Daoist quote "谷神不死，是谓玄牝" (gu shen bu si, shi wei xuan pin), which is attributed to the Han dynasty commentator Heshang Gong (河上公) and sourced from the "老子道德經" (Dao De Jing), specifically the "成象" (Cheng Xiang) chapter six of the SBCK (四部叢刊) edition based on the Changshu Qu family's Song dynasty print.

The quote is categorized under the theme of "无为自然" (Wu Wei / natural action) with the genre being classical prose (古文).

Key content elements:
- Original quote: "谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之门，是谓天地根。绵绵若存，用之不勤。" (The valley spirit never dies; this is called the mysterious feminine. The gate of the mysterious feminine is called the root of heaven and earth. Continuous, as if existing, yet functioning without exertion.)
- The translation provided: "虚空神妙的道，永恒不灭，这就是玄妙的母体。" (The empty and mysterious Dao is eternal and indestructible; this is the mysterious maternal source.)
- Context note: This sentence is described as one of the core expressions of the chapter, elaborating the eternal and original nature of the Dao, reflecting Laozi's profound thinking on the origin of the universe.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之门，是谓天地根。绵绵若存，用之不勤。, 虚空神妙的道，永恒不灭，这就是玄妙的母体。 (The empty and mysterious Dao is eternal and indestructible; this is the mysterious maternal source.), 阐述道的永恒与本源特性，是老子对宇宙生成根源的深刻思考。 (It elaborates the eternal and original nature of the Dao, reflecting Laozi's profound thinking on the origin of the universe.)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Daoism Culture Center Database (道教文化中心資料庫) provides an entry on 《老子道德经开题序诀义疏》 (Laozi Daode Jing Kaiti Xujue Yishu), a work on the Daodejing (Laozi) written by Cheng Xuanying (成玄英), a Daoist scholar of the early Tang Dynasty. The work originally comprised seven volumes, as recorded in the New Book of Tang (《新唐书》) and Comprehensive Treatises on Literature (《通志》). The text was not included in the Zhengtong Daoist Canon (《正统道藏》). Existing copies include three Tang dynasty Dunhuang manuscript fragments (P2353, S5887, and P2517). Selections of Cheng Xuanying's commentary also appear in other works such as 《道德真经注疏》 and 《道德真经玄德纂疏》. The modern scholar Meng Wentong (蒙文通) compiled 《校理老子成玄英疏叙录》 based on the Dunhuang manuscripts and the Daoist Canon texts. The work interprets the Laozi through the "Chongxuan" (Twofold Mystery, 重玄) philosophy of Tang Dynasty Daoism, arguing that the Great Dao (道) is neither being nor non-being, and both being and non-being simultaneously—hence described as "huanghu" (vague/obscure). The text emphasizes that Dao is not separate from things ("道不离物" - Dao is not separate from things; "道外无物" - nothing exists outside Dao). It advocates for transcending both attachment to existence and attachment to non-existence ("有无双遣"), using the concept of "xuan" (玄, mystery) and "xuan zhi you xuan" (玄之又玄, mystery upon mystery) to progressively discard dualistic attachments. This "Chongxuan" doctrine had a significant influence on the development of Tang Dynasty Daoist philosophy. The page is categorized under Dunhuang documents and Tang Dynasty Daoist classics, and cites Hu Fuchen's 《中华道教大辞典》 (1995), p. 316, as a reference source.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"夫道无所不在，所在皆无，荡然无际，有何封域也？" (The Great Dao is everywhere present; where it is present, it is nothing; it is vast and boundless, so what boundaries does it have?), "道不离物，物不离道。道外无物，物外无道。用即道物，体即物道。" (Dao is not separate from things, things are not separate from Dao. There is nothing outside Dao, and no Dao outside things.), "为学之人执于有欲，为道之士又滞无为。虽复深浅不同，而二俱有患。今欲治此两执，故有再损之文。既而前损损有，后损损无，二偏双遣，以至于一中之无为。" (Those who study cling to desire; those who practice the Dao become attached to non-action. Though different in depth, both have afflictions. To cure these two attachments, there is the teaching of further diminishment.), "有滞之人唯滞于有，无滞之士又滞于无，故说一玄以遣双执。又恐学者滞于此玄，今说又玄，更怯后病。既而非但不滞，亦乃不滞于不滞，此则遣之又遣，故曰玄之又玄。" (Those attached cling to being; those unattached cling to non-being, so one mystery (xuan) is taught to dispel both attachments. Fearing students would cling to this mystery, the "further mystery" is taught—not only not clinging, but not clinging to non-clinging—this is the dispelling of dispelling, hence "mystery upon mystery.")
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.airitilibrary.com/Article/Detail/19914822-201106-201108300014-201108300014-179-192

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an academic journal article record from an Airiti Library database (a Chinese academic platform). The article is "成玄英《道德經義疏》重玄思想之探析" (Exploration and Analysis of Cheng Xuan-ying's Twofold Mystery Thoughts in Dao De Jing Yi Shu), written by 林文彬 (Wen-Ping Lin), published in 《興大中文學報》(Journal of the Chinese Department of National Chung Hsing University), Issue 29, June 2011, pages 179-192. DOI: https://doi.org/10.30091/JCDNCHU.201106.0007.

The article examines Cheng Xuan-ying (成玄英), an important representative of the School of Twofold Mystery (重玄學派) in the Early Tang Dynasty. The Dao De Jing Yi Shu is his foundational work, which uses the "Twofold Mystery" (重玄) concept to establish an ontological realm of unobstructed reason (虛通之理) and emphasize cultivation of the mind and nature through wisdom (智悟).

The paper identifies three academic contributions of the work: (1) Regarding Laozi studies, it links academia and religion while summarizing predecessors' theories; (2) In Chinese intellectual history, it represents a third period of Taoist thought development after Wei-Jin Xuanxue, serving as a fusion of Xuanxue (Neo-Taoism) and Buddhist Prajñā (Wisdom); (3) In terms of influence, it is the most philosophically significant school in Taoist history, influencing Song and Yuan dynasty Inner Alchemy (Neidan) and the Science of Mind-Nature, and likely enlightening Neo-Confucianism development.

The historical context notes that Sun Deng of the Eastern Jin Dynasty first annotated Laozi using the Twofold Mystery concept, and from the Southern and Northern Dynasties through the Sui and Tang Dynasties, many Taoists used it to comment on Laozi and Zhuangzi, forming the School of Twofold Mystery.

Keywords: 成玄英 (Cheng Xuan-ying); 重玄 (Twofold Mystery); 道德經 (Dao De Jing); 虛通之理 (unobstructed reason); 眾生之性 (nature of beings).

References cited include works by 牟宗三 (才性與玄理, 1980), 牟鐘鑒/張踐 (中國宗教通史, 2003), 任繼愈 (道藏提要, 1991; 中國道教史, 1990), and 袁保新 (老子哲學之詮釋與重建, 1991), all with Google Scholar links.
</summary>

The content is to discuss Metaphysics with Twofold Mystery and narrate the process of cultivation and realization of pure mind based on mind and nature.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: 成玄英《道德經開題序訣義疏》中的心性論述 - 國文學系 ---
URL: https://www.ch.ntnu.edu.tw/SIS/downloadfile.php?periodicalsPage=2&issue_id=13&paper_id=59

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic paper (published in *Studies in Sinology* / 《中國學術年刊》, Volume 36, Autumn issue, September 2014, pp. 19-42, ISSN 1021-7851) by Chiang Shu-chun (National Taiwan Normal University, Department of Chinese) examining the theory of mind-nature (心性論述, xinxing) in Cheng Xuan-ying's (成玄英) commentary on the Daodejing, titled 《道德經開題序訣義疏》 (Dao Der Jing Kai Ti Xu Jue Yi Shu).

CORE ARGUMENT: The paper analyzes the theoretical structure of Cheng Xuan-ying's discussions of mind (心), nature (性), emotions (情), and desire (欲) in his Daodejing commentary, and explores their deep relationship with Buddhist thought. In the early Tang dynasty, Buddhist mind-nature theory had matured, and Daoist Chongxuan (double mystery, 重玄) studies required development of mind-nature theory, leading Daoist commentators on the Laozi to focus on "mind" and "nature" topics while integrating Buddhist thought.

THREE OBSERVATIONAL APPROACHES (the paper's structure):
1. "Dao-Nature Continuity" (道、性一貫) as the ideological premise: Cheng holds that "Dao" and "nature" are one — the innate natural nature/true nature of all beings derives from the transcendent Dao. He explains "Dao" as "void and penetrating" (虛通), and states "所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也" (the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings). He uses "principle" (理) to characterize Dao, marking a major breakthrough in his Laozi scholarship. Dao's subtle principle, when internalized in humans and things, becomes their nature; hence to "preserve and return to true nature" is the path of self-cultivation.
2. "Forgetting Emotions to Complete Nature" (忘情全性) as the master thesis: In commenting on "道可道，非常道," Cheng details the relations among Dao, nature, emotions, form (形), qi (炁), and spirit (神). Since "性動為情" (nature stirring becomes emotion) and emotions contaminate, nature is damaged and distances from Dao. The key statement: "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性" (Dao gives me life, emotions destroy me; if one forgets emotions, nature is made complete). The dialectical process runs: Dao-Nature originally one → Dao-Nature separated (through stirring emotions, deluded mind chasing external objects) → Dao-Nature re-united through cultivation ("復性歸道" / returning nature to Dao as ultimate aim).
3. "Deluded Mind," "Emotional Contamination," and "Attachment to Objects" (妄心、情染、滯境) and the path of cultivation: Cheng identifies deluded mind, emotional contamination, and attachment to sensory objects as the root causes of losing true nature. His cultivation approach incorporates extensive Buddhist concepts — "empty" (空), "mind abiding nowhere" (無所住心), "three karmas clean" (三業清靜), "liberation of six sense faculties" (六根解脫), the bodhisattva ideal, "three poisons" (貪嗔痴), "dependent arising and emptiness" (緣起性空), etc. He reframes the Daoist sage as a bodhisattva-like figure; explains "returning to root/stillness/mandate" (歸根復命); and advocates for "復於真性，反於惠命" (returning to true nature and inherent mandate).

CONCLUSIONS (two observations):
1. The mind-nature discourse of early Tang Chongxuan studies may have independently influenced the mid-Tang Confucian revival (e.g., Li Ao's (李翱) 《復性書》/ "Essay on Restoring Nature," which also advocates "滅情復性" / extinguishing emotions to restore nature). The paper argues the theory of "restoring nature" (復性) was initiated by Cheng Xuan-ying well before Li Ao, challenging the view that Laozi mind-nature interpretation only fully developed in the Song dynasty.
2. The paper highlights the distinctive features of Cheng Xuan-ying's mind-nature discourse in the 《義疏》 and evaluates his value and status in the history of Laozi scholarship — characterizing the early Tang Chongxuan mind-nature theory as marked by Buddhist-Daoist mutual influence, whereas Song Confucian-Laozi interpretation turned toward Confucian-Daoist convergence.

KEY SCHOLARS CITED: Li Gang (李剛) argues Cheng's theory of restoring nature is richer than Li Ao's and scattered across his Laozi/Zhuangzi commentaries; Tang Yi-jie (湯一介) sees Chongxuan philosophy moving from ontology to mind-nature philosophy, similar to Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism (especially Cheng-Zhu), urging attention to the Chongxuan-Song Neo-Confucianism relationship; Dong En-lin divides Tang Laozi studies into three stages (early: Chongxuan with Buddhist coloring; middle: Tang Xuanzong's politicization; late: compilations by Qiang Siqi and Du Guangting). The paper used the Yan Ling-feng (嚴靈峯) edition of the reconstructed 《義疏》 as primary text.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也。" (卷二章一 Annotated in Cheng Xuan-ying's commentary on the first chapter — "the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings.") , "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性。" (From his commentary on "道可道，非常道" — the master thesis of "forgetting emotions to complete nature.") , "湯一介：『重玄學』以「理」釋「道」，又提出「道者，虛通之理，眾生之正性」……通過「窮理盡性」而實現與道合一。這與宋明理學（特別是程朱派）的路數極為相近。" , "李剛：『對重玄學來說，要體認重玄之道，其途徑就在於從心性入手，做到心空，不起妄心；性真，復歸真性。典型代表是成玄英。』" , "與李翱的復性論比較起來，成玄英具有自己的特色且內容更為豐富，只不過李翱的學說集中於〈復性書〉，而成玄英論復性則散見於他對老莊的解讀中。"
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides information about the Daoist text 《道德真经注》(Annotation on the Classic of the Way and Virtue) by Li Rong (李荣), a Daoist priest of the Tang Dynasty during the reign of Emperor Gaozong (唐高宗). The work comprises four volumes and is included in the Orthodox Daoist Canon (《正统道藏》) in the Dongshendi Yujue category. 

Key facts about the text:
- Title: 道德真经注 (Li Rong's annotation)
- Author: Li Rong (李荣)
- Length: Four volumes (四卷)
- Location in Daoist Canon: 洞神部玉诀类, 絲字号
- Editions: Hanfenlou edition volume 430, Xinwenfeng edition volume 23, Sanjia edition volume 14
- Daozang catalogue number: 717
- Included in the Zhonghua Daozang, volume 9

The surviving edition only contains annotations for chapters 1-36 of the Daodejing. The missing portions can be supplemented using Dunhuang manuscripts and cross-checked against Qiang Siqi's 《道德真经玄德纂疏》to reconstruct the complete version of Li Rong's commentary. The annotation is significant for its emphasis on the "Chongxuan" (Double Mystery/Twofold Profundity) doctrine, making it an important source for studying Tang Dynasty Daoist thought.

The reference source is: Hu Fuchen's 《中华道教大辞典》(Chinese Encyclopedia of Daoism, Beijing: China Social Sciences Press, 1995), page 316. The webpage is categorized under both "洞神部玉诀类" (Dongshen Section Jade Instructions category) and "唐代道教经典" (Tang Dynasty Daoist classics).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
道德真经注，唐高宗时道士李荣撰。四卷，收于《正统道藏》洞神部玉诀类。, 此本仅存第一至三十六章经注，其缺佚部分可据敦煌抄本补，复校以强思齐《道德真经玄德纂疏》，可得李荣注本完帙。, 其注主重玄说，是研究唐代道教思想的重要资料。, 胡孚琛主编：《中华道教大辞典》（北京：中国社会科学出版社，1995年），第316页。

--- SOURCE 8: [PDF] 李榮《道德經注》心性思想研究 - 國文學系- 國立臺灣師範大學 ---
URL: https://www.ch.ntnu.edu.tw/SIS/downloadfile.php?periodicalsPage=2&issue_id=12&paper_id=55

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article, "Study of mind thinking from Li Rong's (李榮) note for TaoDeJing (道德經注)" (published in Studies in Sinology, Vol. 37, Spring 2015, pp. 97-116, by Hsieh, Wan-hsin), examines the mind-nature theory (心性論) in Li Rong's commentary on the Tao Te Ching. Li Rong (號任真子) was a prominent early Tang dynasty Taoist of the Chongxuan (重玄, "Double Mystery") school, equally famous as Cheng Xuanying, and considered a representative figure of Chongxuan learning. The article argues that while Li Rong's academic importance parallels Cheng Xuanying's, he has not received commensurate scholarly attention.

The paper is organized into four main sections. First, on theory of nature (性論), Li Rong distinguishes two levels of nature: the "natural nature" (自然之性), which is innate, pure, self-sufficient, and perfectly complete (本乎自然, 樸，本也), and the "emotional nature" (情性), which derives from yin-yang qi and is subject to desires, deceptions, and sensory attractions. Li Rong advocates "以性制情" (controlling emotions with nature) and returning to one's original nature. His view of nature as the highest moral value aligns with the Cheng-Zhu school's "性即理" (nature is principle) approach.

Second, on theory of mind (心論), Li Rong attributes three functions to the mind: activity (活動義), cognition (認知義), and grasping/clinging (執取義). He calls the mind a "靈臺" (spirit tower) and "玄鏡" (mysterious mirror), which can illuminate and perceive the world, but once the mind stirs and clings to external phenomena, it covers the original nature. The mind can move toward either Dao-action (undirected) or non-Dao-action; cultivation work must therefore begin from the mind itself.

Third, on cultivation practices (心性修養工夫), Li Rong proposes three methods: (1) "制之未動，持心守心" (controlling before movement begins, guarding and keeping the mind), using the analogy of upper, middle, and lower scholars to describe levels of prevention; (2) "虛心復性" (emptying the mind and restoring nature), including "灰心" (ash-heart, extinguishing desires) and "混心" (mixing the mind, eliminating discriminations); and (3) "不滯兩邊，遣之又遣" (not adhering to either extreme, dispelling again and again), a double-dispelling Chongxuan method that transcends all dualities and even forgets the dispelling itself.

The conclusion highlights that Li Rong inherited and developed Cheng Xuanying's ideas—Cheng emphasized "復性" (restoring nature) while Li emphasized "修心" (cultivating the mind)—both predating Li Ao's famous "復性說" in the mid-Tang. Li Rong's philosophy notably shifted away from traditional Daoist immortality-seeking toward spiritual cultivation, even asserting that "心為死地" (the mind is the place of death), meaning that once the mind dies, even a living physical body is as good as a walking corpse. The article includes an abstract in English and extensive bibliographic references in Chinese and English on Chongxuan studies.

<summary>
This is a Chinese Taoist studies encyclopedia page about the "Daode Zhenjing Zhuan (道德真经传)" — a four-volume commentary on the Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) written by Lu Xisheng (陆希声), a Tang Dynasty scholar. The work is included in the Zheng Tong Dao Zang (正统道藏) canon under the Dong Shen Bu Yu Jue category (洞神部玉诀类), and appears at sutra number 680 in the Dao Zang Ti Yao index, located in volume 368 of the Hanfenlou edition, volume 20 of the Xinwenfeng edition, and volume 12 of the Sanjia edition. It is also included in volume 9 of the Zhonghua Daozang under the Four Supplementary Scriptures section.

The book begins with a self-authored preface (自序) in which Lu Xisheng critiques various earlier commentators on Laozi's teachings. He argues that Yang Zhu (杨朱) adhered to Laozi's substance but fell short by excessively valuing the body and despising material things; Zhuangzi (庄周) mastered Laozi's function but went too far by seeking to abandon sageliness and discard wisdom; Shen Buhai and Han Feizi (申韩) lost Laozi's reputation through harsh and punitive governance; and Wang Bi and He Yan (王何) lost Laozi's way by falling into empty nihilism and indolence. Lu considered Sima Qian (司马迁) to be the closest approximation of true Laozi philosophy among ancient writers.

Lu Xisheng further develops his core thesis by connecting Laozi with three sages: he claims Laozi shares the same origin (同原) as Fu Xi, who drew the Eight Trigrams, depicted all phenomena, explored the principles of life, and followed the harmony of virtue; that Laozi shares the overarching lineage (通其宗) with King Wen, who observed the I Ching's yin-yang movements, valued strength and change while emphasizing moderation; and that Laozi's views align in power/application (与其合其权) with Confucius, who emulated Yao and Shun, modeled the Zhou founders Wen and Wu, and guided the people through benevolence and righteousness. Lu concludes that Laozi "transformed and connected with, turned back and merged with" all three sages, making him "utterly divine" (至神). The entire work combines Confucian and Taoist thought to present a political philosophy, making it an important source for late Tang intellectual and ideological history.

The page cites Hu Fuchen's "Zhonghua Daojiao Da Cidian" (Chinese Taoist Encyclopedia, China Social Sciences Press, Beijing, 1995, p. 316) as a reference. The page is categorized under the Dong Shen Bu Yu Jue (洞神部玉诀类) and Tang Dynasty Taoist Classics (唐代道教经典).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Chinese Wikisource (zh.wikisource.org) presents the complete text of 《唐玄宗御註道德真經》(Tang Xuanzong's Imperial Commentary on the True Scripture of the Way and Virtue), an annotated edition of the Tao Te Ching (道德經) written by Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Li Longji (李隆基). The work is part of a series of Tao Te Ching commentaries catalogued on the page, which includes other notable commentaries such as Wang Bi's edition, the He-shang Gong chapter commentary, Song Huizong's royal commentary, Zhu Yuanzhang's commentary, and others.

The document is structured into four volumes (卷之一 through 卷之四) covering the Dao Jing (道經) and De Jing (德經) sections, containing all 81 chapters of the Tao Te Ching. Each chapter presents the original text followed by the Emperor's annotations in angle brackets (〈〉). Volume 1 (道經上) covers chapters 1-19, Volume 2 (道經下) covers chapters 20-37, Volume 3 (德經上) covers chapters 38-59, and Volume 4 (德經下) covers chapters 60-81.

The commentary provides philosophical interpretations grounded in Daoist concepts: the emperor explains key notions such as the Dao as formless and ineffable ("道者，虛極之妙用"), the harmony of yin-yang and qi (沖氣), the virtues of emptiness, stillness, and non-action (無為), and the importance of humility and yielding (守雌). The commentary frequently cites concepts from Zhuangzi and applies the teachings to governance, emphasizing that rulers should practice wu-wei (non-interference), rely on naturalness, avoid excessive warfare, and cultivate moral virtue to bring order to the state. For example, in Chapter 57 the emperor writes that "我無為而民自化，我無事而民自富，我好靜而民自正，我無欲而民自樸" (when I practice non-action the people transform themselves; when I am without affairs the people prosper; when I love stillness the people correct themselves; when I am without desire the people become simple). 

The work is attributed to the Tang dynasty, is classified under Emperor Li Longji, the Zhengtong Daozang, and the Tang dynasty, and is noted to be in the public domain since the author died over 100 years ago and the work was published before January 1, 1931.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
唐玄宗御註道德真經 is a Tang dynasty imperial commentary on the Tao Te Ching authored by Emperor Li Longji (唐玄宗/李隆基), included in the Zhengtong Daozang (正統道藏), "唐玄宗御註道德真經"

<summary>
This is a Chinese Wikipedia article about the 《经典释文》 (Jingdian Shiwen / "Classics Explained"), a comprehensive phonetic annotation work on Chinese classics written by the Sui-Tang dynasty Confucian scholar 陆德明 (Lu Deming). Key facts:

**Background and Purpose:**
- Completed in 583 CE (至德元年 of Southern Chen dynasty / 开皇三年 of Sui dynasty), making it a late 6th-century work, not a Tang dynasty work as sometimes thought
- Authored to address the problem that classical texts had "旧音太简" (old pronunciations were too simple) and divergent interpretations had arisen; Lu Deming compiled it based on collating texts and consulting the Cangjie pian and Erya
- Contains 30 volumes (卷), providing phonetic annotations (mainly using 反切 fanqie method) for both classical texts and their commentaries
- Used and cited over 230 scholars' analyses of sounds and meanings, citing 20 Han and Six Dynasties scholars for phonetic research including 徐邈, 李轨, 刘昌宗, 郭璞, 郭象, 韦昭, 向秀, 王元规, 崔撰, 吕忱, 沈重, 戚衮, 沈旋, 谢峤, 顾野王, 孙炎, 郑玄, 王肃, 何胤, 施干
- Since the Tang dynasty, it served alongside the 《十三经注疏》 (Thirteen Classics with Commentaries) as a basis for reading classics
- Still preserves quotations from many now-lost ancient books

**Linguistic Significance:**
- Scholar 高本汉 (Bernhard Karlgren) called the 《经典释文》 and the 《切韵》 (Qieyun, 601 CE) the two main bases for reconstructing Middle Chinese (中古汉语)
- It is a representative work of southern standard pronunciation slightly earlier than the Qieyun, notable for its numerous polysemous readings (异读)

**Content Structure (30 volumes):**
- Vol 1: Preface/General records (序录)
- Vol 2: Zhouyi phonetic annotations
- Vols 3-4: Shangshu (2 vols)
- Vols 5-7: Maoshi/Book of Songs (3 vols)
- Vols 8-9: Zhouli (2 vols)
- Vol 10: Yili
- Vols 11-14: Liji (4 vols)
- Vols 15-20: Chunqiu Zuozhuan (6 vols)
- Vol 21: Chungqiu Gongyang
- Vol 22: Chunqiu Guliang
- Vol 23: Xiaojing
- Vol 24: Lunyu
- Vol 25: Laozi
- Vols 26-28: Zhuangzi (3 vols)
- Vols 29-30: Erya (2 vols)

**Textual History/Editions:**
- The earliest copies were written in two colors: black for the classic text, red for the annotation; by late Tang this was simplified to single-color writing with red dots above the text, and later to monochrome entirely
- Earliest surviving version: Song dynasty carved edition with Song-Yuan repairs (宋刻宋元递修本), not reprinted during Yuan and Ming dynasties
- Qing Kangxi period: Xu Qianxue's Tongzhitang Jingjie edition, based on a manuscript copy by Ye Linzong of a Song edition (since destroyed) held in Qian Qianyi's Jiangyunlou collection
- Qing Qianlong period: Lu Wenchao's edition with 30-volume 《考证》 (Textual Research) inscribed in the Baowentang Congshu, collated against Ye Linzong's copy with broad use of various scholars' findings
- The Song-Yuan repaired edition was only photographically reprinted by Shanghai Ancient Books Publishing House in 1985
- Comparatively: the Tongzhitang edition is the poorest, the Baowentang edition better but not ideal due to collation issues; the Song edition is high quality in original leaves but its Yuan-dynasty repaired leaves contain many errors
- 2006: Zhonghua Book Company published Huang Zhuo's 《经典释文汇校》 (Collected Collations), based on the Tongzhitang edition, collating against all 30-volume carved editions, 30-volume manuscript copies, and the Yuan-Ming editions of the Thirteen Classics commentaries, incorporating Qing-era collation results; format shows Tongzhitang text on top and collation notes below
- Huang's work is considered the most reliable edition, extensively using Dunhuang manuscripts and fragmentary copies in collation, deemed "天下至慎" (the most cautious in the world) for not making hasty judgments

**References and External Links:**
- References Victor H. Mair's work in The Indiana Companion to Traditional Chinese Literature (1998)
- Links to various scholarly articles and the ctext.org project for different editions

SUMMARY:

This is an academic paper (published in *Studies in Sinology* / 《中國學術年刊》, Volume 36, Autumn issue, September 2014, pp. 19-42, ISSN 1021-7851) by Chiang Shu-chun (National Taiwan Normal University, Department of Chinese) examining the theory of mind-nature (心性論述, xinxing) in Cheng Xuan-ying's (成玄英) commentary on the Daodejing, titled 《道德經開題序訣義疏》 (Dao Der Jing Kai Ti Xu Jue Yi Shu).

CORE ARGUMENT: The paper analyzes the theoretical structure of Cheng Xuan-ying's discussions of mind (心), nature (性), emotions (情), and desire (欲) in his Daodejing commentary, and explores their deep relationship with Buddhist thought. In the early Tang dynasty, Buddhist mind-nature theory had matured, and Daoist Chongxuan (double mystery, 重玄) studies required development of mind-nature theory, leading Daoist commentators on the Laozi to focus on "mind" and "nature" topics while integrating Buddhist thought.

THREE OBSERVATIONAL APPROACHES (the paper's structure):
1. "Dao-Nature Continuity" (道、性一貫) as the ideological premise: Cheng holds that "Dao" and "nature" are one — the innate natural nature/true nature of all beings derives from the transcendent Dao. He explains "Dao" as "void and penetrating" (虛通), and states "所謂無極大道，是眾生之正性也" (the infinite great Dao is the true nature of all beings). He uses "principle" (理) to characterize Dao, marking a major breakthrough in his Laozi scholarship. Dao's subtle principle, when internalized in humans and things, becomes their nature; hence to "preserve and return to true nature" is the path of self-cultivation.
2. "Forgetting Emotions to Complete Nature" (忘情全性) as the master thesis: In commenting on "道可道，非常道," Cheng details the relations among Dao, nature, emotions, form (形), qi (炁), and spirit (神). Since "性動為情" (nature stirring becomes emotion) and emotions contaminate, nature is damaged and distances from Dao. The key statement: "生我者道，滅我者情，茍忘其情，則全乎性" (Dao gives me life, emotions destroy me; if one forgets emotions, nature is made complete). The dialectical process runs: Dao-Nature originally one → Dao-Nature separated (through stirring emotions, deluded mind chasing external objects) → Dao-Nature re-united through cultivation ("復性歸道" / returning nature to Dao as ultimate aim).
3. "Deluded Mind," "Emotional Contamination," and "Attachment to Objects" (妄心、情染、滯境) and the path of cultivation: Cheng identifies deluded mind, emotional contamination, and attachment to sensory objects as the root causes of losing true nature. His cultivation approach incorporates extensive Buddhist concepts — "empty" (空), "mind abiding nowhere" (無所住心), "three karmas clean" (三業清靜), "liberation of six sense faculties" (六根解脫), the bodhisattva ideal, "three poisons" (貪嗔痴), "dependent arising and emptiness" (緣起性空), etc. He reframes the Daoist sage as a bodhisattva-like figure; explains "returning to root/stillness/mandate" (歸根復命); and advocates for "復於真性，反於惠命" (returning to true nature and inherent mandate).

CONCLUSIONS (two observations):
1. The mind-nature discourse of early Tang Chongxuan studies may have independently influenced the mid-Tang Confucian revival (e.g., Li Ao's (李翱) 《復性書》/ "Essay on Restoring Nature," which also advocates "滅情復性" / extinguishing emotions to restore nature). The paper argues the theory of "restoring nature" (復性) was initiated by Cheng Xuan-ying well before Li Ao, challenging the view that Laozi mind-nature interpretation only fully developed in the Song dynasty.
2. The paper highlights the distinctive features of Cheng Xuan-ying's mind-nature discourse in the 《義疏》 and evaluates his value and status in the history of Laozi scholarship — characterizing the early Tang Chongxuan mind-nature theory as marked by Buddhist-Daoist mutual influence, whereas Song Confucian-Laozi interpretation turned toward Confucian-Daoist convergence.

KEY SCHOLARS CITED: Li Gang (李剛) argues Cheng's theory of restoring nature is richer than Li Ao's and scattered across his Laozi/Zhuangzi commentaries; Tang Yi-jie (湯一介) sees Chongxuan philosophy moving from ontology to mind-nature philosophy, similar to Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism (especially Cheng-Zhu), urging attention to the Chongxuan-Song Neo-Confucianism relationship; Dong En-lin divides Tang Laozi studies into three stages (early: Chongxuan with Buddhist coloring; middle: Tang Xuanzong's politicization; late: compilations by Qiang Siqi and Du Guangting). The paper used the Yan Ling-feng (嚴靈峯) edition of the reconstructed 《義疏》 as primary text.

This webpage is the full text of the "唐玄宗御注道德真经" (Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's Annotated Commentary on the Daodejing) hosted on Chinese Wikisource (zh.wikisource.org). The work is authored by Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Li Longji (李隆基), and is collected in the "正统道藏" (Zhengtong Daoist Canon). The page provides complete annotations for all 81 chapters of the Daodejing, organized into four volumes (卷): Volume 1 (道经上, Chapters 1-19), Volume 2 (道经下, Chapters 20-37), Volume 3 (德经上, Chapters 38-59), and Volume 4 (德经下, Chapters 60-81). The work begins with a preface (序) by Emperor Xuanzong.

The annotations provide the emperor's commentary on each chapter of the classic Taoist text, explaining key concepts in the imperial interpretation. Notable commentary themes include: the nature of Dao (道) as formless, nameless, and paradoxical; the value of non-action (无为) in governance; the importance of weakness over strength, and humility over pride; warnings against excessive desire, luxury, and warfare; the ideal of the sage-ruler who governs through moral integrity rather than force. The text emphasizes concepts such as 清静 (purity and stillness), 柔弱 (softness and weakness), 冲和 (harmony), and 玄德 (mysterious virtue).

The work is categorized under 李隆基 (Li Longji), 正统道藏 (Zhengtong Daoist Canon), and 唐朝 (Tang Dynasty). The page also includes a list of other Daodejing commentaries for reference, including those by Wang Bi, Heshang Gong, Emperor Huizong of Song, Zhu Yuanzhang, Zhang Daoling, and others. The work is in the public domain as an ancient text. The page also notes that Wikisource has reached 3 million articles.
</summary>

The article is "成玄英《道德經義疏》重玄思想之探析" (Exploration and Analysis of Cheng Xuan-ying's Twofold Mystery Thoughts in Dao De Jing Yi Shu), written by 林文彬 (Wen-Ping Lin), published in 《興大中文學報》(Journal of the Chinese Department of National Chung Hsing University), Issue 29, June 2011, pages 179-192. DOI: https://doi.org/10.30091/JCDNCHU.201106.0007.

The article examines Cheng Xuan-ying (成玄英), an important representative of the School of Twofold Mystery (重玄學派) in the Early Tang Dynasty. The Dao De Jing Yi Shu is his foundational work, which uses the "Twofold Mystery" (重玄) concept to establish an ontological realm of unobstructed reason (虛通之理) and emphasize cultivation of the mind and nature through wisdom (智悟).

The paper identifies three academic contributions of the work: (1) Regarding Laozi studies, it links academia and religion while summarizing predecessors' theories; (2) In Chinese intellectual history, it represents a third period of Taoist thought development after Wei-Jin Xuanxue, serving as a fusion of Xuanxue (Neo-Taoism) and Buddhist Prajñā (Wisdom); (3) In terms of influence, it is the most philosophically significant school in Taoist history, influencing Song and Yuan dynasty Inner Alchemy (Neidan) and the Science of Mind-Nature, and likely enlightening Neo-Confucianism development.

The historical context notes that Sun Deng of the Eastern Jin Dynasty first annotated Laozi using the Twofold Mystery concept, and from the Southern and Northern Dynasties through the Sui and Tang Dynasties, many Taoists used it to comment on Laozi and Zhuangzi, forming the School of Twofold Mystery.

Keywords: 成玄英 (Cheng Xuan-ying); 重玄 (Twofold Mystery); 道德經 (Dao De Jing); 虛通之理 (unobstructed reason); 眾生之性 (nature of beings).

The content is to discuss Metaphysics with Twofold Mystery and narrate the process of cultivation and realization of pure mind based on mind and nature.

Alongside the Shisanjing Zhushu (Thirteen Classics with Commentaries and Sub-commentaries), it served as a standard basis for reading the classics from the Tang dynasty onward. 《经典释文》是唐代陆德明（约550-630年，名元朗，字德明，以字行，苏州吴县人）所撰的一部30卷字典，是古人读经书时的必备工具书。它以考证古音为主，兼辨训义，引用了《周易》、《尚书》、《毛诗》、《周礼》、《仪礼》、《礼记》、《春秋左传》、《公羊传》、《榖梁传》、《孝经》、《论语》、《老子》、《庄子》、《尔雅》等十四部文献，保存了唐代当时较早的音训，为历代学人所推崇。

【著书背景】陆德明是隋季唐初著名的音韵学和训诂学家。他鉴于当时经典旧音太简、后人竞生穿凿的现象，在校理群书的基础上"精研六典，采纳九流，搜访异同，校之《苍》、《雅》"，著成《经典释文》30卷，于陈后主至德元年（公元583年）开始编纂。

【主要内容】全书首为《序录》，说明本书的内容安排和经学的传授源流。各卷分别为：《周易》一卷、《古文尚书》二卷、《毛诗》三卷、《周礼》二卷、《仪礼》一卷、《礼记》四卷、《春秋左氏传》六卷、《公羊传》一卷、《谷梁传》一卷、《孝经》一卷、《论语》一卷、《老子》一卷、《庄子》三卷、《尔雅》二卷。因唐代《孟子》尚不为经书，故未收入；而《老子》、《庄子》因魏晋以后玄学影响很大，故也收入。

【价值影响】陆德明以"典籍常用，会理合时"为基本原则统一注音，合原则者为正音，不合原则者则为参考。书中对所注之书均标明书名和章节，然后摘录字句注释音义，绝大多数都标明反切或直音。作者不仅为经典本文注音，还为注文注音，全书共收录汉魏六朝二百三十余家的各种音切和诸家训诂。因绝大多数音训原书都已失传，本书保存的资料弥足珍贵，后世治文字、音韵、训诂之学者均崇此书。
